Description of Greece.title: Description of Greece
Description of Greece.lead: Description of Greece is the only surviving work by the ancient geographer Pausanias (c. 110 – c. 180). The work comprises ten books, each dedicated to some part of mainland Greece. It describes Pausanias' own travels, and large parts of Greece are not covered, including the islands. His tour begins in Attica (Ἀττικά) and continues to Athens, including its suburbs or demes. The work continues to Corinthia (Κορινθιακά), Laconia (Λακωνικά), Messenia (Μεσσηνιακά), Elis (Ἠλιακά), Achaea (Ἀχαϊκά), Arcadia (Ἀρκαδικά), Boeotia (Βοιωτικά), Phocis (Φωκικά), and Ozolian Locris (Λοκρῶν Ὀζόλων). The work is erratic in its descriptions of topography. Its main interest is the cultural geography of ancient Greece. It focuses especially on religious sites and the historical and mythological underpinnings of the culture that created them.

history.heading: Reception
history.text: Description of Greece left only faint traces in the known Greek corpus. "It was not read", Habicht relates, "there is not a single quotation from it, not even a single mention of the author, not a whisper before the sixth century (Stephanus Byzantius), and only three or two references to it throughout the Middle Ages." Eighteen surviving manuscripts of Pausanias were known in the 1830s, copies from the fifteenth or sixteenth century, with three perhaps older than the rest. They are full of lacunae and errors, and all appear to depend on a single manuscript, now missing, that managed to be copied. Niccolò Niccoli, a collector of manuscripts from antiquity, had this archetype in Florence around 1418, brought into Italy from Greece by the bibliophile and traveller Cristoforo de' Buondelmonti.

secondary.heading: English translations
secondary.text: Translations into English begin rather late, with Thomas Taylor (London, 1794). A widely known version of the text was translated by William Henry Samuel Jones and is available through the Loeb Classical Library. The translation as Guide to Greece by Peter Levi is popular among English speakers, but is often thought to be a loose translation of the original text: Levi took liberties with his translation that restructured Description of Greece to function like a general guidebook to mainland Greece. Sir James George Frazer also published six volumes of translation and commentary of Description of Greece; his translation remains a credible work of scholarship to readers of Pausanias today.

Q1010778.label: Gitiadas
Q1010778.description: architect of the Chalkioikos at Sparta

Q102561.label: Sisyphus
Q102561.description: king of Ephyra in Greek mythology
Q102561.lead: In Greek mythology, Sisyphus or Sisyphos is the founder and king of Ephyra (now known as Corinth). He reveals Zeus's abduction of Aegina to the river god Asopus, thereby incurring Zeus's wrath.

Q10261.label: Pythagoras
Q10261.description: Greek philosopher and mathematician (c. 570 – c. 495 BC)
Q10261.lead: Pythagoras of Samos was an ancient Ionian Greek philosopher, polymath, and the eponymous founder of Pythagoreanism. His political and religious teachings were well known in Magna Graecia and influenced the philosophies of Plato, Aristotle, and, through them, Western philosophy.

Q10264223.label: Darius
Q10264223.description: Crown Prince of Achaemenid Persia (died 465 BC)
Q10264223.lead: Darius, was crown prince of the Persian Empire. He was the eldest son of the Persian king Xerxes I and his wife Amestris.

Q102884.label: Mnemosyne
Q102884.description: personification of memory in Greek mythology, mother of the nine muses
Q102884.lead: In Greek mythology, Mnemosyne was one of the Titans, who are the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She was the goddess of memory and the mother of the nine Muses by Zeus.

Q10291570.label: Gryllus
Q10291570.lead: Gryllus was the elder son of Xenophon. When the war, which broke out between Elis and Arcadia in 365 BC, on the subject of the Triphylian towns, had rendered a residence at Scillus no longer safe, Gryllus and his brother Diodorus were sent by Xenophon to Lepreum for security.

Q103107.label: Leto
Q103107.description: Greek mythological figure and mother of Apollo and Artemis
Q103107.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Leto is the mother of Apollo and Artemis. She is the daughter of the Titans Coeus and Phoebe, and the sister of Asteria.

Q10323051.label: Magnes
Q10323051.lead: In Greek mythology, Magnes was a son of Argos (son of Phrixus) and Perimele (daughter of Admetus). He lived in the region of Thessaly, in the land which men called after him Magnesia.

Q103975.label: Calliope
Q103975.lead: In Greek mythology, Calliope is the Muse who presides over eloquence and epic poetry, so called from the ecstatic harmony of her voice. Hesiod and Ovid called her the "Chief of all Muses".

Q104002.label: Urania
Q104002.description: Muse of astronomy and astrology in Greek mythology
Q104002.lead: Urania was, in Greek mythology, the muse of astronomy and astrology. In ancient art, her attributes include the globe and the pointer.

Q1045153.label: Cestrinus
Q1045153.description: son of Helenus in Greek mythology
Q1045153.lead: In Greek mythology, Cestrinus is the only son of Helenus and Andromache, two survivors from Troy following its fall and sacking. Cestrinus was born and raised in Epirus, where he also founded his own kingdom after Helenus' death.

Q1045730.label: Thersites
Q1045730.description: son of Agrius, Achean warrior in the Trojan War
Q1045730.lead: In Greek mythology, Thersites was a soldier of the Greek army during the Trojan War.

Q1047047.label: Lycus
Q1047047.description: Greek mythical character, brother of Nycteus and king of Thebes
Q1047047.lead: In Greek mythology, Lycus or Lykos was a ruler of the ancient city of Ancient Thebes (Boeotia). His rule was preceded by the regency of Nycteus and in turn, Lycus was succeeded by the twins Amphion and Zethus.

Q10490777.label: Eupheme
Q10490777.description: ancient Greek nymph, nurse of the Muses

Q1052888.label: Codrus
Q1052888.description: last of the semi-mythical Kings of Athens
Q1052888.lead: Codrus was the last of the semi-mythical Kings of Athens (r. ca 1089–1068 BC).

Q105290.label: Praxiteles
Q105290.lead: Praxiteles of Athens, the son of Cephisodotus the Elder, was the most renowned of the Attic sculptors of the 4th century BC. He was the first to sculpt the nude female form in a life-size statue. While no indubitably attributable sculpture by Praxiteles is extant, numerous copies of his works have survived; several authors, including Pliny the Elder, wrote of his works; and coins engraved with silhouettes of his various famous statuary types from the period still exist.

Q105720836.label: Pyrgo
Q105720836.description: first wife of Alcathous in Greek mythology
Q105720836.lead: In Greek mythology, Pyrgo was the first wife of the Pisatian prince Alcathous, son of King Pelops of Pisa and Hippodamia, daughter of Oenomaus. She may be the mother of some or all of Alcathous children: Ischepolis, Callipolis, Iphinoe and Periboea.

Q105772859.label: Pheno
Q105772859.description: mythical daughter of Clytius of Athens
Q105772859.lead: In Greek mythology, Pheno was the Athenian woman and daughter of Clytius. She married Lamedon, king of Sicyon, and bore him a daughter Zeuxippe.

Q10592638.label: Myrtoessa
Q10592638.lead: In Greek mythology, Myrtoessa was an Arcadian nymph. Along with other nymphs – Neda, Anthracia, Hagno and Anchirhoe – she was a nurse of the god Zeus.

Q105973241.label: Helisson
Q105973241.description: mythical son of Lycaon in Arcadia
Q105973241.lead: In Greek mythology, Helisson was an Arcadian prince as one of the 50 sons of the impious King Lycaon either by the naiad Cyllene, Nonacris or by unknown woman. He was the reputed eponymous founder of the Arcadian town of Helisson, as well as the river of the same name.

Q1061554.label: Polydorus
Q1061554.description: mythological Theban prince, son of Cadmus
Q1061554.lead: In Greek mythology, Polydorus or Polydoros was a king of Thebes.

Q10626527.label: Phanes
Q10626527.description: 6th century BC Greek mercenary and tactician
Q10626527.lead: Phanes of Halicarnassus was a wise council man, a tactician, and a mercenary from Halicarnassus, serving the Egyptian pharaoh Amasis II (570–526 BC). Most of what history recounts of Phanes is from the account of Herodotus in his grand historical text, the Histories.

Q106411249.label: Paroreus son of Tricolonus
Q106411249.description: mythical city founder in ancient Arcadia
Q106411249.lead: In Greek mythology, Paroreus was the youngest son of Tricolonus, son of the impious King Lycaon, and brother of Zoeteus. He was the reputed founder of the Arcadian town of Paroria.

Q106514537.label: Leis
Q106514537.lead: In Greek mythology, Leis was a princess as daughter of King Orus of Oraea (former name of Troezen). By the sea god Poseidon, she became the mother of Althepus who inherited the kingdom and renamed it after him, Althepia.

Q1065774.label: Lacedaemon
Q1065774.lead: Lacedaemon or Lacaedemon was the eponymous king of Lacedaemon (i.e. Sparta) in classical Greek mythology.

Q106779267.label: Androdamon
Q106779267.description: son of Phlias in Greek legend
Q106779267.lead: In Greek mythology, Androdamas was the Sicyonian son of Phlias and Chthonophyle, daughter of King Sicyon.

Q10696861.label: Thisbe
Q10696861.description: daughter of Termessus in Greek mythology
Q10696861.lead: In Greek mythology, Thisbe was a Boeotian nymph, from whom the town of Thisbe derived its name. She may be the naiad of the spring, well or fountain of that town.

Q107102250.label: Synallaxis
Q107102250.description: Greek mythological character, one of the Ionides nymphs whose spring waters were believed to cure diseases
Q107102250.lead: In Greek mythology, Synallaxis or Synallasis was one of the Ionides nymphs whose spring waters were believed to cure diseases. She was an Elean naiad-daughter of the river-god Cytherus and sister to Pegaea, Calliphaea and Iasis.

Q107102289.label: Iasis
Q107102289.description: Greek mythological character, one of the Ionides nymphs whose spring waters were believed to cure diseases
Q107102289.lead: In Greek mythology, Iasis was one of the Ionides nymphs whose spring waters were believed to cure diseases. She was an Elean naiad-daughter of the river-god Cytherus and sister to Synallasis, Pegaea and Calliphaea.

Q107189402.label: Pythios
Q107189402.description: epithet of Apollo connected with Delphi

Q1071946.label: Podalirius
Q1071946.lead: In Greek mythology, Podalirius or Podaleirius or Podaleirios was a son of Asclepius.

Q107240687.label: Phigalus
Q107240687.lead: In Greek mythology, Phigalus was an Arcadian prince as one of the 50 sons of the impious King Lycaon either by the naiad Cyllene, Nonacris or by unknown woman. Otherwise, he was called an autochthon.

Q107240697.label: Thocnus
Q107240697.lead: In Greek mythology, Thocnus was an Arcadian prince as one of the 50 sons of the impious King Lycaon either by the naiad Cyllene, Nonacris or by unknown woman. He was the reputed eponymous founder of the Arcadian city of Thocnia on a hill.

Q107240758.label: Thyraeus
Q107240758.lead: In Greek mythology, Thyraeus was an Arcadian prince, one of the 50 sons of the impious King Lycaon. His mother was either the naiad Cyllene, Nonacris or an unknown woman.

Q1072573.label: Niobe
Q1072573.lead: In Greek mythology, Niobe was a daughter of Phoroneus and Teledice, the sister of Apis, and the mother by Zeus of Argus, who was the eponym of Argos. She may have appeared in the lost genealogical epic Catalogue of Women, as part of the family tree of Inachids, one of the mythological royal dynasties of Argos.

Q107304147.label: Menestratus
Q107304147.lead: In Greek mythology, Menestratus is a Thespian man who dies trying to slay a dragon in an attempt to save his lover from the monster. His story is recounted in Description of Greece, a second-century work by Greek traveller and geographer Pausanias.

Q1074481.label: Chios
Q1074481.description: son of Poseidon, eponym of Chios island, water deity in Greek mythology
Q1074481.lead: In Greek mythology, Chios may refer to two possible eponyms of the island of Chios: Chios, one of the Oceanids as a daughter of the Titan Oceanus possibly by his sister-wife, Tethys. Chios, son of Poseidon and an unnamed Chian nymph.

Q108419.label: Rhea
Q108419.description: female Titan in Greek mythology, mother of Zeus and mother of Hera
Q108419.lead: In Greek mythology, Rhea, Rhia or Rheia was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She was the sister and wife of Cronus, and by him was the mother of Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon, and Zeus.

Q1085790.label: Phorbas
Q1085790.lead: In Greek mythology, Phorbas or Phorbaceus was the sixth king of Argos.

Q109220.label: Boreas
Q109220.description: Greek mythological personification and god of the North wind, storms,, winter, loneliness, solitude, absence, lack, sadness, depression, calmness and serenity
Q109220.lead: Boreas is the Greek god of the cold north wind, storms, and winter. Although he was normally taken as the north wind, the Roman writers Aulus Gellius and Pliny the Elder both took Boreas as a northeast wind, equivalent to the Roman god Aquilo or Septentrio.

Q110289833.label: Orus
Q110289833.description: king of Troezen in Greek mythology

Q1108130.label: Charis
Q1108130.lead: Charis, is a goddess in Greek mythology. She is a member of the Charites (Ancient Greek: Χάριτες) — or Gratiae (Graces) in Roman mythology — who are goddesses of charm, beauty, nature, creativity and fertility.

Q111288806.label: Mygdon
Q111288806.description: eponym of Mygdonia in Greek mythology

Q112001.label: Taygete
Q112001.description: one of the Pleiades in Greek mythology
Q112001.lead: In Classical Greek mythology, Taygete was a nymph, one of the Pleiades according to the Bibliotheca (3.10.1) and a companion of Artemis, in her archaic role as potnia theron, "Mistress of the animals", with its likely roots in prehistory. Mount Taygetos in Laconia, dedicated to the goddess, was her haunt.

Q1125040.label: Eriphyle
Q1125040.description: daughter of Talaus in Greek mythology
Q1125040.lead: Eriphyle was a figure in Greek mythology who, in exchange for the Necklace of Harmonia (also called the Necklace of Eriphyle) given to her by Polynices, persuaded her husband Amphiaraus to join the doomed expedition of the Seven against Thebes. She was then slain by her son Alcmaeon.

Q1125049.label: Eumolpus
Q1125049.description: Thracian king settled at Eleusis in Greek mythology
Q1125049.lead: In Greek Mythology, Eumolpus was a legendary king of Thrace. He was described as having come to Attica either as a bard, a warrior, or a priest of Demeter and Dionysus.

Q1128942.label: Parthenopeus
Q1128942.description: son of Melanion in Greek mythology
Q1128942.lead: In Greek mythology, Parthenopaeus or Parthenopaios was one of the Seven against Thebes, a native of Arcadia, described as young and outstandingly good-looking, but at the same time arrogant, ruthless and over-confident, although an unproblematic ally for the Argives.

Q11294144.label: Castor
Q11294144.description: Greek mythical figure, brother of Pollux

Q1129489.label: Orithyia
Q1129489.lead: In Greek mythology, Orithyia or Oreithyia was an Athenian princess who was raped by Boreas, the north wind, and gave birth to the twin Boreads, Zetes and Calaïs.

Q1129914.label: Libya
Q1129914.description: goddess in Roman and Greek mythology
Q1129914.lead: Libya, Libye, Lybie or Lybee was the daughter of Epaphus, King of Egypt, in both Greek and Roman mythology. She personified the land of Ancient Libya in North Africa, and was considered by the Greeks to be the origin of the name of what is now Libya.

Q1131643.label: Salmoneus
Q1131643.description: son of Aiolos in Greek mythology
Q1131643.lead: In Greek mythology, Salmoneus was 'the wicked' eponymous king and founder of Salmone in Pisatis.

Q1132071.label: Iasus
Q1132071.lead: In Greek mythology, Iasus or Iasius (Ἰάσιος) was a king of Argos.

Q1132777.label: Crotopus
Q1132777.description: king of Argos in Greek mythology
Q1132777.lead: Crotopus or Krotopos, in Greek mythology, was the eighth king of Argos.

Q1136130.label: Idas
Q1136130.description: son of Aphareus, husband of Marpessa, argonaut in Greek mythology
Q1136130.lead: In Greek mythology, Idas, was a Messenian prince. He was one of the Argonauts, a participant in the hunt for the Calydonian Boar, and contender with the gods.

Q1138506.label: Tereus
Q1138506.lead: In Greek mythology, Tereus was a Thracian king, the son of Ares and the naiad Bistonis. He was the brother of Dryas.

Q1139470.label: Procris
Q1139470.lead: In Greek mythology, Procris was an Athenian princess, the third daughter of Erechtheus, king of Athens and his wife, Praxithea. Homer mentions her in the Odyssey as one of the many dead spirits Odysseus saw in the Underworld.

Q1141300.label: Celeus
Q1141300.lead: Celeus or Keleos (pronounced /ke.le.ós/, keh-leh-OSS; ) was the king of Eleusis in Greek mythology, husband of Metaneira and father of several daughters, who are called Callidice, Demo, Cleisidice and Callithoe in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, and Diogeneia, Pammerope and Saesara by Pausanias.

Q114319165.label: Timagoras
Q114319165.lead: In Greek mythology, Timagoras is a foreigner living in Athens, who falls in love with a lovely Athenian boy, Meles. His love is nevertheless rejected by the youth, who depending on versions tasks him to accomplish a number of difficult requests only to turn him down anyway, or bids him to jump from a great height.

Q1145956.label: Phoenix
Q1145956.description: Greek mythological character, son of Agenor and Telephassa, eponym of Phoenicia
Q1145956.lead: In Greek mythology, Phoenix or Phoinix was the eponym of Phoenicia who together with his brothers were tasked to find their abducted sister Europa.

Q1154304.label: Nicostratus
Q1154304.description: son of Menelaus and Helen of Troy
Q1154304.lead: In Greek mythology, Nicostratus is a son of Menelaus, the king of Sparta. He was known to Hesiod and epic poet Cinaethon.

Q1154473.label: Theano
Q1154473.description: priestess of Athena in Troy in Greek mythology
Q1154473.lead: In Greek mythology, Theano was the wife of Antenor and a priestess of Athena at Troy during the Trojan War.

Q115449.label: Philomela
Q115449.description: legendary princess of Athens transformed into a swallow or nightingale
Q115449.lead: Philomela or Philomel is a minor figure in Greek mythology who is frequently invoked as a direct and figurative symbol in literary and artistic works in the Western canon.

Q1158901.label: Almus
Q1158901.description: figure in Greek mythology, son of Sisyphus
Q1158901.lead: In Greek mythology, Halmus or Almus, also Holmos (Ὅλμος), was a Corinthian prince who later founded the Boeotian town of Halmones or Holmones, in the neighborhood of Orchomenus.

Q1158902.label: Sangarius
Q1158902.description: Phrygian river-god of Greek mythology, son of Oceanus and Tethys
Q1158902.lead: Sangarius is a Phrygian river-god of Greek mythology. He is the divine personification of the river Sangarius which flows in Phrygia, a region in northwestern Asia Minor.

Q1164796.label: Procles
Q1164796.description: Procles son of Aristodemus, Spartan king
Q1164796.lead: In Greek legends, Procles was one of the Heracleidae, a great-great-great-grandson of Heracles, and a son of Aristodemus and Argia. His twin was Eurysthenes.

Q1166183.label: Trophonius
Q1166183.description: Greek mythological figure with an oracular cult at Lebadaea
Q1166183.lead: Trophonius was a Greek hero or daimon or god—it was never certain which one—with a rich mythological tradition and an oracular cult at Lebadea (Ancient Greek: Λεβάδεια) in Boeotia, Greece.

Q1167892.label: Doryssus
Q1167892.lead: Doryssus or Dorissus or Doriagus was a king of ancient Sparta, who reigned for 29 years. Pausanias identified him as the son of Labotas or Leobotes and the father of Agesilaus I. He was killed in battle between the Spartans and the Argives.

Q11704754.label: Triopas
Q11704754.description: Greek mythological character, king of Argos
Q11704754.lead: In Greek mythology, Triopas or Triops was the seventh king of Argos. Triopas may be an aspect of the Argive Zeus (sometimes represented with a third eye on his forehead), or may be his human representative.

Q1173681.label: Coön
Q1173681.description: son of Antenor in Greek mythology
Q1173681.lead: In Greek mythology, Coön, also known as Cynon (Κύνων), was the eldest son of Antenor and Theano.

Q1178583.label: Laodice
Q1178583.lead: In Greek mythology, Laodice was the daughter of Priam of Troy and Hecuba. She was described as the most beautiful of Priam's daughters.

Q1178970.label: Porthaon
Q1178970.description: son of Agenor in Greek mythology
Q1178970.lead: In Greek mythology, Porthaon, sometimes referred to as Parthaon or Portheus, was a king of Calydon and son of Agenor or Ares by Epicaste and thus brother of Demonice (also known as Demodice) and possibly Thestius.

Q1186159.label: Critius
Q1186159.lead: Kritios was an Athenian sculptor, probably a pupil of Antenor, working in the early 5th century BCE, whose manner is on the cusp of the Late Archaic and the Severe style of Early Classicism in Attica. He was the teacher of Myron.

Q118992.label: Menander
Q118992.lead: Menander (Ancient Greek: Μένανδρος, romanized: Ménandros; c. 342/341 – c.

Q11904059.label: Acarnanians
Q11904059.description: ancient ethnic group of west Greece

Q11905582.label: Androtion
Q11905582.description: Attidographer, often identified with the homonym orator
Q11905582.lead: Androtion was a historian of ancient Greece. He wrote an Atthis, that is, a work on the history of Attica, which was frequently referred to by ancient writers.

Q11906401.label: Arcadians
Q11906401.description: people of the ancient region of Peloponnese, Arcadia

Q11906538.label: Aristotimus
Q11906538.lead: Aristotimus was a tyrant of the ancient Greek city of Elis. He was installed by the Macedonian king Antigonus II Gonatas in 272 BC and ruled only a few months during which he committed many outrageous crimes, driving 800 citizens into exile.

Q11912529.label: Carmanor
Q11912529.lead: In Greek mythology, Carmanor or Karmanor was a Cretan priest who purified Apollo after he killed the Delphic dragon Python. He was the father of two children: Eubuleus and Chrysothemis, possibly by Demeter.

Q11917255.label: Dionysius
Q11917255.description: ancient Greek sculptor, son of Timarchides

Q11917689.label: Dorceus
Q11917689.description: son of Hippocoon in Greek mythology

Q11917781.label: Dryopes
Q11917781.lead: Dryopes or Dryopians were one of the aboriginal tribes of ancient Greece. According to Herodotus, their earliest abode is said to have been on Mount Oeta in Central Greece and its adjacent valleys, in the district called after them, Dryopis (Δρυοπίς).

Q11925399.label: Henioche
Q11925399.description: daughter of Creon in Greek mythology

Q11926250.label: Hyamus
Q11926250.description: son of Lycorus in Greek mythology
Q11926250.lead: In Greek mythology, Hyamus was a son of Lycorus. It was related of him that after the Great Deluge, he became king over a people dwelling around Mount Parnassus, and founded Hyampolis.

Q11936418.label: Melissa
Q11936418.description: wife of Periander in early Greek history

Q11939298.label: Olbiades
Q11939298.lead: Olbiades was an ancient Greek painter. One of his work was a paint portraying Calippus, the general of the Athenians during the Battle of Thermopylae (279 BC) against the Gauls.

Q11942481.label: Porus
Q11942481.description: Indian king in the age of Alexander the Great
Q11942481.lead: Porus or Poros was an ancient Indian king who ruled over a part of the Punjab region of northwestern South Asia. He is only mentioned in Greek sources.

Q11953845.label: Tellias
Q11953845.description: ancient seer and general of Elis

Q12029578.label: Cleodice
Q12029578.description: Greek mythical character, daughter of Lacedaemon

Q12046224.label: Pollux
Q12046224.description: Greek mythical figure, brother of Castor

Q1205276.label: Polydamas
Q1205276.description: Trojan hero, son of Panthoos in the Iliad
Q1205276.lead: In Greek mythology, Polydamas was a lieutenant and friend of Hector during the Trojan War.

Q12079024.label: Aristonymus
Q12079024.description: tyrant of Sicyon, father of Cleisthenes

Q121409927.label: Amyntas
Q121409927.description: son of Alexander I of Macedonia

Q12163200.label: Timalcus
Q12163200.description: son of Megareus of Onchestus in Greek mythology
Q12163200.lead: In Greek mythology, Timalcus was a Megarian prince as the son of Megareus, eponymous king of Megara.

Q121973.label: Eros
Q121973.description: Greek god of love and sex
Q121973.lead: Eros is the Greek god of love and sex. The Romans referred to him as Cupid or Amor.

Q122248.label: Heracles
Q122248.description: divine hero in Greek mythology, son of Zeus and Alcmene
Q122248.lead: Heracles, born Alcaeus (Ἀλκαῖος) or Alcides (Ἀλκείδης), was the greatest of the Greek heroes. He was considered the son of Zeus and Alcmene, and the foster son of Amphitryon.

Q12271661.label: Alcidamea
Q12271661.description: mythical partner of Hermes, and mother of Bunus
Q12271661.lead: In Greek mythology, Bounos or Bunus was the Corinthian son of Hermes and Alcidamea/Alcidamia.

Q1228764.label: Pamphos
Q1228764.description: ancient Greek author of hymns now lost
Q1228764.lead: Pamphos Ancient Greek Πάμφως (Pamphos) is an Athenian poet, allegedly a contemporary of Linus of Thrace, inventor of the ialémos. Two purported short fragments of his poems survive.

Q1230857.label: Silanion
Q1230857.lead: Silanion was the best-known of the Greek portrait-sculptors working during the fourth century BC. Pliny gives his floruit as the 113th Olympiad, that is, around 328–325 BCE (Natural History, 34.51), and records he had no famous teacher.

Q1231743.label: Procne
Q1231743.description: legendary princess of Athens, sister of Philomele
Q1231743.lead: Procne or Progne is a minor figure in Greek and Roman mythology. Traditionally she is an Athenian princess as the elder daughter of a king of Athens named Pandion.

Q1232483.label: Hegemone
Q1232483.description: one of the Graces, at Athens
Q1232483.lead: In ancient Greek religion, Hegemone was, according to the geographer Pausanias, the name of one of the two Charites worshipped at ancient Athens, the other being Auxo.

Q1233081.label: Pisander
Q1233081.lead: Peisander of Camirus in Rhodes, Ancient Greek epic poet, supposed to have flourished about 640 BC.

Q1233841.label: Polybotes
Q1233841.description: one of the Giants of Greek mythology
Q1233841.lead: In Greek mythology, Polybotes was one of the giants, the offspring of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky). He fought Poseidon during the Gigantomachy, the war between the giants and the gods.

Q1235379.label: Pasithea
Q1235379.description: one of the Charities in Greek mythology
Q1235379.lead: In Greek mythology, Pasithea, Pasithee or Pasitheia was one of the Charites and the wife of Hypnos. In the Dionysiaca, the epic poem of Nonnus (fifth century CE), she and the other Charites are the attendants of Aphrodite.

Q1240680.label: Pronomus of Thebes
Q1240680.description: ancient Greek musician and lyric poet

Q1241666.label: Lachares
Q1241666.lead: Lachares was a demagogue and tyrant of Athens at the turn from the 4th to the 3rd century BC.

Q1245211.label: Thallo
Q1245211.description: mythical character, one of the Horae

Q1246244.label: Pharis
Q1246244.description: son of Hermes in Greek mythology
Q1246244.lead: In Greek mythology, Pharis was the son of Hermes and the Danaid Phylodámeia (Φυλοδάμεια), and founder of Pharae in Messene.

Q1249335.label: Gelanor
Q1249335.description: mythical son of Sthenelas of Argos
Q1249335.lead: In Greek mythology, Pelasgus also known as Gelanor, was an Inachid king of Argos.

Q1251156.label: Dotadas
Q1251156.description: son of Isthmius in Greek mythology

Q1255043.label: Melanthus
Q1255043.description: son of Andropompus in Greek mythology
Q1255043.lead: In Greek mythology, Melanthus was a king of Athens and son of Andropompus and Henioche.

Q125731076.label: Olorus
Q125731076.description: father of Thucydides the Athenian historian

Q1258025.label: Aristomenes
Q1258025.description: leader of ancient Messene in war with Sparta
Q1258025.lead: Aristomenes was a king of Messenia, celebrated for his struggle with the Spartans in the Second Messenian War (685–668 BC), and his resistance to them on Mount Eira for 11 years. At length the mountain fell to the enemy, while he escaped and, according to legend, was snatched up by the gods; in fact he died at Rhodes.

Q1258032.label: Teleclus
Q1258032.lead: Teleclus or Teleklos was the 8th Agiad dynasty king of Sparta during the eighth century BC. He was the son of King Archelaus and grandson of King Agesilaus I. Pausanias reports that Teleclus' reign saw the conquest of Amyclae, Pharis and Geranthrae, towns of the Perioeci or "dwellers round about". Teleclus was killed during a skirmish with the Messanians during a festival at the temple of Artemis Limnatis, an event foreshadowing the First Messenian War.

Q1260484.label: Thalia
Q1260484.lead: In Greek mythology, Thalia or Thaleia was one of the three Charites, along with her sisters Aglaia and Euphrosyne. The Greek word thalia is an adjective applied to banquets, meaning rich, plentiful, luxuriant and abundant.

Q1266218.label: Zeuxidamus
Q1266218.lead: Zeuxidamus can refer to two ancient Spartans. A king of Sparta, and 10th of the Eurypontid dynasty.

Q1266225.label: Anaxidamus
Q1266225.lead: Anaxidamus was a king of Sparta, 11th of the Eurypontids. Anaxidamus was the son of Zeuxidamus and contemporary with Anaxander, and lived to the conclusion of the Messenian Wars, 668 BC (Paus.

Q1266363.label: Eurypon
Q1266363.lead: Eurypon, otherwise called Eurytion, son of Soos and grandson of Procles, was the third king of that house at Sparta, and thenceforward gave it the name of Eurypontidae. Plutarch talks of his having relaxed the kingly power, and played the demagogue; and Polyaenus relates a war with the Arcadians of Mantineia under his command.

Q1269165.label: Hipponous
Q1269165.description: mythical king of Olenus, father of Capaneus

Q1269430.label: Machanidas
Q1269430.lead: Machanidas was a tyrant of Lacedaemon near the end of the 3rd century BC. He was defeated and slain by Philopoemen.

Q1275070.label: Larissa
Q1275070.description: daughter or mother of Pelasgus in Greek mythology
Q1275070.lead: In Greek mythology, Larissa or Larisa (Ancient Greek: Λάρισα, Lárisa, pronounced [ˈlarisa] was the name of two different figures that appears in various accounts:

Q12752432.label: Ischepolis
Q12752432.description: mythical son of Alcathous of Megara

Q12755124.label: Melanion
Q12755124.lead: In Greek mythology, Melanion or Milanion (Ancient Greek: Μειλανίων, romanized: Meilaníōn) is an Arcadian prince who married Atalanta, the fearsome huntress who killed the Calydonian boar. In ancient sources Melanion is often conflated with Atalanta's husband Hippomenes, but is not entirely interchangeable with him, and the two likely originated from independent traditions.

Q12757032.label: Parnassus
Q12757032.description: son of Cleopompus in Greek mythology

Q1276974.label: Sardus
Q1276974.lead: Sardus, also Sid Addir and Sardus Pater ("Sardinian Father") was the eponymous mythological hero of the Nuragic Sardinians. Sardus appears in the writings of various classical authors, like Sallust, Solinus and Pausanias.

Q12777065.label: Syllis
Q12777065.description: nymph, mother of Zeuxippus with Apollo
Q12777065.lead: In Greek mythology, Syllis was a Sicyonian nymph who mothered Zeuxippus by Apollo. Her son succeeded Phaestus as the king of Sicyon when the latter migrated to Crete.

Q1280277.label: Echelaus
Q1280277.description: mythical son of Penthilus and king of Arcadia

Q1280328.label: Echestratus
Q1280328.lead: Echestratus was a King of ancient Sparta from about 900 to 870 BC. He was a son of king Agis I, and third of the Agiad line of Spartan kings. In his reign Sparta gained control of the district of Cynuria on the Argive border.

Q1280725.label: Echion
Q1280725.description: one of the Spartoi, father of Pentheus

Q128176.label: Agamemnon
Q128176.description: son of Atreus in Greek mythology
Q128176.lead: In Greek mythology, Agamemnon was a king of Mycenae who commanded the Achaeans during the Trojan War. He was the son (or grandson) of King Atreus and Queen Aerope, the brother of Menelaus, the husband of Clytemnestra, and the father of Iphigenia, Iphianassa, Electra, Laodike, Orestes and Chrysothemis.

Q12841832.label: Melanippe
Q12841832.description: wife of Itonus and mother of Boeotus

Q12872377.label: Amphiclus
Q12872377.lead: In Greek mythology, Amphiclus may refer to two different characters: Amphiclus, succeeded King Oenopion and his sons on the throne of Chios. He came from Histiaea in Euboea and went to the island of Chios because of an oracle from Delphi.

Q12872565.label: Iops
Q12872565.description: mythical local hero with shrine at Sparta

Q12873065.label: Azeus
Q12873065.description: son of Clymenus in Greek mythology
Q12873065.lead: In Greek mythology, Azeus, also Aezeius (Ancient Greek: Ἀζειός), was a Minyan prince as the youngest among the sons of King Clymenus of Orchomenus.

Q12873129.label: Atherion
Q12873129.description: son of Preugenes in Greek mythology

Q12877440.label: Eumelus
Q12877440.description: companion of Triptolemus, father of Antheias who tried to ride the chariot of Triptolemus but fell off and died

Q12878200.label: Isthmiades
Q12878200.description: mythical husband of Pelarge, involved in worship of the Cabiri

Q12878271.label: Iphinoe
Q12878271.description: daughter of Nisus of Megara in Greek mythology

Q12879099.label: Cleta
Q12879099.lead: In Greek mythology, Cleta was one of the Charites (Graces). The Lakedaemonians say that the Charites are the two who gave them the names of Cleta and Phaenna.

Q12879792.label: Cynus
Q12879792.description: mythical son of Opus in Greek mythology

Q12880867.label: Membliarus
Q12880867.description: mythical leader on Thera left by Cadmus

Q12881148.label: Molpia
Q12881148.description: daughter of Scedasus of Leuctra in Greek mythology

Q12882571.label: Pisus
Q12882571.description: legendary founder of Pisa in Greece

Q12883286.label: Patreus
Q12883286.description: mythical Greek king, founder of Patrae
Q12883286.lead: Patreus was the mythical founder of the city of Patras, Greece.

Q12884308.label: Samia
Q12884308.description: daughter of Maeandrus, wife of Ancaeus in Greek mythology
Q12884308.lead: Samia was the daughter of the river-god Maeander. She became the wife of Ancaeus, the son of Poseidon and Astypalaea, who ruled over Leleges.

Q12885689.label: Philanthus
Q12885689.description: Eleian athlete, murdered at Isthmia according to ancient legend

Q12885691.label: Philander
Q12885691.description: mythical son of Apollo by Acacallis
Q12885691.lead: In Greek mythology, Philander or Philandros was the son of the nymph Acacallis and Apollo, and the brother of Phylacides. Their mother mated with the god in the house of Carmanor in the city of Tarrha.

Q1289213.label: Thersander
Q1289213.lead: In Greek mythology, the name Thersander or Thersandros was one of the Epigoni, who attacked the city of Thebes. This is in retaliation for the deaths of their fathers, the war of the Seven against Thebes, who had attempted the same thing.

Q129165.label: Xerxes I
Q129165.lead: Xerxes I was a Persian ruler who reigned as the fourth King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire, reigning from 486 BC until his assassination in 465 BC. He was the son of Darius the Great and Atossa. In Western history, Xerxes is best known for his invasion of Greece in 480 BC, which ended in Persian defeat.

Q129168.label: Psamathe
Q129168.lead: In Greek mythology, Psamathe was the daughter of King Crotopus of Argos, who became the lover of the god Apollo.

Q1294873.label: Erginus
Q1294873.lead: In Greek mythology, Erginus was a king of Minyan Orchomenus in Boeotia.

Q129772.label: Xenophon
Q129772.description: Greek philosopher, historian, and soldier (c.430–355/354 BC)
Q129772.lead: Xenophon of Athens was a Greek military leader, philosopher, economist, and historian. At the age of 30, he was elected as one of the leaders of the retreating Greek mercenaries, the Ten Thousand, who had been part of Cyrus the Younger's attempt to seize control of the Achaemenid Empire.

Q129866.label: Minotaur
Q129866.description: creature of Greek mythology with the head and tail of a bull and the body of a man
Q129866.lead: In Greek mythology, the Minotaur, also known as Asterion or Asterius, is a mythical creature portrayed during classical antiquity with the head and tail of a bull and the body of a man or, as described by Roman poet Ovid, a being "part man and part bull". He dwelt at the center of the Labyrinth, which was an elaborate maze-like construction designed by the architect Daedalus and his son Icarus, upon command of King Minos of Crete.

Q1304531.label: Hippothoon
Q1304531.description: mythological Greek character, son of Poseidon and Alope, king of Eleusis
Q1304531.lead: Hippothoon or Hippothous is a figure in Greek mythology, often described as the king of Eleusis, succeeding to the throne after the death of Cercyon. He is the Attic hero and the eponym of the Athenian phyle called Hippothoontis (Ιπποθοωντίς).

Q130818.label: Atlas
Q130818.lead: In Greek mythology, Atlas is a Titan condemned to hold up the heavens or sky for eternity after the Titanomachy. Atlas also plays a role in the myths of two of the greatest Greek heroes: Heracles (Hercules in Roman mythology) and Perseus.

Q130832.label: Perseus
Q130832.description: legendary Greek hero and founder of Mycenae, demigod son of Zeus and Danae; famous for beheading the Gorgon Medusa
Q130832.lead: In Greek mythology, Perseus is the legendary founder of the Perseid dynasty. He was, alongside Cadmus and Bellerophon, the greatest Greek hero and slayer of monsters before the days of Heracles.

Q131090.label: Chaos
Q131090.lead: In the context of religious cosmogony, Chaos refers to the division of reality outside or in contrast to the ordered cosmos. As such it refers to a state, place, or time beyond the known, familiar, and reliable world, often said to be inhabited by strange, ominous, or demonic beings.

Q131125.label: Hebe
Q131125.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Hebe is the goddess of youth or of the prime of life. She was the cup-bearer for the gods of Mount Olympus, serving their nectar and ambrosia.

Q131157.label: Clytemnestra
Q131157.description: daughter of Tyndareus in Greek mythology
Q131157.lead: In Greek mythology, Clytemnestra is the wife of Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, and the half-sister of Helen of Troy. With Agamemnon, she is the mother of Iphigenia, Orestes, Electra, and Chrysothemis.

Q131169.label: Polybius
Q131169.lead: Polybius was an ancient Greek historian of the middle Hellenistic period. He is noted for his Histories, a universal history documenting the rise of Rome in the Mediterranean in the third and second centuries BC. It covers the period 264–146, recording in detail events in Italy, Iberia, Greece, Syria, Egypt, and Africa, and documents the Punic Wars and Macedonian Wars among many others.

Q131346.label: Pandora
Q131346.description: mythological figure, first human woman created by Hephaestus
Q131346.lead: In Greek mythology, Pandora was the first human woman, created by Hephaestus on the instructions of Zeus. As Hesiod related it, each deity cooperated by giving her unique gifts.

Q131351.label: Antigone
Q131351.description: mythical daughter of Oedipus and Jocasta
Q131351.lead: In Greek mythology, Antigone was a Theban princess and a character in several ancient Greek tragedies. She was the daughter of Oedipus, king of Thebes; her mother/grandmother was either Jocasta or, in another variation of the myth, Euryganeia.

Q131445.label: Jocasta
Q131445.lead: In Greek mythology, Jocasta, also rendered as Iocaste and Epicaste (Ἐπικάστη Epikástē), was Queen of Thebes through her marriages to Laius and her son, Oedipus. She is best known for her role in the myths surrounding Oedipus and her eventual suicide upon the discovery of his identity.

Q13156677.label: Butes
Q13156677.description: mythical hero in Athens, son of Pandion

Q131575.label: Hecate
Q131575.lead: Hecate is a goddess in ancient Greek religion and mythology. Variously associated with crossroads, night, light, magic, witchcraft, and the Moon, she is most often shown holding a pair of torches, a key, or snakes, or accompanied by dogs, and in later periods she is typically depicted as three-formed or triple-bodied.

Q131585.label: Selene
Q131585.description: ancient Greek goddess and personification of the Moon, daughter of Hyperion and Theia
Q131585.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Selene is the goddess and personification of the Moon. Also known as Mene (Ancient Greek: μήνη pronounced [mɛ̌ː.nɛː] MEH-neh), she is traditionally the daughter of the Titans Hyperion and Theia, and sister of the sun god Helios and the dawn goddess Eos.

Q131588.label: Ganymede
Q131588.description: son of Tros in Greek mythology
Q131588.lead: In Greek mythology, Ganymede ( GAN-im-eed) or Ganymedes is a divine hero whose homeland was Troy. Homer describes Ganymede as the most handsome of mortals and tells the story of how he was abducted by the gods to serve as Zeus's cup-bearer in Olympus.

Q131651.label: Electra
Q131651.lead: In Greek mythology Electra, also spelt Elektra, is a princess of Mycenae and the daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra. Famously, Electra and her brother, Orestes, attack and kill Clytemnestra to avenge their father's murder.

Q131694431.label: Lycomedes
Q131694431.description: son of Apollon and Parthenope in Greek mythology

Q1320718.label: Theseus
Q1320718.description: legendary king of Athens, son of Aegeus and Aethra; famous for slaying the Minotaur
Q1320718.lead: Theseus was a divine hero in Greek mythology, famous for slaying the Minotaur. The myths surrounding Theseus, his journeys, exploits, and friends, have provided material for storytelling throughout the ages.

Q132582.label: Pan
Q132582.description: Greek god of the mountain wilds, shepherds, flocks, rustic music, fertility, spring, and theatrical criticism, with the hindquarters, legs, and horns of a goat
Q132582.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Pan is the god of the wild, shepherds and flocks, rustic music and impromptus, and companion of the nymphs. He has the hindquarters, legs, and horns of a goat, in the same manner as a faun or satyr.

Q1328257.label: Elephenor
Q1328257.lead: In Greek mythology, Elephenor was the king of the Abantes of Euboea.

Q1328260.label: Eleusis
Q1328260.description: eponymous hero of the town of Eleusis
Q1328260.lead: In Greek mythology, Eleusis ( ih-LEW-siss) or Eleusinus was the eponymous hero of the town of Eleusis.

Q1328289.label: Eleuther
Q1328289.description: figure in Greek mythology, son of Apollo and Aethusa

Q133337.label: Solon
Q133337.lead: Solon was an archaic Athenian statesman, lawmaker, political philosopher (philosopher in an etymological sense), and poet. He was one of the Seven Sages of Greece and is credited with laying the foundations for Athenian democracy.

Q1336476.label: Penthilus
Q1336476.lead: Penthilus is the illegitimate or legitimate son of half-siblings Orestes and Erigone in Greek mythology.

Q133806866.label: Asopichus
Q133806866.lead: Asopichus was a male Greek name. Asopichus of Orchomenus, son of Cleodamus and winner of the boy's foot race at the Ancient Olympic Games of 488 BCE. Asopichus, or Asopius, father of the 5th-century BCE Athenian general Phormio.

Q134270.label: Helios
Q134270.description: Greek god and personification of the Sun
Q134270.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Helios is the god who personifies the Sun. His name is also Latinized as Helius, and he is often given the epithets Hyperion ("the one above") and Phaethon ("the shining").

Q1343776.label: Crethon
Q1343776.lead: In Greek mythology, Crethon was an Achaean warrior, from Pharae in Messenia, who participated in the Trojan War.

Q13446048.label: Sphettos
Q13446048.lead: Sphettus or Sphettos was one of the twelve cities of ancient Attica, and subsequently a deme. That it was situated either in the Mesogaea or the Paralia is certain from the legend, that Pallas, who had obtained these districts, marched upon Athens from Sphettus by the Sphettian Way.

Q1345963.label: Enyalius
Q1345963.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Enyalius is a war deity, either as an aspect of Ares or a separate god of combat. The identification of the two gods is early, as they are already interchangeable in the epic Iliad (eighth century BC).

Q1347121.label: Epimedes
Q1347121.description: one of the Dactyls (demi-gods from Mt. Ida in Crete)

Q134929.label: Pindar
Q134929.lead: Pindar was an Ancient Greek lyric poet from Thebes. Of the canonical nine lyric poets of ancient Greece, his work is the best preserved.

Q135224.label: Nausicaa
Q135224.description: daughter of Alcinous in Greek mythology
Q135224.lead: Nausicaa, also spelled Nausicaä or Nausikaa, is a character in Homer's Odyssey. She is the daughter of King Alcinous and Queen Arete of Phaeacia.

Q1352687.label: Eubuleus
Q1352687.description: son of Carmanor in Greek mythology
Q1352687.lead: In ancient Greek religion and myth, Eubuleus or Eubouleus is a god known primarily from devotional inscriptions for mystery religions. The name appears several times in the corpus of the so-called Orphic gold tablets spelled variously, with forms including Euboulos, Eubouleos and Eubolos.

Q1353815.label: Erigone
Q1353815.description: daughter of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra in Greek mythology
Q1353815.lead: In Greek mythology, Erigone is the daughter of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, rulers of Mycenae after the murder of King Agamemnon. Depending on version she was either married to her half-brother Orestes and bore him children, or Orestes tried to kill her when he claimed his throne, but the goddess Artemis saved her.

Q1362371.label: Pratinas
Q1362371.lead: Pratinas was one of the early tragic poets who flourished at Athens at the beginning of the fifth century BCE, and whose combined efforts were thought by critics to have brought the art to its perfection.

Q13635441.label: Mermerus
Q13635441.description: figure in Greek mythology, son of Jason
Q13635441.lead: In Greek mythology, Mermerus and Pheres (Ancient Greek: Φέρης, romanized: Phéres or Phérēs) were the sons of Jason and Medea. They were killed either by the Corinthians or by Medea, for reasons that vary depending on the rendition.

Q1364612.label: Peneus
Q1364612.lead: In Greek mythology, Peneus is a Thessalian river god, one of the three thousand Rivers, a child of Oceanus and Tethys.

Q1367860.label: Talthybius
Q1367860.lead: Talthybius was herald and friend to Agamemnon in the Trojan War. Talthybius is a Greek soldier who serves as both a messenger and a herald during the time of the Trojan War.

Q1370557.label: Tolmides
Q1370557.description: Athenian general during the First Peloponnesian War
Q1370557.lead: Tolmides,, son of Tolmaeus, was a leading Athenian general of the First Peloponnesian War. He rivalled Pericles and Myronides for the military leadership of Athens during the 450s and early 440s BC. In 455 BC, Tolmides was given command of a fleet and a force of 4,000 soldiers in order to sail round the coasts of the Peloponnesus attacking the Spartans and their allies.

Q1371026.label: Eteoclus
Q1371026.description: son of Iphis in Greek mythology
Q1371026.lead: In Greek mythology, Eteoclus was the son of Iphis.

Q1378335.label: Eurotas
Q1378335.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurotas was a king of Laconia.

Q1378407.label: Euryalus
Q1378407.description: son of Mecisteus in Greek Mythology

Q1378566.label: Eurysaces
Q1378566.description: son of Ajax the Great in Greek mythology
Q1378566.lead: Eurysaces in Greek mythology was the son of the Ajax and the enslaved former Teuthranian princess Tecmessa. He was venerated in Athens.

Q1378985.label: Eutychides
Q1378985.lead: Eutychides of Sicyon in Corinthia, Greek sculptor of the early part of the 3rd century BC, was a pupil of Lysippus. His most noted work was a statue of the Tyche of Antioch, a goddess who embodied the idea of the then newly founded city of Antioch.

Q138151.label: Chryse
Q138151.description: daughter of Almus in Greek mythology

Q1381908.label: Aloeus
Q1381908.description: mythical son of Helios and king of Sicyon

Q1387790.label: Micon
Q1387790.lead: Micon the Younger of Athens, simply Micon or Mikon was an ancient Greek painter and sculptor from the middle of the 5th century BC. He was closely associated with Polygnotus of Thasos, in conjunction with whom he adorned the Stoa poikile ("Painted Portico"), at Athens, with paintings of the Battle of Marathon and other battles. He also painted in the Anakeion at Athens.

Q1388093.label: Thyia
Q1388093.lead: In Greek mythology, Thyia was the daughter of Deucalion. Thyia bore to Zeus two sons, Magnes and Makednos, the latter of whom was considered the eponym of Macedonia.

Q1395752.label: Teuthras
Q1395752.lead: In Greek mythology, Teuthras was a king of Mysia, and mythological eponym of the town of Teuthrania.

Q1397559.label: Pagondas
Q1397559.lead: Pagondas, son of Aeolidas, was a Theban general and statesman, who is best known for his command of the Boeotian forces at the Battle of Delium (424 BC) during the Peloponnesian War. His modification of the standard hoplite phalanx and his use of reserve cavalry in that battle constitute what most historians agree is the first recorded use of formal military tactics in human history.

Q1405.label: Augustus
Q1405.description: first emperor of the Roman Empire and founder of the Julio-Claudian dynasty
Q1405.lead: Augustus, also known as Octavian (Latin: Octavianus), was the founder of the Roman Empire and the first Roman emperor from 27 BC until his death in AD 14. The reign of Augustus initiated an imperial cult and an era of imperial peace (the Pax Romana or Pax Augusta) when the Roman world was largely free of armed conflict.

Q1406849.label: Polemocrates
Q1406849.lead: In Greek mythology, Polemocrates was a physician, and son of Machaon and grandson of Asclepius, god of health. He had a sanctuary, at the village of Eua in Argolis and was honoured there as a god or hero of the healing art.

Q1408128.label: Alexanor
Q1408128.description: Greek mythical character, son of Machaon
Q1408128.lead: In Greek mythology, Alexanor a son of Machaon, and grandson of the Greek god Asclepius.

Q1409.label: Caligula
Q1409.lead: Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, also called Gaius or Caligula, was the third Roman emperor, ruling from AD 37 until his assassination in AD 41. He was the son of the Roman general Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder, Augustus's granddaughter, members of the first ruling family of the Roman Empire.

Q1411.label: Claudius
Q1411.lead: Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, or simply Claudius, was a Roman emperor, ruling from AD 41 until his death in AD 54. The fourth ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, Claudius was born to Drusus the Elder, the brother of Emperor Tiberius, and Antonia Minor at Lugdunum in Roman Gaul, where his father was stationed as a military legate.

Q1411680.label: Pleuron
Q1411680.lead: In Greek mythology, Pleuron was a son of Aetolus and Pronoe, daughter of Phorbus, and brother of Calydon. He was married to Xanthippe, daughter of Dorus, by whom he became the father of Agenor, Sterope, Stratonice, and Laophonte.

Q1413.label: Nero
Q1413.description: fifth and last Roman Emperor of Julio-Claudian dynasty (54–68)
Q1413.lead: Nero was Roman emperor from AD 54 until his suicide in AD 68, as the final emperor of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. Nero was born at Antium in AD 37, the son of Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Agrippina the Younger (great-granddaughter of the emperor Augustus).

Q1413020.label: Gordias
Q1413020.description: in Greek mythology, the king of Phrygia
Q1413020.lead: Gordias was the name of at least two members of the royal house of Phrygia. The best-known Gordias was reputedly the founder of the Phrygian capital city Gordium, the maker of the legendary Gordian Knot, and the father of the legendary King Midas who turned whatever he touched to gold.

Q1415180.label: Scylla
Q1415180.description: Greek mythological figure, daughter of Nisos
Q1415180.lead: In Greek mythology, Scylla was a princess of Megara as daughter of King Nisus.

Q1417968.label: Alcathous
Q1417968.lead: Alcathous or Alcathoos was in Greek mythology, a Pisatian prince who became a king of Megara.

Q1419.label: Vespasian
Q1419.description: ninth Roman Emperor and founder of the Flavian dynasty (69–79)
Q1419.lead: Vespasian was Roman emperor from 69 to 79. The last emperor to reign in the Year of the Four Emperors, he founded the Flavian dynasty, which ruled the empire for 27 years.

Q1419140.label: Opheltes
Q1419140.description: son of Lycurgus of Nemea in Greek mythology
Q1419140.lead: In Greek mythology, Opheltes, also called Archemorus (Αρχέμορος, Beginning of Doom), was a son of Lycurgus of Nemea. His mother is variously given as Eurydice, Nemea, or Amphithea.

Q1421201.label: Porphyrion
Q1421201.lead: In Greek mythology, Porphyrion was one of the Gigantes (Giants), who according to Hesiod, were the offspring of Gaia, born from the blood that fell when Uranus (Sky) was castrated by their son Cronus. In some other versions of the myth, the Gigantes were born of Gaia and Tartarus.

Q1425.label: Trajan
Q1425.lead: Trajan was a Roman emperor from AD 98 to 117, remembered as the second of the Five Good Emperors of the Nerva–Antonine dynasty. He was a philanthropic ruler and a successful soldier-emperor who presided over one of the greatest military expansions in Roman history, during which, by the time of his death, the Roman Empire reached its maximum territorial extent.

Q1427.label: Hadrian
Q1427.lead: Hadrian was Roman emperor from 117 to 138. His form of address as Roman emperor was Imperator Caesar Traianus Hadrianus Augustus.

Q1428276.label: Pandareus
Q1428276.description: son of Merops in Greek mythology
Q1428276.lead: In Greek mythology, Pandareus is the son of Merops and a nymph. His residence is usually given as either Ephesus or Miletus, though he is also associated with the island of Crete.

Q1431067.label: Polyxo
Q1431067.lead: In Greek mythology, Polyxo, also known as Philozoë (Ancient Greek: Φιλοζώη, romanized: Philozṓē, lit. 'animal-loving' or 'life-loving'), is the wife of the Trojan War hero Tlepolemus, and later the queen of Rhodes, an island in the southeastern Aegean sea. Following her husband's death during the war, Polyxo took revenge against Helen, whom she blamed for all the sorrows she had suffered.

Q1432941.label: Sosipolis
Q1432941.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Sosipolis was a native god at Elis. His mother was the childbirth-goddess Eileithyia, daughter of Zeus and Hera.

Q1433820.label: Labotas
Q1433820.lead: Labotas, also spelled Leobotas or Leobotes was the son of Echestratus and was the third king of Sparta from the Agiad dynasty. Labotas led a war against the Argives because the Kynouria occupied and supposedly lived in the surrounding areas that the Perioeci had inhabited.

Q143559.label: Lysander
Q143559.description: Spartan military and political leader (died 395 BC)
Q143559.lead: Lysander was a Spartan admiral and statesman who was one of the leading military and political figures of Sparta during the Peloponnesian War.

Q143880.label: Athamas
Q143880.description: son of Minyas or Aeolus in Greek mythology
Q143880.lead: In Greek mythology, Athamas was a Boeotian king.

Q1445864.label: Crisus
Q1445864.description: son of Phocus in Greek mythology
Q1445864.lead: In Greek mythology, Crisus or Crissus was a son of Phocus and twin brother of Panopeus. With Antiphateia, daughter of Naubolus, he became father of Strophius; thus he was the grandfather of Pylades.

Q1446575.label: Orsilochus
Q1446575.description: son of Alpheus in Greek mythology

Q14515330.label: Proserpina
Q14515330.lead: Proserpina or Proserpine ( PROSS-ər-pyne) is an ancient Roman goddess whose iconography, functions and myths are virtually identical to those of the Greek Persephone. Proserpina replaced or was combined with the ancient Roman fertility goddess Libera, whose principal cult was housed in a temple atop Rome's Aventine Hill, which she shared with the grain-goddess Ceres and the wine god Liber (Liber Pater).

Q1454839.label: Aglaophon
Q1454839.lead: Aglaophon was an ancient Greek painter, born on the island of Thasos. He was the father and instructor of Polygnotus.

Q1458587.label: Themisto
Q1458587.lead: In Greek mythology, Themisto was a Thessalian princess as the daughter of King Hypseus of Lapiths and the naiad Chlidanope. Her name is derived from the Ancient Greek word: "θεμιστος" which means "belonging to the law", or "belonging to the customs".

Q1462644.label: Learchus
Q1462644.description: son of Athamas in Greek mythology
Q1462644.lead: In Greek mythology, Learchus or Learches was the son of King Athamas and Ino, daughter of King Cadmus of Thebes. He was the brother of Melicertes.

Q1466343.label: Minyas
Q1466343.lead: In Greek mythology, Minyas was the founder of Orchomenus, Boeotia.

Q1466824.label: Cynortas
Q1466824.description: King of Sparta and son of Amyclas
Q1466824.lead: In Greek mythology, Cynortas or Cynortes (Ancient Greek: Κυνόρτης) or Cynortus was a king of Sparta.

Q14690266.label: Theronice
Q14690266.description: daughter of Dexamenus in Greek mythology
Q14690266.lead: In Greek mythology, Theronice was an Olenian princess as the daughter of King Dexamenus and the twin sister of Theraephone. These maidens were wed to the Molionides, Eurytus and Cteatus.

Q1469237.label: Sciron
Q1469237.lead: In Greek mythology, Sciron, also Sceiron, Skeirôn and Scyron, was one of the malefactors killed by Theseus on the way from Troezen to Athens. He was a famous Corinthian bandit who haunted the frontier between Attica and Megaris.

Q1469456.label: Metanira
Q1469456.lead: In Greek mythology, Metanira or Meganira was a queen of Eleusis as wife of King Celeus. She was the daughter of Amphictyon, the king of Athens.

Q14702439.label: Parthenope
Q14702439.description: daughter of Ancaeus in Greek mythology

Q148030.label: Triton
Q148030.description: Greek god, messenger of the sea
Q148030.lead: Triton is a Greek god of the sea, the son of Poseidon and Amphitrite. Triton lived with his parents in a golden palace on the bottom of the sea.

Q15078598.label: Eteonicus
Q15078598.description: Spartan admiral during the Peloponesian and Corinthian Wars
Q15078598.lead: Eteonicus was a Spartan commander during the Peloponesian and Corinthian Wars. He participated in many key engagements, held important commands and is mentioned multiple times by Thucydides, Xenophon and Diodorus Siculus.

Q150986.label: siren
Q150986.description: creatures half bird and half woman who lured sailors by the sweetness of her song
Q150986.lead: In Greek mythology, sirens are female humanlike beings with alluring voices; they appear in a scene in the Odyssey in which Odysseus saves his crew's lives. Roman poets place them on some small islands called Sirenum Scopuli.

Q15206125.label: Leontomenes
Q15206125.description: son of Tisamenus in Greek antiquity

Q152262.label: Pluto
Q152262.description: god in Roman religion, Plouton in Greek
Q152262.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Pluto was the ruler of the underworld. The earlier name for the god was Hades, which became more common as the name of the underworld itself.

Q1533115.label: Pausias
Q1533115.lead: Pausias was an ancient Greek painter of the first half of the 4th century BCE, of the school of Sicyon.

Q15360381.label: Astyoche
Q15360381.description: person from Greek mythology, daughter of Aktor

Q1536527.label: Aleus
Q1536527.description: in mythology, the king of Arcadia
Q1536527.lead: In Greek mythology, Aleus (or Aleos) was the king of Arcadia, eponym of Alea, and founder of the cult of Athena Alea. He was the grandson of Arcas.

Q1538212.label: Gorge
Q1538212.description: figure in Greek mythology (daughter of Oeneus and Althaea)

Q155063.label: Mardonius
Q155063.description: Achaemenid military commander during Greco-Persian Wars (died 479 BC)
Q155063.lead: Mardonius was a Persian military commander during the Greco-Persian Wars. Though he secured initial victories in the first Persian invasion of Greece, he was ultimately forced to retreat into Anatolia after suffering catastrophic losses in both men and material due to a storm off the coast of Mount Athos, following which he was relieved of his command by Darius the Great.

Q1550960.label: Macaria
Q1550960.description: daughter of Heracles in Greek mythology
Q1550960.lead: In Greek mythology, Macaria is a daughter of the divine hero Heracles. After his immolation, Eurystheus hunted down the descendants of the hero, eventually besieging them in Athens.

Q15543116.label: Aspledon
Q15543116.description: mythical son of Poseidon and Mideia

Q15543873.label: Tenerus
Q15543873.description: mythical Theban king, son of Apollo and Melia
Q15543873.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, the Theban hero Tenerus was the son and prophet of Apollo. His mother was Melia, a daughter of the Titan Oceanus.

Q1559958.label: Cocalus
Q1559958.lead: Cocalus is also a genus of jumping spiders. In Greek mythology, Cocalus is a king of Camicus (Ancient Greek: Καμικός, romanized: Kamikós) in the island of Sicily, according to Greek author Diodorus Siculus.

Q15623026.label: Dontas
Q15623026.description: ancient Lacedaemonian sculptor mentioned by Pausanias, likely a textual corruption

Q15820363.label: Ionidae
Q15820363.description: nymphs of a healing spring near ancient Olympia
Q15820363.lead: In Greek mythology, the Ionides were a sisterhood of water nymphs. Their individual names were Calliphaea, Synallasis (or Synallaxis), Pegaea and Iasis.

Q15838246.label: Onchestus
Q15838246.lead: In Greek mythology, Onchestos or Onchestus was the eponymous founder of the city of Onchestos in Boeotia, where the Onchestian Poseidon had a temple and a statue.

Q159168.label: Themis
Q159168.description: in ancient Greek mythology, a titaness, the personification of divine order, fairness, law, natural law, and custom, whose symbols are the scales of justice
Q159168.lead: In Greek mythology and religion, Themis is the goddess and personification of justice, divine order, law, and custom. She is one of the twelve Titan children of Gaia and Uranus, and the second wife of Zeus.

Q159666.label: Hector
Q159666.description: prince of Troy in Greek mythology
Q159666.lead: In Greek mythology, Hector was a Trojan prince, a hero, and the greatest warrior for Troy during the Trojan War. He is a major character in Homer's Iliad, where he leads the Trojans and their allies in the defense of Troy, killing countless Greek warriors.

Q1601964.label: Telchis
Q1601964.description: son of Europs in Greek mythology
Q1601964.lead: "Telchis" is also the singular form of "Telchines". In Greek mythology, Telchis may refer to two different or the same characters: Telchis or Telchin, the third king of Sicyon who reigned for 20 years.

Q1606756.label: Ancaeus
Q1606756.description: character from Greek mythology, son of Zeus or Poseidon
Q1606756.lead: In Greek mythology, Ancaeus was king of the island of Samos, and an Argonaut: helmsmanship was his special skill.

Q160730.label: Medusa
Q160730.description: in Greek mythology, one of the three Gorgons, described as a woman with snakes in place of hair, beheaded by Perseus
Q160730.lead: In Greek mythology, Medusa, also called Gorgo (Ancient Greek: Γοργώ) or the Gorgon, was one of the three Gorgons. Medusa is generally described as a woman with living snakes in place of hair; her appearance was so hideous that anyone who looked upon her was turned to stone.

Q1613558.label: Hermesianax
Q1613558.lead: Hermesianax of Colophon was an Ancient Greek elegiac poet of the Hellenistic period, said to be a pupil of Philitas of Cos; the dates of his life and work are all but lost, but Philitas is supposed to have been born c. 340 BC. His chief work was a poem in three books, dedicated to his mistress Leontion.

Q161419.label: Oceanus
Q161419.description: ancient Greek god of the earth-encircling river, Oceanos
Q161419.lead: In Greek mythology, Oceanus or Okeanos was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth), and the god of the great river which encircled the entire world. He was the brother and husband of the Titaness Tethys, and by her was the father of the river gods and the Oceanids.

Q16157161.label: Spartans
Q16157161.description: people from or residents of Sparta, Greece

Q161936.label: Death
Q161936.lead: Personifications of death are found in many religions and mythologies. In more modern stories, a character known as the Grim Reaper (usually depicted as a berobed skeleton wielding a scythe) causes the victim's death by coming to collect that person's soul.

Q162163.label: Ion of Chios
Q162163.description: 5th-century BC Greek poet, dramatist and philosopher
Q162163.lead: Ion of Chios (Ancient Greek: Ἴων ὁ Χῖος; c. 490/480 – c.

Q1627764.label: Arne
Q1627764.lead: In Greek mythology, Melanippe, also known as Arne or Antiopa, was the daughter of Aeolus and the precedent Melanippe (or else daughter of Hippotes or of Desmontes). She was the mother by Poseidon, of the twins Aeolus (Hellen) and Boeotus.

Q162797.label: Pegasus
Q162797.lead: Pegasus is a winged horse in Greek mythology, usually depicted as a white stallion. He was sired by Poseidon, in his role as horse-god, and foaled by Medusa, one of three Gorgon sisters.

Q1632703.label: Mantius
Q1632703.description: son of Melampus in Greek mythology
Q1632703.lead: Mantius is also a genus of jumping spiders. In Greek mythology, Mantius was the son of Melampus and Iphianassa and the father of Cleitus, Polypheides and, in some versions, of Oicles.

Q16329997.label: Castalius
Q16329997.description: son of Delphus in Greek mythology

Q16331985.label: Meles
Q16331985.description: cruel Athenian lover in Greek mythology

Q16332133.label: Euamerion
Q16332133.description: deity worshiped at Titane in Greece

Q16332222.label: Phylacides
Q16332222.lead: In Greek mythology, Phylacides or Phylakides was the son of the nymph Acacallis and Apollo, and the brother of Philander. Their mother mated with the god in the house of Carmanor in the city of Tarrha.

Q16332252.label: Physcoa
Q16332252.description: mythical lover of Dionysos and mother of Narcaeus
Q16332252.lead: In Greek mythology, Physcoa was a woman from the deme Orthia of Elis. She was credited with a variety of notable deeds, which are recorded in Pausanias' Description of Greece.

Q1636827.label: Pelasgus
Q1636827.description: ancestor of the Arcadians in Greek mythology

Q1638952.label: Marathon
Q1638952.description: mythical son of Epopeus of Sicyon
Q1638952.lead: In Greek mythology, Marathon, also Marathos or Marathus (Μάραθος), may refer to the same or four distinct characters who gave his name to Marathon, a town in Attica. Marathus, the 14th king of Sicyon who reigned for 20 or 30 years.

Q163920.label: Adonis
Q163920.description: Greek god of beauty and desire
Q163920.lead: In Greek mythology, Adonis was the mortal lover of the goddesses Aphrodite and Persephone. He was considered to be the ideal of male beauty in classical antiquity.

Q164061.label: Helen of Troy
Q164061.description: daughter of Zeus in Greek mythology
Q164061.lead: Helen, commonly known as Helen of Troy and sometimes as Helen of Sparta, is a figure in Greek mythology said to have been the most beautiful woman in the world. She was believed to have been the daughter of Zeus by Leda or Nemesis, and the sister of Clytemnestra, Castor, Pollux, Philonoe, Phoebe and Timandra.

Q16515491.label: Amphidamas
Q16515491.description: Greek mythical character, Argonaut, son of Aleus

Q165170.label: Europa
Q165170.description: Phoenician character in Greek mythology, daughter of Agenor
Q165170.lead: In Greek mythology, Europa was a Phoenician princess said to have been abducted by Zeus in the form of a bull. She was the mother of the Cretan king Minos.

Q16528339.label: Arimnestos
Q16528339.description: commander of the Plataean contingent at the battles of Marathon and Plataea during the Greco-Persian Wars
Q16528339.lead: Arimnestos was the commander of the Plataean contingent at the battles of Marathon and Plataea during the Greco-Persian Wars.

Q1654068.label: Oncius
Q1654068.lead: In Greek mythology, Oncius or Oncus (Ancient Greek: Ὄγκος, romanized: Ónkos, lit. 'point of an arrow') was a son of Apollo and a ruler over Ónkeion (Ὄγκειον), a region of Arcadia adjacent to Thelpusa, as well as eponym of a city Oncae. He owned a herd of horses, in which Demeter tried to hide from Poseidon's advances, changing herself into a mare.

Q1655397.label: Ialmenus
Q1655397.lead: In Greek mythology, Ialmenus or Ialmenos was a son of Ares and Astyoche, and twin brother of Ascalaphus. Together with his brother he sailed with the Argonauts, among the suitors of Helen, and led the Orchomenian contingent in the Trojan War.

Q1655431.label: Iamus
Q1655431.description: son of Evadne in Greek mythology, ancestor of the Iamidae
Q1655431.lead: In Greek mythology, Iamus was the son of Apollo and Evadne, a daughter of Poseidon, raised by Aepytus. In a story told by Pindar, after his mother lies with Apollo and the child is born, he is left in the wilderness.

Q16555097.label: Phayllus
Q16555097.lead: In ancient Greek legend and folklore, Phayllus is a man from Oetaea who stole the cursed necklace of Harmonia from the temple of Athena to gift his mistress. The necklace then brought immense suffering to the woman, its last known owner, and her family.

Q1655690.label: Ianiscus
Q1655690.description: King of Sicyon in Greek mythology

Q16566384.label: Cercyon
Q16566384.description: son of Agamedes in Greek mythology

Q1657298.label: Lelex
Q1657298.lead: In Greek mythology, Lelex was a king of Megara and regarded as the ancestor of the Leleges.

Q165769.label: Penelope
Q165769.description: wife of Odysseus in Greek mythology
Q165769.lead: Penelope is the legendary wife of Odysseus and queen of Ithaca in Homer's Odyssey. She is the daughter of Spartan king Icarius, and the mother of Telemachus.

Q1659401.label: Olympiodorus of Athens
Q1659401.lead: Olympiodoros was a military leader (General) in Athens in ancient Greece. His capacity as a savior of Athens and his self-confident power and serious engagement during political crises were emphasized.

Q16607057.label: Midea
Q16607057.description: nymph, mother of Aspledon by Poseidon

Q1675360.label: Itys
Q1675360.lead: In Greek mythology, Itys is a minor mythological Thracian character, the son of Tereus, a king of Thrace, by his Athenian wife Procne. Itys was murdered by his own mother and aunt and served to be consumed during dinner by his father, as part of a revenge plan against Tereus for assaulting and raping the maiden Philomela, Procne's sister.

Q167646.label: Paris
Q167646.description: mythological son of Priam, king of Troy
Q167646.lead: Paris, also known as Alexander (Ancient Greek: Ἀλέξανδρος, romanized: Aléxandros), is a figure from Greek mythology who appears in the numerous stories about the Trojan War, including the Iliad. He was prince of Troy, son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba, and younger brother of Prince Hector.

Q16821458.label: Anaxias
Q16821458.description: Greek mythical character, son of Castor an Hilaeira
Q16821458.lead: Anaxias or Anaxis (Ἄναξις means 'bringing up, raising up') was in Greek and Roman mythology a son of Castor and Hilaeira, and cousin of Mnasinus, with whom he is usually mentioned. The temple of the Dioscuri at Argos contained also the statues of these two sons of the Dioscuri, and on the throne of Amyclae both were represented riding on horseback.

Q16845943.label: Hydna
Q16845943.lead: Hydna of Scione (alternately called Hydne or Cyana) (Ancient Greek: Ὕδνα; fl.

Q16879570.label: Sesostris
Q16879570.description: king of ancient Egypt, per Herodotus
Q16879570.lead: Sesostris is the name of a king of ancient Egypt who, according to Herodotus, led a military expedition across Asia into parts of Europe. Tales of Sesostris are probably based on the life of Senusret I, Senusret III and perhaps other Pharaohs such as Shoshenq I and Ramesses II. Sesostris's name is also given as Sesoösis or Sesonchosis in other sources.

Q16931911.label: Pandion
Q16931911.description: eponymous hero of the Attic tribe Pandionis
Q16931911.lead: Pandion was the eponymous hero of the Attic tribe Pandionis, which was created as part of the tribal reforms of Cleisthenes at the end of the sixth century BC. He is usually assumed to be one of the two legendary kings of Athens, Pandion I or Pandion II.

Q170053.label: Castalia
Q170053.lead: Castalia, in ancient Greek and Roman mythology, is a young nymph, a daughter of the river-god Achelous, who attracted the god Apollo and who is said to have flung herself into the sacred spring in Delphi when pursued by him. The spring took the name Castalia afterwards.

Q1702894.label: Thelpusa
Q1702894.description: nymph, daughter of Ladon in Greek mythology

Q170379.label: Hydra
Q170379.description: ancient serpent-like chthonic water monster, with reptilian traits, that possessed many heads, in Greek mythology
Q170379.lead: The Lernaean Hydra or Hydra of Lerna, more often known simply as the Hydra, is a serpentine lake monster in Greek mythology and Roman mythology. Its lair was the lake of Lerna in the Argolid, which was also the site of the myth of the Danaïdes.

Q170473.label: Priam
Q170473.description: the legendary and last king of Troy during the Trojan war; son of Laomedon
Q170473.lead: In Greek mythology, Priam was the legendary and last king of Troy during the Trojan War. He was the son of Laomedon.

Q1705660.label: Heleus
Q1705660.description: son of Perseus in Greek mythology
Q1705660.lead: In Greek mythology, Heleus or Heleius, also Helios (Ἕλιος), was a Mycenaean prince.

Q170779.label: Cassandra
Q170779.description: mythological prophetess and princess of Troy
Q170779.lead: In Greek mythology, Cassandra, also spelled Kassandra or Casandra, was a Trojan priestess dedicated to the god Apollo and fated by him to utter true prophecies, but never to be believed. Cassandra lived through the Trojan War and survived the sack of the city, but was murdered by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus when Agamemnon brought her to Mycenae as a pallake.

Q17115359.label: Crison of Himera
Q17115359.description: ancient Greek olympics winner in 5th century B.C.

Q171303.label: Zeno of Citium
Q171303.lead: Zeno of Citium (Koine Greek: Ζήνων ὁ Κιτιεύς, Zēnōn ho Kitieus; c. 334 – c.

Q171839.label: Menelaus
Q171839.description: mythical king of Sparta, husband of Helen of Troy
Q171839.lead: In Greek mythology, Menelaus was a king of Sparta. According to the Iliad, the Trojan War began as a result of Menelaus' wife, Helen, fleeing to Troy with the Trojan prince Paris.

Q171876.label: Antinous
Q171876.lead: Antinous, also called Antinoös, (Ancient Greek: Ἀντίνοος; c. 111 – c.

Q1722503.label: Callirhoe
Q1722503.description: daughter of Achelous in Greek mythology
Q1722503.lead: In Greek mythology, Callirhoe was the daughter of the river god Achelous. She was betrothed of Alcmaeon, son of Amphiaraus of Argos, and mothered by him two sons, Amphoterus and Acarnan.

Q1722514.label: Callon of Aegina
Q1722514.description: Greek sculptor from Aegina, active ca. 500-450 BCE

Q1723235.label: Nicomachus
Q1723235.description: son of Machaon in Greek mythology

Q1723440.label: Canachus
Q1723440.lead: Canachus was a sculptor of Sicyon in Corinthia, in the latter part of the 6th century BCE. He was especially noted as the author of two great statues of Apollo, one in bronze made for the temple at Didyma near Miletus, and one in cedar wood made for Thebes. The coins of Miletus furnish us with copies of the former and show the god to have held a stag in one hand and a bow in the other.

Q172725.label: Ajax the Great
Q172725.description: son of Telamon in Greek mythology
Q172725.lead: Ajax or Aias is a Greek mythological hero, the son of King Telamon and Periboea, and the half-brother of Teucer.

Q17282472.label: Schedius
Q17282472.description: son of Iphitos and ruler of Phocis

Q1734053.label: Carme
Q1734053.lead: In Greek mythology, Carme was the mother of the Cretan goddess Britomartis by Zeus.

Q1738025.label: Cisus
Q1738025.description: king of Argos in Greek mythology
Q1738025.lead: In Greek mythology, Cisus, (or Ceisus), son of Temenus, was a king of Argos. Temenus had initially left his kingdom to his son in law, Deiphontes, despite having natural sons of his own.

Q174278.label: Medea
Q174278.description: daughter of King Aeëtes of Colchis in Greek mythology
Q174278.lead: In ancient Greek mythology, Medea is the daughter of King Aeëtes of Colchis. Medea is known in most stories as a sorceress, an accomplished pharmakís, a worker in pharmakeía (medicinal magic), and is often depicted as a high priestess of the goddess Hecate.

Q174353.label: Orpheus
Q174353.description: legendary musician, poet, and prophet in ancient Greek religion and myth
Q174353.lead: In Greek mythology, Orpheus was a Thracian bard, legendary musician and prophet. He was also a renowned poet and, according to legend, travelled with Jason and the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece, and descended into the underworld to recover his lost wife, Eurydice.

Q174532.label: Hegias of Athens
Q174532.lead: Hegias or Hegesias of Athens was a famous sculptor of Athens, a member of the Late Archaic school of the generation before Pheidias. No surviving work can be securely identified as his, though Pliny mentions a Pyrrhus Supported by Pallas Athena.

Q17454800.label: Orsobia
Q17454800.description: daughter of Deiphontes in Greek mythology

Q17461398.label: Daulis
Q17461398.lead: In Greek mythology, Daulis and at a later stage Daulia (Ancient Greek: Δαυλία) and Daulion (Ancient Greek: Δαύλιον) was the name of a mythological figure and Davleia, the city in Phocis, is named after her. Daulis was the hometown of Tereus, Thracian king and also the city at the end of the road not taken by Oedipus.

Q17516372.label: Argeus
Q17516372.description: mythological Greek character, son of Deiphontes

Q17542231.label: Antimenes
Q17542231.description: son of Deiphontes in Greek mythology

Q176022.label: Charilaus
Q176022.lead: Charilaus, also spelled Charilaos, Charillos, or Charillus, was a king of Sparta in the middle of the 8th century BC. He was probably the first historical king of the Eurypontid dynasty.

Q176758.label: Jason
Q176758.description: Greek mythological hero, son of Aeson
Q176758.lead: Jason was an ancient Greek mythological hero and leader of the Argonauts, whose quest for the Golden Fleece is featured in Greek literature. He was the son of Aeson, the rightful king of Iolcos.

Q177302.label: Phidias
Q177302.description: Greek sculptor, painter and architect (c.480–430 BC)
