Q177302.lead: Phidias or Pheidias was an Ancient Greek sculptor, painter, and architect, active in the 5th century BC. His Statue of Zeus at Olympia was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Phidias also designed the statues of the goddess Athena on the Athenian Acropolis, namely the Athena Parthenos inside the Parthenon, and the Athena Promachos, a colossal bronze which stood between it and the Propylaea, a monumental gateway that served as the entrance to the Acropolis in Athens.

Q1774178.label: Cleopatra
Q1774178.description: Greek mythological person, daughter of Idas and Marpessa
Q1774178.lead: In Greek mythology Cleopatra, sometimes called Alcyone (Ancient Greek: Ἀλκυόνη, romanized: Alkuónē, lit. 'kingfisher') was the daughter of Idas and Marpessa and the wife of Meleager, a Calydonian prince and participant in the Calydonian boar hunt. Together they had a daughter, Polydora.

Q1779164.label: Phyleus
Q1779164.lead: In Greek mythology, Phyleus was an Elean prince and one of the Calydonian boar hunters.

Q178641.label: Peleus
Q178641.description: son of Aeacus in Greek mythology
Q178641.lead: In Greek mythology, Peleus was a hero, king of Phthia, husband of Thetis and the father of their son Achilles.

Q178710.label: Vesta
Q178710.description: goddess of the hearth, home, and family in Roman religion
Q178710.lead: Vesta is the virgin goddess of the hearth, home, and family in Roman religion. She was rarely depicted in human form, and was more often represented by the fire of her temple in the Forum Romanum.

Q1788026.label: Cresphontes
Q1788026.description: king of Messenia in Greek mythology
Q1788026.lead: In Greek mythology, Cresphontes was a son of Aristomachus, husband of Merope, father of Aepytus and brother of Temenus and Aristodemus. He was a great-great-grandson of Heracles and helped lead the fifth and final attack on Mycenae in the Peloponnesus.

Q178831.label: Aurora
Q178831.description: goddess of dawn in Roman mythology
Q178831.lead: In Roman mythology, Aurora is the goddess and personification of the dawn. Aurora is the Latin word for dawn, and she appeared frequently in Latin literature.

Q17892.label: Sappho
Q17892.description: ancient Greek poet from Lesbos (c. 630-c. 570 BC)
Q17892.lead: Sappho was an ancient Greek poet from Eresos or Mytilene on the island of Lesbos. She is known for her lyric poetry, written to be sung while accompanied by music.

Q179014.label: Io
Q179014.description: nymph seduced by Zeus in Greek mythology
Q179014.lead: In Greek mythology, Io was one of the mortal lovers of Zeus. An Argive princess, her descendants included Perseus, Cadmus, Heracles, Minos, Lynceus, Cepheus, Dionysus, and Danaus.

Q179256.label: Narcissus
Q179256.lead: In Greek mythology, Narcissus is a handsome youth who becomes enamoured with his own reflection in a pool of water. In the most famous version of the story, found in Metamorphoses by the Roman poet Ovid (who was active around the beginning of the 1st century AD), Narcissus rejects the advances of numerous suitors, including those of the nymph Echo.

Q1795033.label: Cylarabes
Q1795033.lead: Cylarabes, or Cylarabos, or Cylasabos, son of Sthenelus, was a mythological king of Argos.

Q179543.label: Iapetos
Q179543.lead: In Greek mythology, Iapetus or Iapetos, also Japetus or Japetos, was one of the Titans, the son of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth) and father of Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus, and Menoetius. He was also called the father of Buphagus and Anchiale in other sources.

Q179552.label: Themistocles
Q179552.lead: Themistocles was an Athenian politician and general. He was one of a new breed of non-aristocratic politicians who rose to prominence in the early years of the Athenian democracy.

Q179785.label: Gorgias
Q179785.description: Greek presocratic philosopher and sophist (483–375 BC)
Q179785.lead: Gorgias was an ancient Greek sophist, pre-Socratic philosopher, and rhetorician who was a native of Leontinoi in Sicily. Several doxographers report that he was a pupil of Empedocles, although he would only have been a few years younger.

Q1801511.label: Lamedon
Q1801511.lead: In Greek mythology, Lamedon also known as Laomedon, was the 18th king of Sicyon who reigned for 40 years.

Q18018199.label: Aenetus
Q18018199.description: Greek mythical character, son of Deion and Diomede
Q18018199.lead: In Greek mythology, Aenetus was a Phocian prince as the son of King Deioneus and Diomede, daughter of Xuthus. He was the brother of Cephalus, Actor, Phylacus and Asterodia.

Q180222.label: Amphitrite
Q180222.description: Oceanid or Nereid of Greek mythology
Q180222.lead: In ancient Greek mythology, Amphitrite was the goddess of the sea, the queen of the sea, and her consort is Poseidon. She was a daughter of Nereus and Doris (or Oceanus and Tethys).

Q180262.label: Erinyes
Q180262.lead: The Erinyes, also known as the Eumenides (Εὐμενίδες, the "Gracious ones"), are chthonic goddesses of vengeance in ancient Greek religion and mythology.

Q180287.label: Moirae
Q180287.description: personifications of fate in Greek mythology
Q180287.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, the Moirai—often known in English as the Fates—were the personifications of destiny. In certain accounts, they were considered as three sisters: Clotho (the spinner), Lachesis (the allotter), and Atropos (the inevitable, a metaphor for death), though their number and names varied over time according to the author.

Q1817912.label: Hyrieus
Q1817912.lead: In Greek mythology, Hyrieus was the eponym of Hyria in Boeotia, where he dwelt and where Orion (see below) was born; some sources though place him either in Thrace or on Chios. Most accounts speak of him as a king, although Ovid and Nonnus portray him as a peasant.

Q182019.label: Leda
Q182019.description: daughter of Thestius in Greek mythology
Q182019.lead: In Greek mythology, Leda, also rendered as Lede, was an Aetolian princess who became queen consort of Sparta through her marriage to King Tyndareus. Zeus fell in love with Leda, and to avoid his wife Hera's jealousy, assaulted her while disguised as a swan.

Q1821610.label: Leucothea
Q1821610.lead: Leucothea, sometimes also called Leucothoe (Ancient Greek: Λευκοθόη, romanized: Leukothóê or Leukothoē, lit. 'running white water', Ancient Greek pronunciation: [leu̯.koˈtho.εː]) is a sea goddess in Greek mythology. Myths surrounding Leucothea typically concern her original identity, either as Ino or Halia, and her transformation into a goddess.

Q1823070.label: Libon
Q1823070.description: 5th century BC architect of Ancient Greece
Q1823070.lead: Libon was a 5th-century BC architect of Ancient Greece.

Q182439.label: Pelias
Q182439.description: mythical king of Iolcus, and son of Poseidon who sent Jason on the quest for the Golden Fleece
Q182439.lead: Pelias was king of Iolcus in Greek mythology. He was the one who sent Jason on the quest for the Golden Fleece.

Q182483.label: Cambyses II
Q182483.lead: Cambyses II was the second King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire, reigning from 530 to 522 BCE. He was the son of and successor to Cyrus the Great; his mother was Cassandane. His relatively brief reign was marked by his conquests in North Africa, notably Egypt, which he took by defeating pharaoh Psamtik III (r. 526–525 BC) at the Battle of Pelusium in 525 BC. After his victory in Egypt, he expanded the empire's holdings in Africa by taking Cyrenaica, the coastal region of eastern Libya.

Q182855.label: Polygnotus of Thasos
Q182855.lead: Polygnotus was an ancient Greek painter active in the middle of the 5th century BC. Later scholars of the Classical World considered him to be one of the first great painters, sometimes even the inventor of the artform.

Q183109.label: Leosthenes
Q183109.lead: Leosthenes was an Athenian who was commander of the combined Greek army in the Lamian War. Leosthenes was the son of his namesake father Leosthenes who had suffered exile in 362/1 BC and who had fled to the court of Philip II. It is unknown by what means he had obtained the high reputation he had when he first makes his appearance in history.

Q183417.label: Chiron
Q183417.lead: In Greek mythology, Chiron, also Cheiron or Kheiron, was held to be the superlative centaur amongst his brethren since he was called the "wisest and justest of all the centaurs".

Q18353959.label: Aristodama
Q18353959.lead: Aristodama of Smyrna was a 3rd-century BCE itinerant poet of ancient Ionia. She is most likely born in Smyrna.

Q184176.label: Seleucus I Nicator
Q184176.description: general of Alexander and founder of the Seleucid dynasty
Q184176.lead: Seleucus I Nicator was a Macedonian Greek general, officer and successor of Alexander the Great who went on to found the eponymous Seleucid Empire, led by the Seleucid dynasty. Initially a secondary player in the power struggles following Alexander's death, Seleucus rose to become the total ruler of Asia Minor, Syria, Mesopotamia, and the Iranian plateau, assuming the title of basileus (king).

Q184353.label: Charites
Q184353.description: Greek goddesses of grace and beauty
Q184353.lead: The Charites are goddesses of Greek mythology who personify beauty and grace. According to Hesiod, their names were Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia and were the daughters of Zeus and Eurynome, the daughter of Oceanus.

Q184437.label: Thetis
Q184437.lead: Thetis is a figure from Greek mythology with varying mythological roles. She mainly appears as a sea nymph, a goddess of water, and one of the 50 Nereids, daughters of the ancient sea god Nereus.

Q184874.label: Ariadne
Q184874.description: the daughter of Minos in Greek mythology
Q184874.lead: In Greek mythology, Ariadne was a Cretan princess as the daughter of King Minos. There are multiple variations of Ariadne's myth, but she is best known for helping Theseus escape from the Minotaur and being abandoned by him on the island of Naxos.

Q185126.label: Mithridates VI of Pontus
Q185126.description: ruler of the Kingdom of Pontus from 120 to 63 BC
Q185126.lead: Mithridates or Mithradates VI Eupator sometimes known as Mithridates the Great was the Hellenistic ruler of the Kingdom of Pontus from 120 to 63 BC. He proved to be one of the Roman Republic's most formidable and determined opponents. He sought to dominate Anatolia and the Black Sea region, waging several hard-fought but ultimately unsuccessful wars to break Roman dominion over Asia and the Hellenic world.

Q1851846.label: Medus
Q1851846.description: son of Medea with either Aegeas or Jason
Q1851846.lead: In Greek mythology, Medus, also Medeus or Medeius (Μήδειος, Mḗdeios, lit. 'son of Medea', 'from Media', 'Median' or 'appertaining to the Medes'), was an Athenian prince as the son of King Aegeus, thus a half-brother of the hero Theseus.

Q18551588.label: Otus
Q18551588.description: mythological giant son of Poseidon or Aloeus

Q185670.label: Echidna
Q185670.description: ancient Greek mythological monster, the mother of monsters
Q185670.lead: In Greek mythology, Echidna was a monster, half-woman and half-snake, who lived alone in a cave. She was the mate of the fearsome monster Typhon and was the mother of many of the most famous monsters of Greek myth.

Q185747.label: Nemesis
Q185747.lead: In ancient Greek religion and myth, Nemesis, also called Rhamnousia (or Rhamnusia; Ancient Greek: Ῥαμνουσία, romanized: Rhamnousía, lit. 'the goddess of Rhamnous'), was the goddess who personified retribution for the sin of hubris: arrogance before the gods.

Q1862383.label: Melantho
Q1862383.description: daughter of Dolius in Greek mythology
Q1862383.lead: In Greek mythology, Melantho is one of the minor characters in the Odyssey. She was one of the maidservants of Odysseus who was loyal to the suitors of Penelope.

Q187602.label: Circe
Q187602.lead: In Greek mythology, Circe is a witch and goddess. In most accounts, Circe is described as a daughter of the sun god Helios and the Oceanid Perse.

Q187982.label: Alcibiades
Q187982.lead: Alcibiades was an Athenian statesman and general.

Q1886507.label: Merope
Q1886507.description: daughter of Cypselus of Arcadia in Greek mythology
Q1886507.lead: Merope was a Queen of Messenia in Greek mythology, daughter of King Cypselus of Arcadia and wife of Cresphontes, the Heraclid king of Messenia. After the murder of her husband and her two older children by Polyphontes (another Heraclid), Merope was forced to marry the murderer, but she managed to save her youngest son Aepytus, whom she sent secretly to Aetolia.

Q1887300.label: Mopsus
Q1887300.description: Greek mythological seer. son of Manto,
Q1887300.lead: In Greek mythology, Mopsus, a celebrated seer and diviner, was the son of Manto, daughter of the mythic seer Tiresias, and of Rhacius of Caria or of Apollo himself, the oracular god. Greeks of the Classical age accepted Mopsus as a historical figure, though the anecdotes concerning him bridge legend and myth.

Q189527.label: Nereus
Q189527.lead: In Greek mythology, Nereus was the eldest son of Pontus (the Sea) and Gaia (the Earth). Nereus and Doris became the parents of 50 daughters (the Nereids) and a son (Nerites), with whom Nereus lived in the Aegean Sea.

Q189872.label: Bellerophon
Q189872.description: Hero in Greek myth who rode Pegasus and killed the Chimera
Q189872.lead: Bellerophon or Bellerophontes or Hipponous (Ancient Greek: Ἱππόνοος, lit. 'horse-knower'), was a divine Corinthian hero of Greek mythology, the son of Poseidon and Eurynome, and the foster son of Glaukos. He was "the greatest hero and slayer of monsters, alongside Cadmus and Perseus, before the days of Heracles".

Q190055.label: Roxana
Q190055.description: Bactrian princess and wife of Alexander the Great
Q190055.lead: Roxana sometimes known as Roxanne, Roxanna, Roxzana, and Roxane, was a Bactrian or Sogdian princess who married Alexander the Great after he invaded Persia and defeated Darius, ruler of the Achaemenid Empire.

Q190103.label: Castor and Pollux
Q190103.lead: Castor and Pollux (or Polydeuces) are twin half-brothers in Greek and Roman mythology, known together as the Dioscuri or Dioskouroi. Their mother was Leda, but they had different fathers; Castor was the mortal son of Tyndareus, the king of Sparta, while Pollux was the divine son of Zeus, who seduced Leda in the guise of a swan.

Q190323.label: Atalanta
Q190323.description: Greek mythological character, the only female Argonaut
Q190323.lead: Atalanta is a heroine in Greek mythology. There are two versions of the huntress Atalanta: one from Arcadia, whose parents were Iasus and Clymene and who is primarily known from the tales of the Calydonian boar hunt and the Argonauts; and the other from Boeotia, who is the daughter of King Schoeneus and is primarily noted for her skill in the footrace.

Q190436.label: Epaminondas
Q190436.lead: Epaminondas was a Greek general and statesman of the 4th century BC who transformed the Ancient Greek city-state of Thebes, leading it out of Spartan subjugation into a pre-eminent position in Greek politics called the Theban Hegemony. In the process, he broke Spartan military power with his victory at Leuctra and liberated the Messenian helots, a group of Peloponnesian Greeks who had been enslaved under Spartan rule for some 230 years following their defeat in the Second Messenian War ending in 600 BC. Epaminondas reshaped the political map of Greece, fragmented old alliances, created new ones, and supervised the construction of entire cities.

Q190543.label: Alkmene
Q190543.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcmene or Alcmena ( alk-MEE-nə; Doric Greek: Ἀλκμάνα, romanized: Alkmána; Latin: Alcumena; meaning "strong in wrath") was the wife of Amphitryon, by whom she bore two children, Iphicles and Laonome. She is best known as the mother of Heracles, whose father was the god Zeus.

Q1917132.label: Megaros
Q1917132.description: son of one of the Sithnide nymphs and Zeus
Q1917132.lead: Greek mythology describes various great floods throughout ancient history. Differing sources refer to the flood of Ogyges, the flood of Deucalion, and the flood of Dardanus, though often with similar or even contradictory details.

Q191725.label: Aegeus
Q191725.lead: Aegeus was one of the kings of Athens in Greek mythology, who gave his name to the Aegean Sea, was the father of Theseus, and founded Athenian institutions.

Q191962.label: Achaeans
Q191962.description: inhabitants of the region of Achaea in the northern Peloponnese
Q191962.lead: The Achaeans were one of the four major tribes into which Herodotus divided the Greeks, along with the Aeolians, Ionians and Dorians. They inhabited the region of Achaea in the northern Peloponnese, and played an active role in the colonization of Italy, founding important cities such as Sybaris, Kroton and Metapontum.

Q192211.label: Myron
Q192211.lead: Myron of Eleutherae (Ancient Greek: Μύρων, Myrōn [mý.rɔːn]; c. 485 – c.

Q192222.label: Lysippos
Q192222.lead: Lysippos was a Greek sculptor of the 4th century BC. Together with Scopas and Praxiteles, he is considered one of the three greatest sculptors of the Classical Greek era, bringing transition into the Hellenistic period. Problems confront the study of Lysippos because of the difficulty in identifying his style in the copies which survive.

Q192313.label: Pyrrho
Q192313.description: Greek philosopher and founder of Pyrrhonism (c.360-c.270 BC)
Q192313.lead: Pyrrho of Elis was a Greek philosopher of Classical antiquity, credited as being the first Greek skeptic philosopher and founder of Pyrrhonism.

Q192407.label: Orestes
Q192407.description: son of Agamemnon in Greek mythology
Q192407.lead: In Greek mythology, Orestes or Orestis was the son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, and the brother of Electra and Iphigenia. He was also known by the patronymic Agamemnonides (Ἀγαμεμνονίδης), meaning "son of Agamemnon." He is the subject of multiple Ancient Greek plays (including Aeschylus' Oresteia), which depict his revenge, madness, and ritual purification.

Q1924155.label: Messene
Q1924155.lead: In Greek mythology, Messene was the daughter of Triopas, king of Argos (alternately, daughter of Phorbas and sister of Triopas). She was married to Polycaon, son of king Lelex, of Laconia.

Q192469.label: Atreus
Q192469.description: king of Mycenae, father of Agamemnon
Q192469.lead: In Greek mythology, Atreus was a king of Mycenae in the Peloponnese, the son of Pelops and Hippodamia, and the father of Agamemnon and Menelaus. His descendants became known collectively as the Atreidae (Ancient Greek: Ἀτρείδαι Atreidai).

Q192485.label: Pelops
Q192485.description: son of Tantalus in Greek mythology, king of Pisa in the Peloponnesus region
Q192485.lead: In Greek mythology, Pelops was king of Pisa in the Peloponnesus region (Πελοπόννησος, lit. "Pelops's Island").

Q1929263.label: Ocnus
Q1929263.description: figure in Greek mythology, punished in the underworld for sloth or hesitation
Q1929263.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Ocnus or Bianor (Ancient Greek: Βιάνωρ) was a son of Manto and Tiberinus Silvius, king of Alba Longa. He founded modern Mantua in honor of his mother.

Q192946.label: Tyndareus
Q192946.lead: In Greek mythology, Tyndareus was a Spartan king.

Q193267.label: Nestor
Q193267.description: wise ruler of Pylos in Greek mythology, son of Neleus
Q193267.lead: In Greek mythology, Nestor of Gerenia was a legendary king of Pylos. He is a prominent secondary character in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, where he appears as an elderly warrior who frequently offers advice to the other characters.

Q1934135.label: Mikythos
Q1934135.lead: Micythus, son of Choerus, was a 5th-century BC tyrant of Rhegium (modern Reggio Calabria) and Zancle (modern Messina) in Magna Graecia. He also founded the city of Pyxus (c.

Q193422.label: Polykleitos
Q193422.lead: Polykleitos was an ancient Greek sculptor, active in the 5th century BCE. Alongside the Athenian sculptors Pheidias, Myron and Praxiteles, he is considered as one of the most important sculptors of classical antiquity. The 4th century BCE catalogue attributed to Xenocrates (the "Xenocratic catalogue"), which was Pliny's guide in matters of art, ranked him between Pheidias and Myron.

Q193433.label: Hecuba
Q193433.lead: In Greek mythology, Hecuba was the wife of King Priam and queen of Troy during the Trojan War. With Priam, she was the mother of the warriors Hector and Troilus; Helen's suitor Paris; and the prophetess Cassandra.

Q193609.label: Rhadamanthus
Q193609.description: Greek mythology character, son of Zeus and Europa
Q193609.lead: In Greek mythology, Rhadamanthus or Rhadamanthys was a wise king of Crete. As the son of Zeus and Europa he was considered a demigod.

Q19376.label: Andromache
Q19376.description: wife of Hector in Greek mythology
Q19376.lead: In Greek mythology, Andromache was the wife of Hector, daughter of Eetion, and sister to Podes. She was born and raised in the city of Cilician Thebe, over which her father ruled.

Q194015.label: Daphne
Q194015.lead: Daphne, a figure in Greek mythology, was in various retellings a mortal woman or a nymph, daughter of a river god. The god Apollo fell in love with Daphne and chased her against her wishes, but before he caught her, Daphne prayed for escape, and was transformed into a laurel tree.

Q1951047.label: Mousos
Q1951047.description: Greek sculptor with work at Olympia

Q1956583.label: Mycene
Q1956583.description: daughter of Inachus in Greek mythology
Q1956583.lead: In Greek mythology, Mycene, was a daughter of Inachus, king of Argos and wife of Arestor. Mycene was said to be the eponym of Mycenae.

Q1956649.label: Myles
Q1956649.description: Ancient King of Laconia in Greek mythology
Q1956649.lead: In Greek mythology, Myles was an ancient king of Laconia. He was the son of the King Lelex and possibly the naiad Queen Cleocharia, and brother of Polycaon.

Q1968413.label: Mecisteus
Q1968413.description: son of Talaus and Lysimache in ancient Greek mythology
Q1968413.lead: In Greek mythology, Mecisteus was the son of Talaus and Lysimache. He was the father of Euryalus by Astyoche.

Q196865.label: Zethos
Q196865.lead: Amphion and Zethus (Ancient Greek: Ζῆθος, romanized: Zêthos) were, in ancient Greek mythology, the twin sons of Zeus (or Theobus) by Antiope. They are important characters in one of the two founding myths of the city of Thebes, because they constructed the city's walls.

Q197033.label: Zeuxippus
Q197033.lead: In Greek mythology, Zeuxippus was the successor of Phaestus as king of Sicyon and in turn succeeded by Hippolytus, grandson of the former ruler.

Q1977078.label: Nemea
Q1977078.description: naiad, mythical daughter of Asopus or Zeus
Q1977078.lead: In Greek mythology, Nemea was the eponymous nymph of Nemea, a district between Cleonae and Phlius in Argolis. She is sometimes depicted bringing water to Heracles after his fight with the Nemean Lion.

Q19822828.label: Aroanios
Q19822828.description: tributary of the Erymanthos in Greece

Q1985130.label: Orneus
Q1985130.description: in Greek mythology, son of King Erechtheus and Praxithea
Q1985130.lead: In Greek mythology, Orneus may refer to two different personages: Orneus, an Athenian prince as the son of King Erechtheus and probably Praxithea, daughter of Phrasimus and Diogeneia. His possible siblings were Protogeneia, Pandora, Creusa, Procris, Oreithyia, Chthonia, Merope, Cecrops, Pandorus, Metion, Thespius, Eupalamus and Sicyon.

Q19946249.label: Eurymachus
Q19946249.description: son of Antenor in Greek mythology

Q1995961.label: Thalpius
Q1995961.description: king of Elis in Greek mythology

Q1996222.label: Melaneus
Q1996222.description: son of Apollo in Greek mythology
Q1996222.lead: In Greek mythology, Melaneus was the founder of Oechalia (Oikhalia), variously located in Thessaly, Messenia or Euboea and also king of the Dryopes.

Q199923.label: Dione
Q199923.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Dione is an oracular goddess and Titaness. She is primarily known from Book V of Homer's Iliad, where she tends to the wounds suffered by her daughter Aphrodite.

Q200382.label: Phorcys
Q200382.lead: In Greek mythology, Phorcys or Phorcus is a primordial sea god, generally cited (first in Hesiod) as the son of Pontus and Gaia (Earth). Classical scholar Karl Kerenyi conflated Phorcys with the similar sea gods Nereus and Proteus.

Q200401.label: Antigonus I Monophthalmus
Q200401.description: Macedonian general, founder of Antigonid dynasty (382–301 BC)
Q200401.lead: Antigonus I Monophthalmus was a Macedonian Greek general and successor of Alexander the Great who founded the Antigonid dynasty, which ruled over Macedonia until its conquest by the Roman Republic in 168 BC. A prominent military leader in Alexander's army, he went on to control large parts of Alexander's former empire. He assumed the title of basileus (king) in 306 BC and reigned until his death.

Q2006592.label: Neis
Q2006592.description: mythical child of Zethus of Thebes
Q2006592.lead: In Greek mythology Neis is a princess from the ancient Greek city-kingdom of Thebes and the namesake of the Neitian Gate, one of the seven gates of Thebes. Neis is the daughter of either one of Thebes' twin kings, Amphion and Zethus, by their wives Niobe or Aëdon respectively.

Q20100712.label: Helice
Q20100712.description: figure in Greek mythology, daughter of Selinous

Q20102055.label: Tisagoras
Q20102055.lead: Tisagoras may refer to the: A brother of Miltiades according to Cornelius Nepos. Cornelius Nepos describes Tisagoras as the brother of Miltiades who conducted Miltiades defense when he was put on trial in Athens after his failed expedition to Paros.

Q201261.label: Orion
Q201261.lead: In Greek mythology, Orion was a giant huntsman whom Zeus or Artemis placed among the stars as a constellation. He was venerated as a hero in the region of Boeotia, and there is one etiological passage which says that Orion was responsible for the present shape of the Strait of Sicily.

Q202113.label: Perdiccas
Q202113.lead: Perdiccas was a Macedonian general and bodyguard (somatophylax) of Alexander the Great, and the regent of Alexander's empire after his death.

Q202257.label: Hygieia
Q202257.description: goddess in Greek mythology, personification of health
Q202257.lead: Hygieia is a goddess from Greek mythology. Hygieia is a goddess of health (Greek: ὑγίεια – hygíeia), cleanliness and hygiene.

Q2031315.label: Ornytion
Q2031315.description: son of Sisyphus and king of Corinth in Greek mythology
Q2031315.lead: In Greek mythology, Ornytion or Ornytus (Ὄρνυτος) may refer to two different characters: Ornytion, also known as Porphyrion, a Corinthian prince who later succeeded his father, King Sisyphus, as the ruler of the Ephyraean land. His mother was the Pleiad Merope, daughter of the Titan Atlas.

Q2031409.label: Xanthus
Q2031409.lead: Xanthos, son of Ptolemy, was the king of Thebes, the 16th and final monarch that ruled the city. He was possibly king only temporarily, being shown at times as the king of the Boeotians, the King of the Thebians.

Q203480.label: Phaethon
Q203480.description: son of Helios from Greek mythology
Q203480.lead: Phaethon, also spelled Phaëthon, is the son of the Oceanid Clymene and the sun god Helios in Greek mythology. According to most authors, Phaethon is the son of Helios who, out of a desire to have his parentage confirmed, travels to the sun god's palace in the east.

Q203673.label: Callisto
Q203673.lead: In Greek mythology, Callisto was a nymph (an Arcadian mountain nymph; an Oread), or the daughter of King Lycaon; the myth varies in such details. She was believed to be one of the followers of Artemis (Diana for the Romans) who was pursued by Zeus.

Q204760.label: Antipater
Q204760.lead: Antipater was a Macedonian general, regent and statesman under the successive kingships of Philip II of Macedon and his son, Alexander the Great.

Q2049871.label: Panthalis
Q2049871.description: attendant of Helen, represented in Iliupersis painting at Delphi

Q205233.label: Maia
Q205233.lead: In ancient Greek mythology, Maia, also spelled Maie, is one of the Pleiades and the mother of the messenger god Hermes by Zeus. Maia was identified with the Roman earth goddess Maia, the mother of Mercury.

Q205251.label: Plutus
Q205251.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Plutus is the god and the personification of wealth, and the son of the goddess of agriculture Demeter and the mortal Iasion.

Q206187.label: Aeacus
Q206187.description: son of Zeus in Greek mythology
Q206187.lead: Aeacus was a king of the island of Aegina in Greek mythology. He was a son of Zeus and the nymph Aegina, and the father of the heroes Peleus and Telamon.

Q206214.label: Amphitryon
Q206214.description: figure in Greek mythology, husband of Alcmene
Q206214.lead: Amphitryon, in Greek mythology, was a son of Alcaeus, king of Tiryns in Argolis. His mother was named either Astydameia, the daughter of Pelops and Hippodamia, or Laonome, daughter of Guneus, or else Hipponome, daughter of Menoeceus.

Q2065138.label: Lycortas
Q2065138.lead: Lycortas of Megalopolis, son of Thearidas, was a politician of the Achaean League active in the first half of the 2nd century BC. He was the father of the historian Polybius. A political ally of Philopoemen, he shared the latter's view that the Romans should be dealt with according to the strict letter of their treaty with the League, and that no more assistance should be given to them than was necessary.

Q2066030.label: Diaeus
Q2066030.lead: Diaeus of Megalopolis was the last strategos of the Achaian League in ancient Greece before the League was disbanded by the Romans. He served as the League's general from 150 to 149 BC and from 148 BC until his death.

Q206878.label: Priapus
Q206878.lead: In Greek mythology, Priapus is a minor rustic fertility god, protector of livestock, fruit plants, gardens, and male genitalia. Priapus is marked by his oversized penis, and his permanent erection, which gave rise to the medical term priapism.

Q207183.label: Cassander
Q207183.lead: Cassander was king of the Ancient Greek kingdom of Macedonia from 305 BC until 297 BC, and de facto ruler of southern Greece from 317 BC until his death.

Q207273.label: Hyacinth
Q207273.lead: Hyacinth or Hyacinthus is a deified hero and a lover of Apollo in Greek mythology. His cult at Amyclae southwest of Sparta dates from the Mycenaean era.

Q207663.label: Augeias of Elis
Q207663.description: son of Phorbas in Greek mythology
Q207663.lead: In Greek mythology, Augeas, also called Aegeus, was king of Elis and father of Epicaste. Some ancient authors say that Augeas was one of the Argonauts.

Q207715.label: Deucalion
Q207715.description: son of Prometheus in Greek mythology
Q207715.lead: In Greek mythology, Deucalion was the son of Prometheus; ancient sources name his mother as Clymene, Hesione, or Pronoia. He is closely connected with a flood myth in Greek mythology.

Q208017.label: Acrisius
Q208017.lead: In Greek mythology, Acrisius was a king of Argos. He was the grandfather of the famous Greek demi-god Perseus through his only daughter Danaë.

Q208531.label: Actaeon
Q208531.description: son of Aristaeus in Greek mythology
Q208531.lead: In Greek mythology, Actaeon was the son of the priestly herdsman Aristaeus in Boeotia, and a famous Theban hero. Through his mother Autonoë he was a member of the ruling House of Cadmus.

Q2088105.label: Philocles
Q2088105.description: Athenian military commander at Aegospotami 405 BCE

Q2089459.label: Epione
Q2089459.description: wife of Asclepius in Greek mythology
Q2089459.lead: In Greek mythology, Epione is a minor health goddess, the wife of Asclepius, the Greek god of healing and medicine.

Q2097546.label: Saron
Q2097546.lead: In Greek mythology, Saron is a king of Troezen who gave his name to the Saronic Gulf. He was the third king of Troezen, following Althepus.

Q2097787.label: Pergamus
Q2097787.lead: In Greek mythology, Pergamus was the son of the warrior Neoptolemus and Andromache. Pergamus's parents both figure in the Trojan War, described in Homer's The Iliad: Neoptolemus was the son of Achilles and fought on the Greek side, while Andromache was the Trojan prince Hector's wife.

Q210258.label: Seres
Q210258.lead: Serica was one of the easternmost countries of Asia known to the Ancient Greek and Roman geographers. It is generally taken as referring to North China during its Zhou, Qin, and Han dynasties, as it was reached via the overland Silk Road in contrast to the Sinae, who were reached via the maritime routes.

Q210303.label: Hippolyta
Q210303.description: queen of the Amazons in Greek mythology
Q210303.lead: In Greek mythology, Hippolyta, or Hippolyte, was the queen of the Amazons and a daughter of Ares and Otrera. Her sisters were Antiope and Melanippe.

Q210350.label: Miltiades
Q210350.description: Greek Athenian statesman and general (c.550–489 BC)
Q210350.lead: Miltiades, also known as Miltiades the Younger, was an Athenian general and statesman known mostly for his role in the Battle of Marathon, as well as for his downfall afterwards.

Q210883.label: Danaus
Q210883.lead: In Greek mythology, Danaus was the king of Libya. His myth is a foundation legend of Argos, one of the foremost Mycenaean cities of the Peloponnesus.

Q211411.label: Chrysippus of Soli
Q211411.lead: Chrysippus of Soli (Ancient Greek: Χρύσιππος ὁ Σολεύς, Chrusippos ho Soleus; c. 279 – c.

Q211430.label: Demades
Q211430.lead: Demades was an Athenian orator and demagogue.

Q211953.label: Anchises
Q211953.description: father of Aeneas in Greek mythology, lover of Aphrodite
Q211953.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Anchises was a member of the royal family of Troy. He was said to have been the son of King Capys of Dardania and Themiste, daughter of Ilus, who was son of Tros.

Q212087.label: Eurystheus
Q212087.description: king of Mycenae in Greek mythology
Q212087.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurystheus was king of Tiryns, one of three Mycenaean strongholds in the Argolid, although other authors including Homer and Euripides cast him as ruler of Argos.

Q212091.label: Aegisthus
Q212091.description: son of Thyestes in Greek mythology
Q212091.lead: Aegisthus was a figure in Greek mythology. Aegisthus is known from two primary sources: the first is Homer's Odyssey, believed to have been first written down by Homer at the end of the 8th century BC, and the second from Aeschylus's Oresteia, written in the 5th century BC. Aegisthus also features heavily in the action of Euripides's Electra (c.

Q212827.label: Philoctetes
Q212827.lead: Philoctetes or Philocthetes, according to Greek mythology, was the son of Poeas, king of Meliboea in Thessaly, and Demonassa or Methone. He was a Greek hero, famed as an archer, and a participant in the Trojan War.

Q212872.label: Alcaeus of Mytilene
Q212872.lead: Alcaeus of Mytilene was a lyric poet from the Greek island of Lesbos who is credited with inventing the Alcaic stanza. He was included in the canonical list of nine lyric poets by the scholars of Hellenistic Alexandria.

Q213484.label: Anacreon
Q213484.description: ancient Greek lyric poet, notable for his drinking songs and hymns
Q213484.lead: Anacreon was an Ancient Greek lyric poet, notable for his drinking songs and erotic poems. Later Greeks included him in the canonical list of Nine Lyric Poets.

Q214554.label: Serapis
Q214554.lead: Serapis or Sarapis is a Graeco-Egyptian god. A syncretic deity derived from the worship of the Egyptian gods Osiris and Apis, Serapis was extensively popularized in the third century BC on the orders of Greek Pharaoh Ptolemy I Soter, as a means to unify the Greek and Egyptian subjects of the Ptolemaic Kingdom.

Q21548762.label: Aristomache
Q21548762.lead: In Greek mythology, Aristomache was a Trojan princess, the daughter of King Priam. She was married to Critolaus, son of Hicetaon.

Q21552855.label: Aristogiton
Q21552855.lead: Harmodius and Aristogeiton (Ἀριστογείτων, Aristogeíton; both died 514 BC) were two lovers in Classical Athens who became known as the Tyrannicides (τυραννόκτονοι, tyrannoktonoi) for their assassination of Hipparchus, the brother of the tyrant Hippias, for which they were executed. A few years later, in 510 BC, the Spartan king Cleomenes I forced Hippias to go into exile, thereby opening the way to the subsequent democratic reforms of Cleisthenes.

Q21567935.label: Pierus
Q21567935.description: king of Emathia, father of the Pierides, eponym of Pieria
Q21567935.lead: In Greek mythology, Pierus was the king of Emathia in Macedonia. He was the eponym of Pieria and Mt.

Q21616165.label: Tithorea
Q21616165.description: nymph for whom Tithorea polis named
Q21616165.lead: In Greek mythology, Tithorea a Phocian nymph of Mount Parnassus, from whom the town of Tithorea, previously called Neon, was believed to have derived its name. She was possibly a dryad.

Q21616290.label: Auxesia
Q21616290.lead: Auxesia was in Greek mythology the goddess who grants growth and prosperity to the fields, sometimes distinct and sometimes an epithet of the goddess Persephone. Her name is the Greek word for "increase".

Q2167123.label: Taras
Q2167123.description: son of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q2167123.lead: In Greek mythology, Taras was the eponymous founder of the Greek colony of Taras (Tarentum, modern Taranto), in Magna Graecia (today Southern Italy).

Q216822.label: Apelles
Q216822.lead: Apelles of Kos was a renowned painter of ancient Greece.

Q218102.label: Cimon
Q218102.lead: Cimon was an Athenian strategos (general and admiral) and politician. He was the son of Miltiades, also an Athenian strategos.

Q2194100.label: Leitus
Q2194100.lead: In Greek mythology, Leitus was a leader of the Boeotians and admiral of 12 ships which sailed against Troy.

Q2196048.label: Creusa
Q2196048.lead: In Greek mythology, Creusa was an Athenian princess.

Q221182.label: Isocrates
Q221182.lead: Isocrates was an ancient Greek rhetorician, one of the ten Attic orators. Among the most influential Greek rhetoricians of his time, Isocrates made many contributions to rhetoric and education through his teaching and written works.

Q221787.label: Anaximenes of Lampsacus
Q221787.lead: Anaximenes of Lampsacus was a Greek rhetorician and historian. He was one of the teachers of Alexander the Great and accompanied him on his campaigns.

Q221925.label: Acarnan
Q221925.description: son of Alcmaeon in Greek mythology
Q221925.lead: In Greek mythology, Acarnan was son of Alcmaeon and Callirrhoe, and brother of Amphoterus.

Q223134.label: Olympias
Q223134.lead: Olympias was an ancient Greek princess of the Molossians, the eldest daughter of King Neoptolemus I of Epirus, and the sister of Alexander I of Epirus.

Q223152.label: Adrastus
Q223152.lead: In Greek mythology, Adrastus or Adrestus was a king of Argos, and leader of the Seven against Thebes. He was the son of the Argive king Talaus, but was forced out of Argos by his dynastic rival Amphiaraus.

Q223690.label: Ino
Q223690.lead: In Greek mythology, Ino was a Theban princess who later became a queen of Boeotia. After her death and transfiguration, she was worshiped as a goddess under her epithet Leucothea, the "white goddess." Alcman called her "Queen of the Sea" (Ancient Greek: θαλασσομέδουσα, romanized: thalassomédousa), which, if not hyperbole, would make her a goddess parallel to Amphitrite.

Q2244996.label: Thrasyllus
Q2244996.lead: Thrasyllus was an Athenian strategos (general) and statesman who rose to prominence in the later years of the Peloponnesian War. First appearing in Athenian politics in 410 BC, in the wake of the Athenian coup of 411 BC, he played a role in organizing democratic resistance in an Athenian fleet at Samos.

Q2259929.label: Cisseus
Q2259929.description: Greek mythological character, Thracian king and father of Theano
Q2259929.lead: In Greek mythology, Cisseus may refer to the following personages: Cisseus, an Egyptian prince as one of the sons of King Aegyptus. His mother was the naiad Caliadne and thus full brother of Eurylochus, Phantes, Peristhenes, Hermus, Potamon, Dryas, Lixus, Imbrus, Bromius, Polyctor and Chthonius.

Q22906256.label: Lamia
Q22906256.lead: In Greek mythology, Lamia was a daughter of Poseidon, and mother, by Zeus, of the Libyan Sibyl. It was perhaps this Lamia who, according to Stesichorus, was the mother of Scylla.

Q2293816.label: Endeïs
Q2293816.description: daughter of Sciron in Greek mythology
Q2293816.lead: In Greek mythology, Queen Endeïs was the wife of King Aeacus and mother of the heroes Telamon and Peleus (since Peleus was the father of Achilles and Telamon was the father of Ajax the Great and Teucer, Endeïs was the grandmother of Achilles, Ajax and Teucer). The name is a dialect variant of Engaios (Ἐγγαῖος, "in the earth").

Q229483.label: Octavia the Younger
Q229483.lead: Octavia the Younger was the elder sister of the first Roman emperor (Augustus, also known as Octavian), the half-sister of Octavia the Elder, and the fourth wife of Mark Antony. She was also the great-grandmother of the Emperor Caligula and Empress Agrippina the Younger (who was empress during the reign of Claudius), maternal grandmother of Claudius and his brother Germanicus, and paternal great-grandmother and maternal great-great-grandmother of the Emperor Nero.

Q2296243.label: Sparta
Q2296243.description: daughter of Eurotas, in Greek mythology
Q2296243.lead: In Greek mythology, Sparta was the ancient Queen of Sparta, which was named in her honour.

Q22965372.label: Alopecus
Q22965372.description: mythical son of Irbus of Sparta

Q2300199.label: Meges
Q2300199.lead: In Greek mythology, Mégês Phyleïdês was the commander of Epeans and/or Dulichians during the Trojan War.

Q2303713.label: Anax
Q2303713.lead: In Greek mythology, Anax was a king of Anactoria (Miletus). He was the son of Gaea (Earth) and father of Asterius.

Q2305446.label: Caanthus
Q2305446.lead: Caanthus is also a synonym of the cylindrical bark beetle genus Ciconissus. In Greek mythology, Caanthus or Kaanthos was the son of Oceanus and Tethys, and the brother of Melia, who was the consort of Apollo, and an important cult figure at Thebes.

Q23168.label: Minos
Q23168.description: Greek mythology character, son of Zeus and Europa, king of Crete
Q23168.lead: In Greek mythology, Minos was a king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa. Every nine years, he made King Aegeus pick seven young boys and seven young girls to be sent to Daedalus's creation, the labyrinth, to be eaten by the Minotaur.

Q2317917.label: Helicaon
Q2317917.lead: In Greek mythology, Helicaon or Helikaon was a Trojan warrior and son of the elder Antenor and the priestess Theano. He was the brother of Crino, including Acamas, Agenor, Antheus, Archelochus, Coön, Demoleon, Eurymachus, Glaucus, Hippolochus, Hypsipylus, Iphidamas, Laodamas, Laodocus, Medon, Polybus, and Thersilochus.

Q2319055.label: Rhianus
Q2319055.description: ancient Greek poet and grammarian, a native of Crete, friend and contemporary of Eratosthenes (275 BC – 195 BC)
Q2319055.lead: Rhianus was a Greek poet and grammarian, a native of Crete, friend and contemporary of Eratosthenes (275–195 BC).

Q232128.label: Artemisia I of Caria
Q232128.description: 5th century BC queen of Halicarnassus, Kos, Nisyros and Kalymnos
Q232128.lead: Artemisia I of Caria (Ancient Greek: Ἀρτεμισία, transl. Ártemisía; fl.

Q2322495.label: Amphissa
Q2322495.description: Greek mythical character, daughter of Macareus, lover of Apollo
Q2322495.lead: In Greek mythology, Amphissa, also called Issa (/ˈiːsɑː/; Ἴσσα) was the daughter of Macareus and a lover of Apollo. She was the eponym of the city Amphissa in Ozolian Locris, where her memory was perpetuated by a splendid monument.

Q232790.label: Phryne
Q232790.lead: Phryne was an ancient Greek hetaira (courtesan). Born Mnesarete, she was from Thespiae in Boeotia, but seems to have lived most of her life in Athens.

Q2329005.label: Phegeus
Q2329005.lead: In Greek mythology, Phegeus was the king of Psophis in Arcadia who purified Alcmaeon after the murder of his own mother, Eriphyle. The town of Phegeia, which had before been called Erymanthus, was believed to have derived its name from him.

Q2335647.label: Licymnius
Q2335647.description: son of Electryon in Greek mythology
Q2335647.lead: In Greek mythology, Licymnius was a good friend of Heracles and an illegitimate son of Electryon, King of Tiryns and Mycenae in the Argolid (which makes him half-brother of Alcmene, mother of Heracles). His mother is given as Mideia, a Phrygian woman.

Q2335996.label: Polyeidos
Q2335996.description: mythical seer, who revived Glaucus son of Minos
Q2335996.lead: In Greek mythology, Polyidus also known as Polyeidus, is the son of Coeranus, and a famous seer from Argos or Corinth.

Q233771.label: Eurydice of Egypt
Q233771.lead: Eurydice was the third known wife to Ptolemy I Soter and as such a queen of Egypt.

Q233783.label: Barsine
Q233783.lead: Barsine was the daughter of a Persian father, Artabazus, satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia, and a Greek Rhodian mother, the sister of mercenaries Mentor of Rhodes and Memnon of Rhodes.

Q2338787.label: Phormio
Q2338787.lead: Phormio, the son of Asopius, was an Athenian general and admiral before and during the Peloponnesian War. A talented naval commander, Phormio commanded at several famous Athenian victories in 428 BC, and was honoured after his death with a statue on the acropolis and a state funeral.

Q2349443.label: Salamis
Q2349443.lead: Salamis was a nymph in Greek mythology, the daughter of the river-god Asopus.

Q237136.label: Berenice
Q237136.lead: Berenice (c.275 BC–246 BC), also called Berenice Phernophorus ("Dowry Bearer") or Berenice Syra, was an Egyptian princess and a Seleucid queen regent. She was a Seleucid queen by marriage to Antiochus II Theos, and regent during the minority of her son Antiochus in 246.

Q2395266.label: Phytalus
Q2395266.description: King of Attica who gave Demeter hospitality
Q2395266.lead: In Greek mythology, Phytalus was a hero and king of Attica who gave Demeter hospitality when she was searching for her daughter, Persephone. Demeter thanked Phytalus for his kindness by giving him a fig-tree.

Q2401584.label: Telegone
Q2401584.lead: In Greek mythology, Telegone was the daughter of Pharis, son of Hermes and the Danaid Phylodameia. She bore to the river-god Alpheus, a son, Orsilochus who later became the father of Diocles.

Q241120.label: Anyte of Tegea
Q241120.lead: Anyte of Tegea was a Hellenistic poet from Tegea in Arcadia. Little is known of her life, but twenty-four epigrams attributed to her are preserved in the Greek Anthology, and one is quoted by Julius Pollux; nineteen of these are generally accepted as authentic.

Q241132.label: Corinna
Q241132.description: ancient Greek poet whose lifetime is unclear and controversial
Q241132.lead: Corinna or Korinna was an ancient Greek lyric poet from Tanagra in Boeotia. Although ancient sources portray her as a contemporary of Pindar (born c. 518 BC), not all modern scholars accept the accuracy of this tradition.

Q241971.label: Aeëtes
Q241971.description: son of Helios in Greek mythology
Q241971.lead: Aeëtes, or Aeeta, was the ruler of the eponymous realm of Aea in Greek mythology, a wondrous realm which from the fifth century B.C.E. onward became identified with the kingdom of Colchis east in the Black Sea. The name comes from the ancient Greek word αἰετός (aietós, "eagle").

Q2421647.label: Thoas
Q2421647.description: king of Corinth, son of Ornytion
Q2421647.lead: In Greek mythology, Thoas was a prince of Corinth who succeeded his father Ornytion to the throne.

Q242172.label: Pisistratus
Q242172.description: 6th century BC tyrant of ancient Athens
Q242172.lead: Pisistratus was a politician in ancient Athens, ruling as tyrant in the late 560s, the early 550s and from 546 BC until his death. His unification of Attica, the triangular peninsula of Greece containing Athens, along with economic and cultural improvements laid the groundwork for the later pre-eminence of Athens in ancient Greece.

Q242835.label: Amphion
Q242835.description: mythical musician and ruler at Thebes
Q242835.lead: Amphion and Zethus (Ancient Greek: Ζῆθος, romanized: Zêthos) were, in ancient Greek mythology, the twin sons of Zeus (or Theobus) by Antiope. They are important characters in one of the two founding myths of the city of Thebes, because they constructed the city's walls.

Q244318.label: Briseis
Q244318.description: daughter of Briseus in Greek mythology
Q244318.lead: Briseis, also known as Hippodameia (Ἱπποδάμεια, [hippodámeːa]), is a significant character in the Iliad. Her role as a status symbol is at the heart of the dispute between Achilles and Agamemnon that initiates the plot of Homer's epic.

Q2446699.label: Rhacius
Q2446699.description: cretan son of Lebes who settled in Caria
Q2446699.lead: In Greek mythology, Rhacius was the Cretan son of Lebes, who led a group of Greek settlers to Colophon in Asia Minor. With his wife Manto, daughter of the seer Tiresias, he became the father of Mopsus, a renowned seer.

Q2446711.label: Pamphylus
Q2446711.description: son of Aegimius in Greek mythology
Q2446711.lead: In Greek mythology, Pamphylus was a Dorian hero. He was considered to be the eponymous hero of one of the three tribes (phylai) of the Dorians, the Pamphyloi; his brothers, Dymas and Hyllos, were associated with the remaining two.

Q2460883.label: Taxiles
Q2460883.lead: Taxiles was a general in the service of Mithridates VI of Pontus, and one of those in whom he reposed the highest confidence.

Q2462054.label: Orestheus
Q2462054.lead: Orestheus, in Greek mythology, was a name attributed to two individuals. Orestheus, a king of the Ozolian Locrians in Aetolia.

Q2466253.label: Amarynceus
Q2466253.description: son of Pyttius in Greek mythology
Q2466253.lead: Amarynceus was in Greek mythology, a chief of the Eleans.

Q2470261.label: Miletus
Q2470261.lead: Miletus was a character from Greek mythology, the eponymous mythical founder of the city of Miletus.

Q2473927.label: Anaxilas
Q2473927.description: tyrant of Rhegium from 494 to 476 BC
Q2473927.lead: Anaxilas or Anaxilaus, son of Cretines, was a tyrant of Rhegium (modern Reggio Calabria) in Magna Graecia. He was originally from Messenia, a region in the Peloponnese.

Q247617.label: Curetes
Q247617.description: minor Minoan and Greek deities, servants of Rhea

Q2479189.label: Ischys
Q2479189.description: son of Elatus and lover of Coronis in Greek mythology
Q2479189.lead: In Greek mythology, Ischys was the son of Elatus.

Q252387.label: Palamedes
Q252387.lead: Palamedes was a Euboean prince, son of King Nauplius in Greek mythology. He joined the rest of the Greeks in the expedition against Troy.

Q2537664.label: Prytanis
Q2537664.lead: Prytanis (Ancient Greek: Πρύτανις; reigned from c. 865 to c.

Q2551733.label: Peteus
Q2551733.lead: In Greek mythology, Peteus or Peteos or Petes (Πέτης) was a member of the Athenian royal family as the son of Orneus, son of King Erechtheus. In some versions of the myth, Petes was originally an Egyptian, who later obtained Athenian citizenship.

Q256115.label: Hemithea
Q256115.description: daughter of Cycnus in Greek mythology

Q2584301.label: Onomarchus
Q2584301.lead: Onomarchus was general of the Phocians in the Third Sacred War, brother of Philomelus and son of Theotimus. After his brother's death he became commander of the Phocians and pursued a warmongering policy defeating in battle even Philip II of Macedon until his final defeat by him.

Q2608087.label: Thasus
Q2608087.lead: In Greek mythology, Thasus or Thasos was a son of Poseidon (in other versions, Agenor, Phoenix or Cilix). He was a Phoenician prince and one of those who set out from Phoenicia in search of Europa (Thasus' sister).

Q2608554.label: Molpadia
Q2608554.lead: In Greek mythology, Molpadia may refer to the two different women: Molpadia, an Amazon who was said to have fought for both Antiope and Orithyia. She was a participant in the Attic War, where she witnessed her queen Antiope sustain heavy injuries.

Q262016.label: Attis
Q262016.lead: Attis was the consort of Cybele, in Phrygian and Greek mythology. His priests were eunuchs, the Galli, as explained by origin myths pertaining to Attis castrating himself.

Q2622614.label: Molossus
Q2622614.lead: In Greek mythology, Molossus was the son of Neoptolemus and Andromache. He was the eponymous founder of the Molossians, an ancient Greek tribe that inhabited the region of Epirus located in northwestern Greece.

Q26296.label: Electryon
Q26296.description: son of Perseus in Greek mythology
Q26296.lead: In Greek mythology, Electryon was a king of Tiryns and Mycenae or Medea in Argolis.

Q2640491.label: Schoeneus
Q2640491.description: father of Atalante in Greek mythology

Q2647446.label: Alcinoe
Q2647446.description: mythological Greek character, daughter of Polybus
Q2647446.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcinoë is a young princess of Corinth, daughter of King Polybus of Corinth, and sister to Oedipus. Greek grammarian Parthenius of Nicaea preserves her story in his Erotica Pathemata ("sorrows about love"), which he attributes to the Hellenistic poetess Moero.

Q2661436.label: Norax
Q2661436.description: son of Hermes in Greek mythology
Q2661436.lead: Norax was a mythological hero mentioned in the writings of ancient Greek and Roman writers. He was said to be the son of the god Hermes and Erytheia, the daughter of Geryon.

Q26690189.label: Antinoe
Q26690189.description: Greek mythical character, daughter of Pelias

Q267195.label: Cynisca
Q267195.lead: Cynisca was a wealthy Spartan princess. She is famous for being the first woman to win at the Olympic Games.

Q268229.label: Echembrotus
Q268229.lead: Echembrotus was an ancient Arcadian Greek lyricist and poet. According to Pausanias, Echembrotus offered a bronze tripod to Heracles when the latter won at the Amphictyonic Games.

Q26825.label: Herodotus
Q26825.lead: Herodotus was a Greek historian and geographer from the Greek city of Halicarnassus (now Bodrum, Turkey), under Persian control in the 5th century BC, and a later citizen of Thurii in modern Calabria, Italy. He wrote the Histories, a detailed account of the Greco-Persian Wars, among other subjects such as the rise of the Achaemenid dynasty of Cyrus.

Q269058.label: Glauce
Q269058.description: mythical character; daughter of Creon in Greek mythology
Q269058.lead: In Greek mythology, Creusa or Glauce (Γλαυκή "blue-gray"), Latin Glauca, was a princess of Corinth as the daughter of King Creon.

Q269243.label: Triptolemus
Q269243.description: mythical promulgator of agriculture at Eleusis
Q269243.lead: Triptolemus, also known as Buzyges (Ancient Greek: Βουζύγης, romanized: Bouzýgēs, lit. 'Bull-hitcher'), was a hero of Eleusis in Greek mythology, central to the Eleusinian Mysteries and is worshipped as the inventor and patron of agriculture. Triptolemus is credited with being the first to sow seed for cultivation after being taught by Demeter and is credited for the use of oxen and the plough.

Q2714687.label: Eunomus
Q2714687.lead: Eunomus (Ancient Greek: Εὔνομος; reigned from c. 805 to c.

Q271850.label: Agesilaus II
Q271850.lead: Agesilaus II was king of Sparta from c. 400 to c.

Q271949.label: Procrustes
Q271949.description: son of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q271949.lead: In Greek mythology, Procrustes, also known as Prokoptas, Damastes (Δαμαστής, "subduer") or Polypemon, was a rogue smith and bandit from Attica who attacked people by stretching them or cutting off their legs, so as to force them to fit the size of an iron bed. The word Procrustean is thus used by analogy to describe, for example, situations where an arbitrary standard is used to measure success, while completely disregarding obvious harm that results from the effort.

Q272000.label: Deianira
Q272000.description: wife of Heracles in Greek mythology
Q272000.lead: Deianira, Deïanira, or Deianeira, also known as Dejanira, is a Calydonian princess in Greek mythology whose name translates as "man-destroyer" or "destroyer of her husband". She was the wife of Heracles and, in late Classical accounts, his unwitting murderer, killing him with the poisoned Shirt of Nessus.

Q272047.label: Endymion
Q272047.description: son of Aethlius in Greek mythology
Q272047.lead: In Greek mythology, Endymion was variously a handsome Aeolian shepherd, hunter, or king who was said to rule and live at Olympia in Elis. He was also venerated and said to reside on Mount Latmus in Caria, on the west coast of Asia Minor.

Q2723619.label: Agasthenes
Q2723619.description: son of Augeas, and his successor in the kingdom of Elis
Q2723619.lead: In Greek mythology, Agasthenes was the son of Augeas, and his successor in the kingdom of Elis. The government was shared between Amphimachus, Thalpius and Agasthenes.

Q273003.label: Simonides of Ceos
Q273003.lead: Simonides of Ceos was a Greek lyric poet, born in Ioulis on Ceos.

Q2754601.label: Cleone
Q2754601.lead: In Greek mythology, Cleone or Cleonai (Κλεωναὶ, Kleonai) was one of the daughters of the river-god Asopus and possibly Metope, the river-nymph daughter of the river Ladon. She was the sister of Pelasgus (Pelagon), Ismenus, Chalcis, Corcyra, Salamis, Sinope, Aegina, Peirene, Thebe, Tanagra, Thespia, Asopis, Ornea and Harpina.

Q27613.label: Cadmus
Q27613.description: mythological founder of Thebes, son of Agenor
Q27613.lead: In Greek mythology, Cadmus was the legendary founder of Boeotian Thebes. He was, alongside Perseus and Bellerophon, the greatest hero and slayer of monsters before the days of Heracles.

Q278711.label: Praxilla
Q278711.description: poet of the 5th century; there is very little surviving of her works
Q278711.lead: Praxilla, was a Greek lyric poet of the 5th century BC from Sicyon on the Gulf of Corinth. Five quotations attributed to Praxilla and three paraphrases from her poems survive.

Q27892928.label: Lyciscus
Q27892928.lead: Lyciscus, a Messenian, was descended from Aepytus. In the First Messenian War, the Messenians, having consulted the Delphic oracle, were told that to save their country, they must offer by night, to the gods below, an unstained virgin of the blood of the Aepytidae.

Q278930.label: Epeius
Q278930.description: mythical character, Achean soldier who built the Trojan Horse
Q278930.lead: Epeius or Epeus was a mythological Greek soldier during the Trojan War or, in some accounts, one of the Achaean Leaders, at the head of a contingent of 30 ships from the islands of the Cyclades. He was also the architect of the Wooden Horse, by means of which the Achaeans took Troy; he was himself among those warriors who hid inside it.

Q27949366.label: Megapenthes
Q27949366.description: figure in Greek mythology, son of Proetus, king of Argos
Q27949366.lead: In Greek mythology, Megapenthes was a king of Argos.

Q27999483.label: earth goddess
Q27999483.lead: This is a list of earth deities. An Earth god or Earth goddess is a deification of the Earth associated with a figure with chthonic or terrestrial attributes.

Q2803572.label: Tisamenus
Q2803572.lead: Tisamenus, in Greek mythology, was a son of Orestes and Hermione, daughter of Menelaus, or Erigone, daughter of Aegisthus who were first cousins twice over (their mothers were half-sisters and their fathers were brothers), so Tisamenus had only five great-grandparents, instead of the usual eight. Tisamenus succeeded his father to the thrones of Argos, Mycenae and Sparta.

Q28122362.label: Chloris
Q28122362.description: wife of Neleus and daughter of Amphion
Q28122362.lead: In Greek mythology, Chloris was a Minyan princess.

Q28126889.label: Periphetes
Q28126889.lead: In Greek mythology, Periphetes, also called Corynetes (Ancient Greek: Κορυνήτης, romanized: Korunḗtēs, lit. 'club-carrier'), is one of the several bandits encountered and defeated by the hero Theseus on his way to Athens. Periphetes would roam the roads and attack and rob travellers before killing them with his club.

Q281670.label: Pero
Q281670.description: Greek mythical figure, daughter of Neleus
Q281670.lead: In Greek mythology, Pero was a princess of Pylos.

Q28224981.label: Leches
Q28224981.description: mythical son of Poseidon, eponym of Lechaeum
Q28224981.lead: In Greek mythology, Leches or Lekhes was the mortal son of Peirene and Poseidon.

Q2861408.label: Aristion
Q2861408.lead: Aristion was a philosopher who became tyrant of Athens from c. 88 BC until he was executed in 86 BC. Aristion joined forces with King Mithridates VI of Pontus against Greece's overlords, the Romans, fighting alongside Pontic forces during the First Mithridatic War, but to no avail.

Q28626.label: Draco
Q28626.description: first legislator of Athens in Ancient Greece
Q28626.lead: Draco was the first legislator of Athens in Ancient Greece according to Athenian tradition and was active about 625 to 600 BC. He replaced the system of oral law and blood feud by the Draconian constitution, a written code to be enforced only by a court of law. His laws were supposed to have been very harsh, establishing the death penalty for most offenses.

Q287216.label: Telesilla
Q287216.description: late 6th century and early 5th century BC Greek poet
Q287216.lead: Telesilla was an ancient Greek lyric poet from Argos, active in the fifth century BC. She is known for her role in the defence of Argos in 494 BC. The historicity of this episode continues to be disputed. Only a few fragments of her poetry survive, several of which reference the gods Apollo and Artemis.

Q289276.label: Lysandra
Q289276.description: Ptolemaic princess, queen consort of Macedonia
Q289276.lead: Lysandra was a Queen of Macedonia, daughter of Ptolemy I Soter to Eurydice or Berenice. She was married first to her maternal cousin Alexander, one of the sons of Cassander, King of Macedonia.

Q2943528.label: Caystrus
Q2943528.lead: In Greek mythology, Cayster, also Causter or Caystrus, is a river god, deification of the river by the same name flowing in Lydia and Ionia (now called Küçük Menderes, in modern Turkey).

Q294840.label: Polycrates
Q294840.lead: Polycrates, son of Aeaces, was the tyrant of Samos from the 540s BC to 522 BC. He had a reputation as both a fierce warrior and an enlightened tyrant.

Q296325.label: Ctesias
Q296325.lead: Ctesias, also known as Ctesias of Cnidus, was a Greek physician and historian from the town of Cnidus in Caria, then part of the Achaemenid Empire.

Q296857.label: Mausolus
Q296857.description: Satrap of Caria from 377 BCE to 353 BCE
Q296857.lead: Mausolus was a ruler of Caria (377–353 BCE) and a satrap of the Achaemenid Empire. He enjoyed the status of king or dynast by virtue of the powerful position created by his father Hecatomnus (Carian: 𐊴𐊭𐊪𐊳𐊫 K̂tmño), who was the first satrap of Caria from the hereditary Hecatomnid dynasty.

Q29686726.label: Anthracia
Q29686726.lead: In Greek mythology, Anthracia was an Arcadian nymph. According to Pausanias, she was depicted holding a torch on a table at a temple in Megalopolis, alongside the nymphs Neda, Hagno, Anchiroe and Myrtoessa, and the young Zeus, with her presumably being shown as one of the nurses of the infant god.

Q297366.label: Eumenes
Q297366.lead: Eumenes was a Greek general, satrap, and successor of Alexander the Great. He participated in the Wars of Alexander the Great, serving as Alexander's personal secretary and later on as a battlefield commander.

Q29856413.label: Prosymna
Q29856413.lead: In Greek mythology, Prosymna was one of the Argive daughters of the river-god Asterion. She and her sisters, Acraea and Euboea, were the nurses of Hera.

Q298850.label: Alcman
Q298850.lead: Alcman was an Ancient Greek choral lyric poet from Sparta.

Q2993240.label: Phemonoe
Q2993240.lead: In Greek mythology, Phemonoe was a Greek poet of the ante-Homeric period. She was said to have been the daughter of Apollo, his first priestess at Delphi, or of his possible son Delphus, and the inventor of the hexameter verses, a type of poetic metre.

Q2993260.label: Echemus
Q2993260.description: son of Aeropus in Greek mythology
Q2993260.lead: In Greek mythology, Echemus was the Tegean king of Arcadia who succeeded Lycurgus. His name was derived from the Greek verb ἔχω (echō), meaning "to have, hold, or keep," combined with elements denoting posture or retention.

Q299387.label: Ptolemy Ceraunus
Q299387.lead: Ptolemy Ceraunus was a member of the Ptolemaic dynasty and briefly king of Macedon.

Q301219.label: Erechtheus
Q301219.lead: Erechtheus in Greek mythology was a king of Athens, the founder of the polis and, in his role as god, attached to Poseidon, as "Poseidon Erechtheus". The name Erichthonius is carried by a son of Erechtheus, but Plutarch conflated the two names in the myth of the begetting of Erechtheus.

Q3040215.label: Dryops
Q3040215.lead: In Greek mythology, Dryops was the eponym of the Dryopians.

Q304525.label: Caletor
Q304525.description: Greek mythological character, son of Clytius

Q305524.label: Abantidas
Q305524.description: Tyrant of the Greek city-state of Sicyon from 264 to 252 BC
Q305524.lead: Abantidas (died 252 BC), the son of Paseas, became tyrant of the ancient Greek city-state of Sicyon in 264 BC after murdering Cleinias, the father of Aratus. After the assassination, Abantidas had the remaining friends and relations of Cleinias banished or put to death.

Q305567.label: Abaris the Hyperborean
Q305567.description: semi-legendary Greek physician, magician, and prophet of Apollo
Q305567.lead: In Greek mythology, Abaris the Hyperborean, son of Seuthes (Σεύθης), was a legendary sage, healer, and priest of Apollo known to the Ancient Greeks. He was supposed to have learned his skills in his homeland of Hyperborea, which he fled during a plague.

Q305607.label: Abas
Q305607.lead: In Greek mythology, Abas was the twelfth king of Argos. He was the great-grandfather of Perseus, and the founder of the towns Abae and Argos Pelasgikon.

Q308398.label: Midas
Q308398.description: king with the power to turn whatever he touches to gold
Q308398.lead: Midas was a king of Phrygia with whom many myths became associated, as well as two later members of the Phrygian royal house. His father was Gordias, and his mother was Cybele.

Q308902.label: Victoria
Q308902.lead: In ancient Roman religion, Victoria or Victory is the deified personification of victory. She first appeared during the first Punic War, seemingly as a Romanised re-naming of Nike, the goddess of victory associated with Rome's Greek allies in the Greek mainland and in Magna Graecia.

Q309579.label: Scopas
Q309579.lead: Scopas was an ancient Greek sculptor and architect, most famous for his statue of Meleager, the copper statue of Aphrodite, and the head of goddess Hygieia, daughter of Asclepius.

Q3099662.label: Ismenias
Q3099662.lead: Ismenias was an ancient Theban politician of the 4th century BC, leader of the Theban democratic faction. He rose to power in 403 BC, a year after the end of the Peloponnesian War, and pursued an anti-Spartan policy, which included harboring exiles fleeing from the Thirty Tyrants in Athens.

Q311502.label: Ictinus
Q311502.lead: Ictinus was an architect active in the mid 5th century BC. Ancient sources identify Ictinus and Callicrates as co-architects of the Parthenon. He co-wrote a book on the project – which is now lost – in collaboration with Carpion.

Q311536.label: Aristomachus
Q311536.description: one of the Heracleidae, a great-grandson of Heracles

Q311742.label: Brasidas
Q311742.lead: Brasidas was a Spartan general and statesman and is considered to be the most distinguished Spartan commander of the first decade of the Peloponnesian War. He died during the Second Battle of Amphipolis while winning one of his most spectacular victories.

Q311835.label: Pittacus of Mytilene
Q311835.lead: Pittacus of Mytilene (Ancient Greek: Πιττακός; c. 650 – c.

Q312425.label: Berossus
Q312425.description: 3rd-century BC Babylonian writer, priest and astronomer
Q312425.lead: Berossus or Berosus was an early-3rd-century BC Hellenistic-era Babylonian writer, priest of Bel Marduk, and astronomer who wrote in the Koine Greek language. His original works, including the Babyloniaca (Ancient Greek: Βαβυλωνιακά), are lost, but fragments survive in some quotations, largely in the writings of the fourth-century AD early Christian writer Eusebius.

Q31256.label: Corinthos
Q31256.description: king of Corinth in Greek Mythology
Q31256.lead: In Greek mythology, Corinthus may refer to the following personages: Corinthus, the eponymous founder of the city of Corinth and the adjacent land. According to the local Corinthian tradition, he was a son of Zeus, but this tradition was not followed elsewhere.

Q312689.label: Nabis
Q312689.description: Last king of Sparta from 207 to 192 BC
Q312689.lead: Nabis was the last king of independent Sparta. He was probably a member of the Heracleidae, and he ruled from 207 BC to 192 BC, during the years of the First and Second Macedonian Wars and the "War against Nabis" named for being against him.

Q312893.label: Artaphernes
Q312893.description: late 6th/early 5th-century BC Persian general and satrap
Q312893.lead: Artaphernes was a brother of the Achaemenid king Darius I and held power circa 513–492 BC. He was appointed satrap of Lydia, which he governed from its capital of Sardis. As satrap of Lydia he had to deal with the Greeks, and played an important role in both the Siege of Naxos and in suppressing the Ionian Revolt.

Q31320071.label: Marmax
Q31320071.lead: In Greek mythology, Marmax was one of the suitors of Hippodameia, who was slain by Oenomaus, and was buried with his two horses, Parthenia and Eripha.

Q313467.label: Hippias
Q313467.description: Tyrant of Athens from 527 to 510 BC
Q313467.lead: Hippias was the last tyrant of Athens, ruling from 527 to 510 BC. He was one of the Peisistratids, a group of tyrants from the same family in ancient Greece. His father was Pisistratus, who preceded him as ruler of Athens, while his brother Hipparchus may have ruled jointly with him.

Q3136179.label: Hippotes
Q3136179.description: son of Mimas in Greek Mythology

Q314447.label: Hypereides
Q314447.lead: Hypereides or Hyperides was an Athenian logographer (speech writer).

Q314518.label: Pausanias
Q314518.description: Spartan general and regent (died c. 477 BC)
Q314518.lead: Pausanias was a Spartan regent and a general. In 479 BC, as a leader of the Hellenic League's combined land forces, he won a pivotal victory against the Achaemenid Empire in the Battle of Plataea.

Q3147753.label: Ida
Q3147753.lead: In Greek mythology, Ida or Ide was one of the nurses of the infant Zeus on Crete.

Q31537.label: Thurimachus
Q31537.description: king of Sicyon in Greek Mythology

Q31545.label: Thelxion
Q31545.lead: In Greek mythology, Thelxion is the name of two Greek mythological figures associated with a king named Apis. These two figures may be indistinct.

Q315822.label: Nicias
Q315822.description: 5th c. BCE Athenian politician and general, son of Niceratus
Q315822.lead: Nicias was an Athenian politician and general, who was prominent during the Peloponnesian War.

Q316059.label: Pelopidas
Q316059.lead: Pelopidas was an important Theban statesman and general in Greece, instrumental in establishing the mid-fourth century Theban hegemony.

Q316094.label: Tyrtaeus
Q316094.lead: Tyrtaeus was a Greek elegiac poet from Sparta whose works were speculated to fill five books.

Q316129.label: Mimnermus
Q316129.lead: Mimnermus was a Greek elegiac poet from either Colophon or Smyrna in Ionia, who flourished about 632–629 BC (i.e. in the 37th Olympiad, according to Suda).

Q317061.label: Phrynichus
Q317061.lead: Phrynichus, son of Polyphradmon and pupil of Thespis, was one of the earliest of the Greek tragedians. Some ancients regarded him as the real founder of tragedy.

Q317331.label: Aratus of Sicyon
Q317331.description: Greek statesman, general and Achaean League strategos (271-213 BC)
Q317331.lead: Aratus of Sicyon was a politician and military commander of Hellenistic Greece. He was elected strategos of the Achaean League 17 times, leading the League through numerous military campaigns including the Cleomenean War and the Social War.

Q319406.label: Epimenides of Crete
Q319406.description: 7th/6th-century BC Greek seer, philosopher, and poet
Q319406.lead: Epimenides of Crete was a semi-mythical 7th- or 6th-century BC Greek seer and philosopher-poet, from Knossos or Phaistos.

Q3200444.label: Harpina
Q3200444.description: Naiad nymph, daughter of Phliasian Asopus and Metrope
Q3200444.lead: In Greek mythology, Harpina was a daughter of Phliasian Asopus and of Metope.

Q320449.label: Alcestis
Q320449.description: daughter of Pelias in Greek mythology
Q320449.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcestis or Alceste, was a princess of Iolcus known for her love of her husband. Her life story was described by Pseudo-Apollodorus in his Bibliotheca, and a version of her death and return from the dead was also popularized by Euripides' tragedy Alcestis.

Q320660.label: Chrysaor
Q320660.lead: In Greek mythology, Chrysaor was the brother of the winged horse Pegasus, often depicted as a young man, the son of Poseidon and Medusa, born when Perseus decapitated the Gorgon Medusa.

Q320830.label: Abia
Q320830.lead: In Greek mythology, Abia served as the nursemaid of Hyllus, the son of Heracles and Deianira. In some translations, the child she nursed is referred to as Glenus.

Q32133.label: Lysimachus
Q32133.description: Macedonian officer, one of Alexander's successor kings
Q32133.lead: Lysimachus was a Thessalian officer and successor of Alexander the Great who became king of Thrace in 306 BC, western Asia Minor in 301 BC and Macedon in 288 BC. Born into a Thessalian noble family, Lysimachus was one of Alexander's immediate bodyguards and accompanied him in his Persian and Indian campaigns.

Q321541.label: Meleager
Q321541.description: son of Oeneus in Greek mythology, king of Calydon
Q321541.lead: Meleager was a hero in Greek mythology, venerated in his temenos at Calydon in Aetolia. He was famed as the host of the Calydonian boar hunt in the epic tradition that was reworked by Homer, and was also mentioned as one of the Argonauts.

Q322639.label: Neoptolemus
Q322639.lead: In Greek mythology, Neoptolemus, originally called Pyrrhus at birth (Πύρρος, Pýrrhos, 'red'), was the son of the mythical warrior Achilles and the princess Deidamia, and the brother of Oneiros. He became the progenitor of the ruling dynasty of the Molossians of ancient Epirus.

Q323430.label: Leochares
Q323430.lead: Leochares was an ancient Greek sculptor from Athens, who lived in the 4th century BC.

Q326269.label: Mnesitheus
Q326269.lead: Mnesitheus of Athens, was a Greek physician, who probably lived in the 4th century BC, as he is quoted by the comic poet Alexis. He belonged to the Dogmatic school of medicine.

Q328354.label: Hippodamia
Q328354.description: Greek mythical character, daughter of Oenomaus and wife of Pelops
Q328354.lead: Hippodamia was a Greek mythological figure, the daughter of Oenomaus. She was the queen of Pisa, Greece and the wife of Pelops, appearing with Pelops at a potential cult site in Ancient Olympia.

Q328793.label: Periander
Q328793.lead: Periander was the second tyrant of the Cypselid dynasty that ruled over ancient Corinth.

Q328853.label: Apollodorus of Acharnae
Q328853.lead: Apollodorus of Acharnae in Attica was an Athenian politician known from several ancient forensic speeches which were preserved as part of the Demosthenic corpus. He was the son of Pasion, a wealthy banker who had been granted Athenian citizenship in thanks for the gifts he had made to the city of Athens.

Q3291388.label: Timandra
Q3291388.description: Greek mythological character, daughter of Leda and Tyndareus
Q3291388.lead: In Greek mythology, Timandra was a Spartan princess and later queen of Arcadia. Her name is derived from two ancient Greek root words: timē (meaning honor or respect) and aner or andros (meaning man).

Q330584.label: Amphiaraus
Q330584.lead: Amphiaraus or Amphiaraos was in Greek mythology the son of Oicles, a seer, and one of the leaders of the Seven against Thebes. Amphiaraus at first refused to go with Adrastus on this expedition against Thebes as he foresaw the death of everyone who joined the expedition.

Q331327.label: Telamon
Q331327.description: one of the Argonauts of Jason, in Greek mythology
Q331327.lead: Telamon in Greek mythology was the son of King Aeacus of Aegina, and Endeïs, a mountain nymph. The elder brother of Peleus, Telamon sailed alongside Jason as one of his Argonauts, and was present at the hunt for the Calydonian Boar.

Q331602.label: Abrupolis
Q331602.description: 2nd-century BC king of the Thracian Sapaei
Q331602.lead: Abrupolis (fl. 2nd century BC) was a king of the Thracian Sapaei, and ally of the Romans.

Q332324.label: Laomedon
Q332324.lead: In Greek mythology, Laomedon was a Trojan king, son of Ilus and thus nephew of Ganymede and Assaracus. Laomedon was variously identified with different parents and siblings, as well as numerous children, including Priam and Tithonus.

Q334235.label: Callinus
Q334235.lead: Callinus (Ancient Greek: Καλλῖνος, Kallinos; fl. mid-7th c.

Q334478.label: Demaratus
Q334478.description: Eurypontid king of Sparta from c.515 to 491 BC
Q334478.lead: Demaratus was a king of Sparta from around 515 BC to 491 BC. He was the 15th ruler of the Eurypontid dynasty and the firstborn son of King Ariston. During his reign, Demaratus is best known for his opposition to his co-ruler, King Cleomenes I of the Agiad dynasty.

Q334817.label: Polynices
Q334817.lead: In Greek mythology, Polynices (also Polyneices) was the son of Oedipus and either Jocasta or Euryganeia, and the brother of Eteocles, Antigone, and Ismene. When Oedipus discovered that he had killed his father and married his mother, he blinded himself and left Thebes, leaving Polynices and Eteocles to rule jointly.

Q3357641.label: Othryades
Q3357641.lead: Othryades and Othryadas (Ancient Greek: Ὀθρυάδας) was the last surviving Spartan of the 300 Spartans selected to fight against 300 Argives in the Battle of the 300 Champions. Ashamed by surviving his comrades, he committed suicide on the field following the battle.

Q336428.label: Hellen
Q336428.lead: In Greek mythology, Hellen is the eponymous progenitor of the Hellenes. He is the son of Deucalion (or Zeus) and Pyrrha, and the father of three sons, Dorus, Xuthus, and Aeolus.

Q3365.label: Antiochus III the Great
Q3365.lead: Antiochus III the Great was the sixth ruler of the Seleucid Empire, reigning from 223 BC to 187 BC. Ascending to the throne at the age of eighteen, Antiochus inherited an empire in turmoil after the death of his brother, Seleucus III Ceraunus.

Q338201.label: Hippolytus
Q338201.description: son of Theseus in Greek mythology
Q338201.lead: Hippolytus in Greek mythology is the son of Theseus and an Amazon, either Hippolyta or Antiope. His downfall at the hands of Aphrodite is recounted by the playwright Euripides.

Q338948.label: Milo of Croton
Q338948.description: 6th-century BC wrestler from the Magna Graecian city of Croton
Q338948.lead: Milo or Milon of Croton was a famous ancient Greek athlete from Croton, which is today in the Magna Graecia region of southern Italy. Milo was a six-time winner at the Olympics, once for boys' wrestling in 540 BC at the 60th Olympics and later five times for wrestling at the 62nd to 66th Olympics.

Q34041.label: Icarus
Q34041.description: Greek mythological figure, son of Daedalus
Q34041.lead: In Greek mythology, Icarus was the son of the master craftsman Daedalus, the architect of the labyrinth of Crete, and his wife Naucrate.
