After Theseus, king of Athens and enemy of King Minos, escaped from the labyrinth, Minos suspected that Icarus and Daedalus had revealed the labyrinth's secrets and thus imprisoned the two, either in a large tower overlooking the ocean or in the labyrinth itself, depending upon the account.

Q3411223.label: Pylas
Q3411223.lead: In Greek mythology, Pylas, also called Pylon or Pylos, was a king of Megara and successor of his father Cteson, son of Lelex.

Q34201.label: Zeus
Q34201.description: Greek god of the sky and king of the gods
Q34201.lead: Zeus is the supreme deity of the Greek pantheon. He is a sky and thunder god in ancient Greek religion and mythology, who rules as king of the gods on Mount Olympus.

Q342279.label: Hippocoon
Q342279.description: king of Sparta, son of Oebalus
Q342279.lead: In Greek mythology, Hippocoön was a Spartan king.

Q342343.label: Perieres
Q342343.lead: In Greek mythology, Perieres was the 'overbold' king of Messene, an ancient polis in southern Peloponnese.

Q347164.label: Leonnatus
Q347164.lead: Leonnatus was a Macedonian officer of Alexander the Great and one of the diadochi.

Q348668.label: Acamas
Q348668.lead: In Greek mythology, Acamas or Akamas was a hero in the Trojan War.

Q3514925.label: Tanagra
Q3514925.lead: In Greek mythology, Tanagra was a naiad or nymph and the namesake of the ancient city of Tanagra in Boeotia, Greece. She was of such great beauty that both the god of war Ares and the god of thieves, Hermes fell for her.

Q354403.label: Thrasybulus
Q354403.lead: Thrasybulus was a Greek general and democratic leader.

Q354424.label: Iphicrates
Q354424.lead: Iphicrates (c. 418 – c. 353 BC) was an Athenian general, who flourished in the earlier half of the 4th century BC. He is credited with important infantry reforms that revolutionized ancient Greek warfare by regularizing light-armed peltasts. Cornelius Nepos wrote that Iphicrates was such a leader, that he was not only comparable to the first commanders of his own time, but no one even of the older generals could be set above him.

Q35500.label: Aphrodite
Q35500.description: Greek goddess of love, beauty, pleasure, and procreation
Q35500.lead: Aphrodite is an ancient Greek goddess associated with love and beauty. Aphrodite's main cult centers were Cythera, Cyprus, Corinth, and Athens.

Q3555328.label: Acichorius
Q3555328.lead: Acichorius was one of the leaders of the Gauls, who invaded Thrace and Macedonia in 280 BC. He and Brennus commanded the division that marched into Paionia. In the following year, 279, he accompanied Brennus in his invasion of Greece.

Q355727.label: Tissaphernes
Q355727.description: Persian Satrap of Lydia and Ionia (445–395 BC)
Q355727.lead: Tissaphernes was a Persian commander and statesman, satrap of Lydia and Ionia. His life is mostly known from the works of Thucydides and Xenophon.

Q3560453.label: Argyra
Q3560453.description: Greek nymph, one of the Naiads
Q3560453.lead: In Greek mythology, Argyra was one of the Naiads, a nymph who lived in a well. There was a city in ancient Achaea, also named Argyra, that was the site of a spring.

Q3563956.label: Preugenes
Q3563956.lead: Preugenes was a mythical king of Achaea in Greece. He was a descendant of King Lacedaemon of Sparta, and the son of Agenor.

Q3564602.label: Andropompus
Q3564602.description: Greek mythology character, father of King Melanthus
Q3564602.lead: In Greek mythology, Andropompus was one of the descendants of Neleus, king of Thessaly, as son of Penthilus and Anchirhoe. He was the father of King Melanthus of Athens.

Q3565120.label: Telete
Q3565120.lead: In Greek mythology, Telete is the daughter of the wine-god Dionysus and Nicaea, a Naiad daughter of the river-god Sangarius and Cybele, a mother goddess.

Q3565937.label: Selinus
Q3565937.lead: In Greek mythology, Selinus was a native king of Aegalea (Ἀιγάλεια Aigáleia) in Achaea. The kingdom which used to exist is located in the present-day Aigio.

Q3606663.label: Hagno
Q3606663.lead: In Greek mythology, Hagno was the Arcadian nymph who together with other nymphs, Neda, Anthracia, Anchirhoe and Myrtoessa, were nurses of the god Zeus. She was depicted to have a water-pot in one hand and a bowl in the other.

Q3608994.label: Alcimedon
Q3608994.description: mythological Greek character, son of Laerkes
Q3608994.lead: Alcimedonte or Alcimedon is a character from Greek mythology. He was the son of Laerces and one of the five leaders of the Myrmidons in the contingent led by Achilles during the Trojan War, mentioned by Homer in the Iliad, Books XVI and XVII. When the combat to the death between Patroclus, who was wearing Achilles' armor, and Hector ended with Hector's victory, Alcimedonte took over Achilles' chariot, drawn by the immortal horses Xanthus and Balius, as he was described as an excellent charioteer.

Q3618450.label: Anthas
Q3618450.description: son of Poseidon and Alcyone in Greek mythology
Q3618450.lead: In Greek mythology, Anthas or Anthes was a son of Poseidon and Alcyone, and brother of Hyperes. The brothers were eponymous founders and first kings of the cities Hyperea and Anthea in a region they reigned over; later on these two cities were merged into the historical Troezen.

Q3618680.label: Antiphemus
Q3618680.lead: Antiphemus was a man from ancient Greece from Rhodes who was the founder of Gela, around 690 BCE. The colony was composed of Rhodians and Cretans, the latter led by Entimus the Cretan, the former chiefly from Lindus, and to this town Antiphemus himself belonged. From the Etymologicum Magnum and Aristaenetus in Stephanus of Byzantium it appears the tale ran that Antiphemus and his brother Lacius, the founder of Phaselis, were, when at Delphi, suddenly bid to go forth, one eastward, one westward; and from his laughing at the unexpected response, the city took its name.

Q362068.label: Andriscus
Q362068.lead: Andriscus, also often referenced as Pseudo-Philip, was a Greek pretender who became the last independent king of Macedon in 149 BC as Philip VI (Ancient Greek: Φίλιππος, Philipos), based on his claim of being Philip, a now-obscure son of the last legitimate Macedonian king, Perseus.

Q3621412.label: Archander
Q3621412.lead: Archander was a son of Achaeus and brother of Architeles. Together with his brother he carried on a war against the king Lamedon.

Q3621840.label: Ardalus
Q3621840.lead: Ardalus was, in Greek mythology, a son of the god Hephaestus who was said to have invented the flute, and to have built a sanctuary of the Muses at Troezen, who derived from him the surname Ardalides or Ardaliotides. This story is recorded in the works of Pausanias, and in some obscure fragments of Hesychius of Alexandria.

Q3621995.label: Nomia
Q3621995.lead: In Greek mythology, Nomia was a nymph of Arcadia, where the local people believed the Nomian Mountains to have been named after her.

Q3622659.label: Aristias
Q3622659.lead: Aristias, son of Pratinas, was a dramatic poet of ancient Greece whose tomb Pausanias saw at Phlius, and whose satyric dramas, with those of his father, were considered to be surpassed only by those of Aeschylus. Aristias is mentioned in the life of Sophocles as one of the poets with whom the latter contended.

Q3624035.label: Phlias
Q3624035.description: Greek mythical character, father of Dameon
Q3624035.lead: Phlias or Phlius or Phliasus was the son of Dionysus and Ariadne, and husband of Chthonophyle in Greek mythology. A native of Araithyrea in Argolis, he is mentioned as one of the Argonauts.

Q36303.label: Thales
Q36303.lead: Thales of Miletus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Miletus in Ionia, Asia Minor. Thales was one of the Seven Sages, founding figures of Ancient Greece.

Q3636218.label: Baton
Q3636218.lead: Baton is a character from Greek mythology. He was said to have been the charioteer of the hero Amphiaraus, and that both belonged to the house of the legendary seer Melampus.

Q363832.label: Conon
Q363832.lead: Conon (before 443 BC – c. 389 BC) was an Athenian general at the end of the Peloponnesian War, who led the Athenian naval forces when they were defeated by a Peloponnesian fleet in the crucial Battle of Aegospotami; later he contributed significantly to the restoration of Athens' political and military power.

Q364492.label: Callimachus
Q364492.description: Athenian polemarch at Battle of Marathon in 490 BC
Q364492.lead: Callimachus was the Athenian polemarch at the Battle of Marathon, which took place during 490 BC. According to Herodotus, he was from the Attica deme of Aphidna.

Q36456.label: Hannibal
Q36456.lead: Hannibal was a Carthaginian general and statesman who commanded the forces of Carthage in their battle against the Roman Republic during the Second Punic War. Hannibal lived during a period of great tension in the Mediterranean Basin, triggered by the emergence of the Roman Republic as a great power with its defeat of Carthage in the First Punic War.

Q3646522.label: Buphagus
Q3646522.lead: In Greek mythology, Buphagus, son of Iapetus and Thornax, was an Arcadian hero and husband of Promne. He received the wounded Iphicles, the brother of Heracles, into his house, and took care of him until he died.

Q366117.label: Philopoemen
Q366117.lead: Philopoemen was a skilled Greek general and statesman, who was Achaean strategos on eight occasions. From the time he was appointed as strategos in 209 BC, Philopoemen helped turn the Achaean League into an important military power in Greece.

Q3664982.label: Ceramus
Q3664982.description: mythical figure, gave name to Cerameicus

Q3676567.label: Cydon
Q3676567.description: son of Tegeates in Greek mythology

Q3680531.label: Cleostratus
Q3680531.lead: In Greek mythology, Cleostratus is a teenage boy from Thespiae, a town in Boeotia, who is chosen to be offered to a dragon in a yearly sacrifice to the monster, until he is saved by his lover Menestratus. His and Menestratus's myth is known thanks to the Description of Greece, a second-century work by Greek traveller and geographer Pausanias.

Q3680855.label: Clitor
Q3680855.description: son of Arcas and king in Arcadia

Q3681782.label: Cnageus
Q3681782.description: mythical Spartan, founder of Artemis cult

Q3697283.label: Chrysanthis
Q3697283.lead: In Greek mythology, Chrysanthis was a female figure associated with the goddess Demeter.

Q3698275.label: Crocon
Q3698275.lead: In Greek mythology, Crocon was the husband of Saesara, daughter of Celeus of Eleusis. This couple became the parents of Meganeira, mother of Apheidas and Elatus by Arcas, son of Zeus and Callisto.

Q3699000.label: Cteatus
Q3699000.description: son of Actor son of Phorbas in Greek mythology

Q3706015.label: Dexamenus
Q3706015.description: mythical king of Olenus in Achaea

Q371564.label: Pleistoanax
Q371564.description: 5th century BC Agiad King of Sparta
Q371564.lead: Pleistoanax, also spelled Plistoanax, was Agiad king of Sparta from 458 to 409 BC. He was the leader of the peace party in Sparta at a time of violent confrontations against Athens for the hegemony over Greece. The son of Pausanias, Pleistoanax was still a minor in 458 BC, so his uncle Nicomedes acted as regent.

Q3726853.label: Epidaurus
Q3726853.description: son of Apollo in Greek mythology
Q3726853.lead: In Greek mythology, Epidaurus was the presumed eponym of the polis Epidaurus. His parentage varies from one local version of the myth to another: the Argive version gives him as the son of Argus (himself son of Zeus) and Evadne; people of Elis believed him to be a son of Pelops; finally, the Epidaurians themselves considered him to be a son of Apollo.

Q37340.label: Apollo
Q37340.description: god in Greek and later Roman mythology
Q37340.lead: Apollo is one of the Olympian deities in ancient Greek religion and mythology. His numerous functions include light, healing, prophecy, music, poetry, and archery.

Q373685.label: Lycurgus of Athens
Q373685.description: 4th century BCE Greek politician and orator
Q373685.lead: Lycurgus (Ancient Greek: Λυκοῦργος Λυκόφρονος Βουτάδης, romanized: Lykourgos Lykophronos Boutadēs; c. 390 – c.

Q3738300.label: Phaenna
Q3738300.description: one of the Graces in Greek mythology
Q3738300.lead: In Greek mythology, Phaenna was one of the Charites (the Graces). She was worshipped in Laconia, the region in ancient Greece where Sparta was located.

Q3744925.label: Phylas
Q3744925.description: in Greek mythology, king of the Dryopes

Q3748280.label: Phormis
Q3748280.description: one of the originators of ancient Greek comedy

Q377669.label: Adristas
Q377669.description: inventor of weaving in Greek mythology

Q379828.label: Penthesilea
Q379828.description: Amazonian queen in Greek mythology, daughter of Ares and Otrera
Q379828.lead: Penthesilea was an Amazonian queen in Greek mythology, the daughter of Ares and Otrera and the sister of Hippolyta, Antiope, and Melanippe. She assisted Troy in the Trojan War, during which she was killed by Achilles or Neoptolemus.

Q379863.label: Hystaspes
Q379863.description: 6th century BC Persian strap of Bactria and Persis
Q379863.lead: Hystaspes or Guštāsp (Persian: گشتاسپ Guštāsp) (fl. 550 BC), was a Persian satrap of Bactria and Persis.

Q38012.label: Hera
Q38012.description: Greek goddess, wife and sister of Zeus
Q38012.lead: In ancient Greek religion, Hera is the goddess of marriage, women, and family, and the protector of women during childbirth. In Greek mythology, she is queen among the twelve Olympians on Mount Olympus, sister and wife of Zeus, and daughter of the Titans Cronus and Rhea.

Q380401.label: Xanthippus
Q380401.description: Athenian politician and father of Pericles (c.525–475 BC)
Q380401.lead: Xanthippus was a wealthy Athenian politician and general during the Greco-Persian Wars.

Q3804539.label: Ithome
Q3804539.description: nymph in Greek mythology, nurse of Zeus
Q3804539.lead: In Greek mythology, Ithome was a Messenian nymph and one of the nurses of the child Zeus.

Q381931.label: Aethlius
Q381931.description: son of Zeus in Greek mythology
Q381931.lead: Aethlius or Aithlios or Aethnos was, in Greek mythology, the first king of Elis.

Q3827232.label: Las
Q3827232.description: mythical founder of Las in Lakonia, Greece
Q3827232.lead: Las was regarded by the inhabitants of the town of Las in Laconia as the founder of their city. His tomb, surmounted by a statue, was located at a place called Arainus near the town of Las.

Q3832028.label: Lycorus
Q3832028.description: mythical son of Apollo and Corycia

Q38366.label: Apis
Q38366.description: king of Sicyon in Greek Mythology
Q38366.lead: In Greek mythology, Apis was the fourth king of Sicyon who reigned for 25 years.

Q3874208.label: Neaera
Q3874208.description: mythological Greek character, daughter of Pereus

Q3889357.label: Palamaon
Q3889357.description: son of Metion in Greek mythology

Q3893378.label: Panopeus
Q3893378.description: son of Phocus in Greek mythology
Q3893378.lead: In Greek mythology, Panopeus was a son of Phocus by Asteria or Asterodia, and twin brother of Crisus. The two brothers were so inimical towards each other that they began fighting while still in their mother's womb, just like Proetus and Acrisius did.

Q3899772.label: Pereus
Q3899772.lead: In Greek mythology, Pereus was an Arcadian prince as the son of King Elatus and Laodice, daughter of King Cinyras. He had four brothers namely, Stymphalus, Aepytus, Ischys and Cyllen.

Q390448.label: Aganippe
Q390448.description: nymph of a spring near Mt. Helicon
Q390448.lead: In Greek mythology, Aganippe was the name of both a spring and the Naiad (a Crinaea) associated with it. The spring is in Boeotia, near Thespiae, at the base of Mount Helicon, and was associated with the Muses who were sometimes called Aganippides.

Q390492.label: Agapenor
Q390492.description: son of Ancaeus in Greek mythology
Q390492.lead: In Greek mythology, Agapenor was a leader of the Arcadians in the Trojan War.

Q390789.label: Alalcomenia
Q390789.description: daughter of King Ogyges in Greek mythology
Q390789.lead: Alalcomenia was, in Greek mythology, one of the daughters of Ogyges and the eponym of Alalcomenae. She and her two sisters, Thelxionoea and Aulis, were regarded as supernatural beings who watched over oaths and saw that they were not taken rashly or thoughtlessly.

Q391091.label: Pentheus
Q391091.description: mythical king of Thebes, son of Echion and Agave
Q391091.lead: In Greek mythology, Pentheus was a king of Thebes. His father was Echion, the wisest of the Spartoi.

Q391379.label: Achelous
Q391379.lead: Achelous (also Acheloos or Acheloios) was the god in ancient Greek religion and mythology associated with the Achelous River, the largest river in Greece. According to Hesiod, he was the son of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys.

Q391454.label: Agathocles
Q391454.description: son of Lysimachus, general in Thrace
Q391454.lead: Agathocles was a prince of Macedonian and Thessalian descent. He was the son of Lysimachus and his first wife, Nicaea a daughter of Antipater, the regent of Alexander the Great's Empire.

Q392120.label: Agdistis
Q392120.description: deity of Greek, Roman and Anatolian mythology
Q392120.lead: Agdistis is a deity of Greek, Roman, and Anatolian mythology who was a hermaphrodite, having been born with both male and female reproductive organs. The deity was closely associated with the Phrygian goddess Cybele.

Q392435.label: Aristaeus
Q392435.lead: Aristaeus was the mythological culture hero credited with the discovery of many rural useful arts and handicrafts, including beekeeping. He was the son of the huntress Cyrene and Apollo.

Q392631.label: Agenor
Q392631.description: mythical Phoenician king, father of Cadmus
Q392631.lead: Agenor was in Greek mythology and history a Phoenician king of Tyre or Sidon. The Greek historian Herodotus (c.

Q393058.label: Agesipolis
Q393058.description: son of Cleombrotus II of Sparta

Q393261.label: Cyrene
Q393261.description: nymph, mother of Aristaeus by Apollo
Q393261.lead: In Greek mythology, Cyrene, also spelled Kyrene, was the etymon of the Greek colony of Cyrene, Libya. She was said to have been a Thessalian princess and huntress who became the queen regnant of Cyrene, founded and named in her honor by the god Apollo.

Q39503.label: Artemis
Q39503.description: goddess of the hunt and the wild in ancient Greek religion and mythology
Q39503.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Artemis is the goddess of hunting, the wilderness, wild animals, transitions, nature, vegetation, childbirth, care of children, and chastity. She was often said to roam the forests and mountains, attended by an entourage of nymphs.

Q3951778.label: Scephrus
Q3951778.description: son of Tegeates in Greek mythology

Q395236.label: Agon
Q395236.description: personification of Struggle/Contest in ancient Greece

Q395404.label: Agoracritus
Q395404.lead: Agoracritus was a famous sculptor in ancient Greece.

Q39576.label: Ptolemy II Philadelphus
Q39576.description: king of the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt (308–246 B.C.)
Q39576.lead: Ptolemy II Philadelphus was the pharaoh and basileus of the Ptolemaic Kingdom from 284 to 246 BC. He was the son of Ptolemy I, the Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who founded the Ptolemaic Kingdom after the death of Alexander, and Queen Berenice I, originally from Macedon. During Ptolemy II's reign, the material and literary splendour of the Alexandrian court was at its height.

Q3963012.label: Smilis
Q3963012.description: ancient Greek sculptor, son of Eucleides
Q3963012.lead: Smilis, was a legendary ancient Greek sculptor, the contemporary of Daedalus, whose name was associated with the archaic cult figure at the Heraion of Samos. Smilis was born on the island of Aegina and his father was named Euclides.

Q3965190.label: Sostratus of Pellene
Q3965190.lead: Sostratus was an Ancient Greek athlete from Pellene, Achaea. He won the footrace for boys at the Ancient Olympic Games.

Q396862.label: Agrius
Q396862.lead: In Greek mythology, Agrius was the son of the Calydonian king Porthaon and Euryte, and the brother of Oeneus, Alcathous, Melas, Leucopeus, and Sterope.

Q3973090.label: Sthenelaidas
Q3973090.lead: Sthenelaidas was a Spartan who held the office of ephor in 432 BC. He is best known for having spoken in favour of initiating the Peloponnesian War against Athens.

Q3982573.label: Tegeates
Q3982573.description: mythological Greek figure, son of Lycaon
Q3982573.lead: In Greek mythology, Tegeates was an Arcadian prince as son of King Lycaon, and the reputed eponymous founder and of Tegea.

Q3984506.label: Thero
Q3984506.description: daughter of Phylas and Leipephilene, and sister of Hippotes

Q4058052.label: Aeropus
Q4058052.description: mythical son of Ares and Aerope

Q4063102.label: Althepus
Q4063102.description: son of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q4063102.lead: In Greek mythology, Althepus was a king of Troezen. Althepia named after him.

Q40730.label: Demeter
Q40730.description: Greek goddess of the harvest, grains, and agriculture
Q40730.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Demeter is the Olympian goddess of the harvest and agriculture, presiding over crops, grains, food, and the fertility of the earth. Although Demeter is mostly known as a grain goddess, she also appeared as a goddess of health, birth, and marriage, and had connections to the Underworld.

Q40901.label: Ares
Q40901.description: Greek god of war and combat
Q40901.lead: Ares is the Greek god of war and courage. He is one of the Twelve Olympians, and the son of Zeus and Hera.

Q40939.label: Aeschylus
Q40939.lead: Aeschylus was an ancient Greek tragedian, often described as the father of tragedy. Academic knowledge of the genre begins with his work, and understanding of earlier Greek tragedy is largely based on inferences made from reading his surviving plays.

Q410748.label: Aetolus
Q410748.lead: Aetolus was, in Greek mythology, a son of Endymion, great-great-grandson of Deucalion, and a Naiad nymph (Neis), or Iphianassa.

Q41127.label: Poseidon
Q41127.description: one of the twelve Olympians presiding over the sea, storms, earthquakes and horses
Q41127.lead: Poseidon is one of the twelve Olympians in ancient Greek religion and mythology, presiding over the sea, storms, earthquakes and horses. He was the protector of seafarers and the guardian of many Hellenic cities and colonies.

Q41328.label: Datis
Q41328.description: early 5th-century BC Median/Persian noble and admiral
Q41328.lead: Datis or Datus was a Median noble and admiral who served the Persian Empire during the reign of Darius the Great (522–486 BC). He is known for his role in leading the Persian amphibious expedition against Greece in 490 BC during the Greco-Persian Wars.

Q41484.label: Hermes
Q41484.description: Olympian god in Greek religion and mythology; the emissary and messenger of the gods; the god of trade, heraldry, merchants, commerce, roads, thieves, trickery, sports, travelers, and athletes; the son of Zeus and the Pleiad Maia
Q41484.lead: Hermes is an Olympian deity in ancient Greek religion and mythology considered the herald of the gods. He is also widely considered the protector of human heralds, travelers, thieves, merchants, and orators.

Q415491.label: Acacus
Q415491.lead: Acacus, in Greek mythology, was a king of Acacesium (Ἀκακήσιον) in Arcadia. He was one of the 50 sons of the impious King Lycaon either by the naiad Cyllene, Nonacris or by unknown woman.

Q4157689.label: Demos
Q4157689.description: Greek deity, personification of the People

Q4162118.label: Dysaules
Q4162118.description: mythical importer of the Eleusinian mysteries to Phlius

Q416384.label: Acastus
Q416384.lead: Acastus is a character in Greek mythology. He sailed with Jason and the Argonauts, and participated in the hunt for the Calydonian Boar.

Q41680.label: Dionysus
Q41680.description: ancient Greek god of winemaking and wine
Q41680.lead: In ancient Greek religion and myth, Dionysus is the god of wine-making, orchards, fruit, vegetation, fertility, festivity, insanity, ritual madness, religious ecstasy, and theatre. He was also known as Bacchus (Ancient Greek: Βάκχος Bacchos) by the Greeks (a name later adopted by the Romans) for a frenzy he is said to induce called baccheia.

Q41683.label: Thucydides
Q41683.lead: Thucydides was an Athenian historian and general. His History of the Peloponnesian War recounts the 5th century BC war between Sparta and Athens until the year 411 BC. Thucydides has been dubbed the father of "scientific history" by those who accept his claims to have applied strict standards of impartiality and evidence-gathering and analysis of cause and effect, without reference to intervention by the gods, as outlined in his introduction to his work.

Q41746.label: Achilles
Q41746.description: Greek mythological hero of the Trojan War
Q41746.lead: In Greek mythology, Achilles or Achilleus (Ancient Greek: Ἀχιλλεύς, romanized: Achilleús) was a hero of the Trojan War who was known as being the greatest of all the Greek warriors. The central character in Homer's Iliad, he was the son of the Nereid Thetis and Peleus, king of Phthia and famous Argonaut.

Q4187165.label: Zarex
Q4187165.description: son of Carystus in Greek mythology
Q4187165.lead: Zarex or Zarax (Ζάραξ) is the name of a hero of ancient Greek mythology, son of Carystus (Carycus) or by the latter's son Petraeus.

Q4200286.label: Immaradus
Q4200286.description: son of Eumolpus in Greek mythology
Q4200286.lead: In Greek mythology, Immaradus is a Thracian prince as the son of King Eumolpus of Thrace and the Oceanid nymph Daeira.

Q4202635.label: Iodame
Q4202635.description: daughter of Itonus in Greek mythology
Q4202635.lead: In Greek mythology, Iodame or Iodama was a Thessalian princess as the daughter of King Itonus of Iton in Phthiotis. She was the granddaughter of Amphictyon.

Q4205332.label: Itonus
Q4205332.lead: In Greek mythology, Itonus, also Itonius, may refer to two individuals: Itonus, king of Iton in Phthiotis and son of Amphictyon. He was married to Melanippe, a nymph, and had a son Boeotus and two daughters, Chromia and Iodame.

Q421184.label: Acrotatus
Q421184.description: Agiad King of Sparta from 265 to 262 BC
Q421184.lead: Acrotatus II was an Agiad King of Sparta from 265 to 262 BC. He was the son of Areus I, and grandson of Acrotatus I. He had unlawful intercourse with Chilonis, the young wife of Cleonymus, uncle of his father Areus. It was this, together with the disappointment of not obtaining the throne, which led Cleonymus to invite Pyrrhus to Sparta in 272.

Q421808.label: Actaeus
Q421808.description: Greek mythical character, first king of Attica
Q421808.lead: In Greek mythology, Actaeus, also called Actaeon, was the first king of Attica, according to Pausanias.

Q4218933.label: Ceyx
Q4218933.lead: In Greek mythology, Ceyx was a king of Trachis in Thessaly.

Q4233066.label: Corybas
Q4233066.lead: In Greek mythology, Corybas is the son of Iasion and the goddess Cybele, who gave his name to the Corybantes (Koribantes), or dancing priests of Phrygia. The Korybantes were associated with Orpheus, another son of Apollo and a Mousa, founder of the closely related Orphic Mysteries.

Q423894.label: Acusilaus
Q423894.lead: Acusilaus, Acusilas, Acousileos, or Akousilaos of Argos, son of Cabas or Scabras, was a Greek logographer and mythographer who lived in the latter half of the 6th century BC but whose work survives only in fragments and summaries of individual points. He is one of the authors (= FGrHist 2) whose fragments were collected in Felix Jacoby's Die Fragmente der griechischen Historiker.

Q4259170.label: Lepreus
Q4259170.description: mythical son of Pyrgeus or Poseidon and Astydameia
Q4259170.lead: In Greek mythology, Lepreus was a son of Caucon (Glaucon) or Pyrgeus, and grandson of Poseidon; one account calls him a son of Poseidon. His mother was Astydameia, daughter of Phorbas.

Q426788.label: Tenes
Q426788.lead: In Greek mythology, Tenes or Tennes was the eponymous hero of the island of Tenedos.

Q4300425.label: Molione
Q4300425.description: Mythological character, mother of the Moliones
Q4300425.lead: In Greek mythology, Molione or Moline (Μολίνη) was a member of the Aetolian royal family.

Q430157.label: Eryx
Q430157.description: in Greek mythology, king of the city Eryx in Sicily

Q430688.label: Cypselus
Q430688.description: first tyrant of Corinth in the 7th century BC
Q430688.lead: Cypselus was the first tyrant of Corinth in the 7th century BC. With increased wealth and more complicated trade relations and social structures, Greek city-states tended to overthrow their traditional hereditary priest-kings; Corinth, the richest archaic polis, led the way. Like the signori of late medieval and Renaissance Italy, the tyrants usually seized power at the head of some popular support.

Q43353.label: Aristophanes
Q43353.description: Classical Athenian comic playwright (c. 446 – c. 386 BC)
Q43353.lead: Aristophanes was an Ancient Greek comic playwright from Athens. He wrote forty plays, of which eleven survive virtually complete.

Q435531.label: Hipparchus
Q435531.description: tyrant of Athens from c. 528 BC to 514 BC
Q435531.lead: Hipparchus was a member of the ruling class of Athens and one of the sons of Pisistratus.

Q43986.label: Peratos
Q43986.description: ruler of Sicyon, and mythical son of Poseidon
Q43986.lead: In Greek mythology, Peratus, also called Eratus (Ἔρατος), was the 10th king of Sicyon who reigned for 46 years.

Q441736.label: Lais of Corinth
Q441736.lead: Lais of Corinth (fl. 425 BC) was a famous hetaira or courtesan of ancient Greece, who was probably born in Corinth.

Q44204.label: Cronus
Q44204.description: ruler of the Titans in Greek mythology
Q44204.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Cronus, Cronos, or Kronos was the leader and youngest of the Titans, the children of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky). Cronus castrated and overthrew his father and then ruled during the mythological Golden Age until he himself was overthrown by his son, Zeus, and imprisoned in Tartarus.

Q44228.label: Leonidas I
Q44228.description: King of Sparta from c. 489 BC to 480 BC
Q44228.lead: Leonidas I was Greek king of the Ancient Greek city-state of Sparta. He was the son of king Anaxandridas II and the 17th king of the Agiad dynasty, a Spartan royal house which claimed descent from Heracles.

Q44233.label: Hesiod
Q44233.description: ancient Greek poet of the archaic period
Q44233.lead: Hesiod was an Ancient Greek poet generally thought to have been active between 750 and 650 BC, around the same time as Homer.

Q4439972.label: Aglaea
Q4439972.description: one of the Graces (Charites) in Greek mythology
Q4439972.lead: In Greek mythology, Aglaia, Aglaïa or Aglaea is a goddess, one of the Charites (known as the Graces in Roman mythology). She is the goddess of splendor, brilliance and brightness.

Q44420027.label: Meda
Q44420027.description: mythological Greek character, daughter of Phylus

Q4453665.label: Teuthis
Q4453665.description: mythical Arcadian leader in the Trojan War
Q4453665.lead: In Greek mythology, Teuthis, also called Ornytus (Ancient Greek: Ὄρνυτος, romanized: Órnutos) is an Arcadian general from the city-state of Teuthis in the Peloponnese, southern Greece. Although not appearing in Homeric works, Teuthis is one of the Achaean leaders who gathered their armies to wage war against Troy in order to retrieve Helen, the queen of Sparta.

Q44887.label: Euryleonis
Q44887.description: Spartan, owner of Olympic winner chariot
Q44887.lead: Euryleonis was a woman honored with a statue in Sparta as the owner of a victorious pair of horses in the chariot races at the Ancient Olympic Games probably in 368 BC. Euryleonis would have been a wealthy aristocrat. She was the second female stephanite (crowned victor) in the long history of the ancient Olympics.

Q450334.label: Alypus
Q450334.lead: Alypus was a sculptor of ancient Greece, a native of Sicyon. He studied under Naucydes of Argos.

Q451066.label: Apama II
Q451066.description: 3rd century BC consort of Magas of Cyrene
Q451066.lead: Apama II, sometimes known as Apame II was a Syrian Greek princess of the Seleucid Empire, queen of Cyrenaica by marriage to King Magas of Cyrene.

Q452536.label: Ageladas
Q452536.lead: Ageladas or Hagelaedas (Ancient Greek: Ἁγελᾴδας Hagelā́idās) was a celebrated Greek (Argive) sculptor, who flourished in the latter part of the 6th and the early part of the 5th century BC. Ageladas' fame is enhanced by his having been the instructor of the three great masters, Phidias, Myron, and Polykleitos. The determination of the period when Ageladas flourished has given rise to a great deal of discussion, owing to the apparently contradictory statements of the writers who mention his name.

Q453968.label: Nicesipolis
Q453968.description: Wife or concubine of king Philip II of Macedon
Q453968.lead: Nicesipolis or Nicasipolis of Pherae, was a Thessalian woman, native of the city Pherae, wife or concubine of king Philip II of Macedon and mother of Thessalonike of Macedon. There is not much surviving evidence about her background and life but she is likely to have been of noble Thessalian origin and maybe she was a niece of Jason of Pherae.

Q454695.label: Gobryas
Q454695.lead: Gobryas was father of Mardonius and lance-bearer of Darius I. Gobryas was one of the six helpers of Darius in killing Gaumāta in September 522 BC mentioned by Herodotus. He was appointed as Darius' lance carrier (arštibara).

Q457294.label: Pallas
Q457294.lead: In Greek mythology, Pallas or Pallantes was the son of the Titans Crius and Eurybia, the brother of Astraeus and Perses, the husband of Styx, and the father of Zelus, Nike, Kratos, and Bia. Hyginus says that Pallas, whom he calls "the giant", also fathered with Styx: Scylla, Fontus ("Fountains") and Lacus ("Lakes").

Q459517.label: Eupolis
Q459517.description: Athenian playwright of Old Comedy (5th-century BC)

Q45967.label: Persephone
Q45967.description: Greek goddess of the seasons and the queen of the underworld; married with Hades
Q45967.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Persephone is the daughter of Zeus and Demeter. She became the queen of the underworld after her abduction by her uncle Hades, the king of the underworld, who later took her into marriage.

Q460094.label: Lilaea
Q460094.lead: In Greek mythology, Lilaea or Lilaia may refer to two different women: Lilaea, a Naiad of a spring of the same name. She was the daughter of the river god Cephissus.

Q461439.label: Antiope
Q461439.description: Greek mythological figure; daughter of Nycteus and mother of Amphion
Q461439.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Antiope is the mother of the twin heroes Amphion and Zethus by Zeus the king of the gods. Although stated in early sources to be a daughter of the Boeotian river god Asopus, most authors made her a child of king Nycteus of Thebes.

Q462684.label: Harpagus
Q462684.lead: Harpagus, also known as Harpagos, was a Median general during the 6th century BC, credited by Herodotus as having put Cyrus the Great on the throne through his defection during the Battle of Pasargadae.

Q462994.label: Harpalus
Q462994.lead: Harpalus, son of Machatas, was a Macedonian aristocrat and childhood friend of Alexander the Great in the 4th century BC. Harpalus was repeatedly entrusted with official duties by Alexander and absconded with large sums of money on three occasions. Alexander appointed him treasurer of his empire in Babylon in 330 BC. In 324 BC he fled from Babylon to Athens with a large sum of money.

Q463107.label: Autolycus
Q463107.description: son of Daedalion in Greek mythology
Q463107.lead: In Greek mythology, Autolycus was a robber who had the power to metamorphose or make invisible the things he stole. He had his residence on Mount Parnassus and was renowned among men for his cunning and oaths.

Q463301.label: Evagoras
Q463301.description: king of Salamis on Cyprus from 411 to 373 BC
Q463301.lead: Evagoras or Euagoras was the king of Salamis in Cyprus from 411 to 374 BC, and was known especially from the work of Isocrates, who presents him as a model ruler.

Q463898.label: Laius
Q463898.description: mythological king of Thebes, father of Oedipus
Q463898.lead: In Greek mythology, King Laius ( L(A)Y-əs) or Laios of Thebes was a key personage in the Theban founding myth. Son of King Labdacus, Laius fathered Oedipus with Jocasta and was later killed by Oedipus, although Oedipus did not know Laius was his father at the time.

Q464091.label: Silenus
Q464091.description: figure in Greek mythology; tutor to Dionysus
Q464091.lead: In Greek mythology, Silenus was a companion and tutor to the wine god Dionysus. He is typically older than the satyrs of the Dionysian retinue (thiasos), and sometimes considerably older, in which case he may be referred to as a Papposilenus.

Q46491.label: Osiris
Q46491.description: god of the afterlife in Egyptian mythology
Q46491.lead: Osiris (from Egyptian wsjr) was the god of fertility, agriculture, the afterlife, the dead, resurrection, life, and vegetation in ancient Egyptian religion. He was classically depicted with a pharaoh's beard, partially mummy-wrapped at the legs, wearing a distinctive atef crown and holding a symbolic crook and flail.

Q466866.label: Nessus
Q466866.lead: In Greek mythology, Nessus was a famous centaur who was killed by Heracles, and whose poisoned blood in turn killed Heracles. He was the son of Centauros.

Q466951.label: Clitomachus
Q466951.lead: Clitomachus or Cleitomachus was a Greek philosopher, originally from Carthage, who came to Athens in 163/2 BC and studied philosophy under Carneades. He became head of the Academy around 127/6 BC. He was an Academic skeptic like his master.

Q468608.label: Gelo
Q468608.lead: Gelon, son of Deinomenes, was a Greek tyrant of the Sicilian cities Gela and Syracuse, first of the Deinomenid rulers.

Q468821.label: Bilistiche
Q468821.lead: Bilistiche or Belistiche was a Hellenistic hetaira of Ptolemy II Philadelphus and winner of the 264 BC Olympic Games in tethrippon and synoris.

Q4688387.label: Aerope
Q4688387.lead: In Greek mythology, Aerope was a daughter of Cepheus of Arcadia, who was king of Tegea. She had a son (Aeropus?) by Ares, but herself died in labor.

Q4692869.label: Aglaus
Q4692869.lead: Aglaus was a semi-mythological poor citizen of Psophis in Arcadia. When King Gyges, king of Lydia asked the Delphic oracle whether any man was happier than he was, the oracle pronounced Aglaus to be happier on account of his contentedness.

Q47231.label: Odysseus
Q47231.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Odysseus, also known by the Latin variant Ulysses (UK also ; Latin: Ulysses, Ulixes), is a legendary Greek king of Ithaca and the hero of Homer's epic poem, the Odyssey. Odysseus also plays a key role in Homer's Iliad and other works in that same epic cycle.

Q4726821.label: Alipherus
Q4726821.description: son of Lycaon in Greek mythology
Q4726821.lead: Alipherus or Halipherus was in Greek mythology, an Arcadian prince as one of the 50 sons of the impious King Lycaon either by the naiad Cyllene, Nonacris or by unknown woman.

Q472774.label: Sicyon
Q472774.description: son of Marathon in Greek mythology
Q472774.lead: In Greek mythology, Sicyon is the eponym of the polis of the same name, which was said to have previously been known as Aegiale and, earlier, Mecone.

Q472784.label: Hypermnestra
Q472784.description: daughter of Danaus in Greek mythology
Q472784.lead: In Greek mythology, Hypermnestra was by birth a Libyan princess and by marriage a queen of Argos. She is a daughter of King Danaus, and one of the 50 Danaids.

Q474854.label: Amphictyon
Q474854.description: son of Deucalion in Greek mythology
Q474854.lead: In Greek mythology, Amphictyon was a king of Thermopylae and later Athens. In one account, he was the ruler of Locris.

Q474888.label: Amphilochus
Q474888.lead: In Greek mythology, Amphilochus was an Argive hero and one of the Epigoni.

Q4784290.label: Aras
Q4784290.lead: In Greek mythology, Aras was an autochthon who was believed to have built Arantea, the most ancient town in Phliasia, Peloponnese.

Q4790873.label: Arisbas
Q4790873.lead: In Greek mythology, the name Arisbas may refer to: Arisbas, father of Molurus. Arisbas, father of the Achaean warrior Leiocritus who was killed by Aeneas in the Trojan War.

Q4797369.label: Artayctes
Q4797369.lead: Artaÿctes is a historical figure described in Herodotus' The Histories. Artaÿctes, the son of Cherasmis, was a Persian general who commanded the Macrones and Mossynoeci forces in the army of Xerxes during the second Persian invasion of Greece in 480-479 BC. During that period, Artaÿctes was also a tyrant in Sestos where he was captured and crucified by Athenian forces in 479.

Q4810678.label: Asterion
Q4810678.lead: In Greek mythology, Asterion was a river-god of Argos.

Q4811170.label: Astrabacus
Q4811170.lead: In Greek mythology, Astrabacus is a Spartan, the son of Irbus (son of Amphisthenes, son of Amphicles, son of Agis I). He and his brother Alopecus found a wooden image of the goddess Artemis Orthia under a bush of willows; it was surrounded in such a way that it stood upright.

Q4818054.label: Attaginus
Q4818054.lead: Attaginus, son of Phrynon, was one of the leading Theban oligarchs, who betrayed their city to Xerxes I on the Second Persian invasion of Greece, and took an active part in favour of the Persians. He invited Mardonius and 50 of the noblest Persians in his army to a splendid banquet at Thebes, shortly before the Battle of Plataea in 479 BC. After the battle, the Greeks marched against Thebes, and required Attaginos and Timegenidas, and other members of the Persian party, to be delivered up to them.

Q482039.label: Amyclas of Sparta
Q482039.description: Greek mythological character; King of Sparta
Q482039.lead: In Greek mythology, Amyclas or Amyclus was a king of Sparta and the son of Lacedaemon. The town of Amyclae in Laconia was said to have been founded by and named after him.

Q482096.label: Amymone
Q482096.description: daughter of Danaus in Greek mythology
Q482096.lead: In Greek mythology, Amymone was one of the 50 Danaids as a daughter of Danaus, king of Libya. As the "blameless" Danaid, her name identifies her as, perhaps, identical to Hypermnestra ("great wooing" or "high marriage"): the one Danaid who did not assassinate her husband on their wedding night.

Q482134.label: Amythaon
Q482134.description: son of Cretheus in Greek mythology
Q482134.lead: In Greek mythology, Amythaon is the son of Cretheus, the king of Iolcus.

Q4826358.label: Autolaus
Q4826358.description: son of Arcas in Greek mythology
Q4826358.lead: In Greek mythology, Autolaus was the illegitimate son of King Arcas of Arcadia. He found and brought up the infant god Asclepius when the infant was exposed in Thelpusa.

Q48305.label: Euripides
Q48305.lead: Euripides was a Greek tragedian of classical Athens. Along with Aeschylus and Sophocles, he is one of the three authors of Greek tragedy whose name is ascribed to surviving plays.

Q483783.label: Sulla
Q483783.lead: Lucius Cornelius Sulla Felix, commonly known as Sulla, was a Roman general and statesman of the late Roman Republic. He came to prominence for his military exploits and was the first general during the late republic to march on Rome and win a civil war.

Q4843985.label: Pirene
Q4843985.lead: In Greek mythology, Pirene or Peirene, a nymph, was either the daughter of the river god Asopus, Laconian king Oebalus, or the river god Achelous, in different sources. By Poseidon she became the mother of Lecheas and Cenchrias.

Q486698.label: Omphale
Q486698.description: daughter of Iardanus, in Greek mythology
Q486698.lead: In Greek mythology, Omphale was princess of the kingdom of Lydia in Asia Minor. Diodorus Siculus provides the first appearance of the Omphale theme in literature, though Aeschylus was aware of the episode.

Q48688514.label: Arcesilaus
Q48688514.description: 5th c. BCE sculptor, son of Aristodicus

Q488558.label: Anaxagoras
Q488558.lead: In Greek mythology, Anaxagoras was a king of Argos. He was the son and successor of either King Megapenthes or by the latter's son, King Argeus.

Q488602.label: Anaxander
Q488602.lead: Anaxander or Anaxandros was the 12th Agiad King of Sparta (ruled c. 640–615 BC).

Q4939448.label: Bolina
Q4939448.lead: In Greek mythology, Bolina or Boline (Βολίνη) was a nymph. According to Pausanias, Bolina was once a mortal maiden of Achaea.

Q494886.label: Pylades
Q494886.lead: In Greek mythology, Pylades was a Phocian prince as the son of King Strophius and Anaxibia, the daughter of Atreus and sister of Agamemnon and Menelaus. He is mostly known for his relationship with his cousin Orestes, son of Agamemnon.

Q495133.label: Atthis
Q495133.description: daughter of Cranaus in Greek mythology
Q495133.lead: In Greek mythology, Atthis or Attis (Ancient Greek: Ἄττις) was the eponymous heroine of Attica.

Q496595.label: Alcinous
Q496595.description: mythical character, King of the Phaeacians, son of Nausithous and brother of Rhexenor
Q496595.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcinous was a son of Nausithous and brother of Rhexenor. After the latter's death, he married his brother's daughter Arete who bore him Nausicaa, Halius, Clytoneus and Laodamas.

Q499025.label: Eurybiades
Q499025.description: Spartan commander in a Greco-Persian War (480–479 BC)
Q499025.lead: Eurybiades was the Spartan navarch in charge of the Greek navy during the Second Persian invasion of Greece (480–479 BC).

Q4998063.label: Bura
Q4998063.lead: In Greek mythology, Bura was a daughter of Ion, son of Xuthus, and Helice. She was the eponym of the city Boura in Achaea.

Q500739.label: Cecrops I
Q500739.lead: Cecrops was a legendary king of Attica which derived from him its name Cecropia, according to the Parian Chronicle having previously borne the name of Acte or Actice (from Actaeus). He was the founder and the first king of Athens itself though preceded in the region by the earth-born king Actaeus of Attica.

Q5011.label: Cupid
Q5011.lead: In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of desire, erotic love, attraction and affection. He is often portrayed as the son of the love goddess Venus and the god of war Mars.

Q501667.label: Lycaon
Q501667.description: Greek mythical character, king of Arcadia, son of Pelasgus and Meliboea
Q501667.lead: In Greek mythology, Lycaon was a king of Arcadia who, in the most popular version of the myth, killed and cooked his son Nyctimus and served him to Zeus, to see whether the god was sufficiently all-knowing to recognize human flesh. Disgusted, Zeus transformed Lycaon into a wolf, while Nyctimus was restored to life.

Q502156.label: Pirithous
Q502156.description: son of Ixion in Greek mythology
Q502156.lead: Pirithous, in Greek mythology, was the King of the Lapiths of Larissa in Thessaly, as well as best friend to Theseus.

Q503500.label: Andreus
Q503500.description: mythical character, son of the river-god Peneus

Q504076.label: Iolaos
Q504076.description: nephew of Heracles in Greek mythology
Q504076.lead: In Greek mythology, Iolaus was a Theban divine hero. He was famed for being Heracles's charioteer and squire, and for helping with some of his Labors, as well as for being one of the Argonauts.

Q5044177.label: Carnus
Q5044177.lead: In Greek mythology, Carnus (also spelled Carneus and Carneius) was a seer from Acarnania, who was instructed in the art of divination by Apollo. According to the poet Praxilla, he was a son of Europa, who was brought up by Apollo and Leto.

Q504744.label: Hellanicus of Mytilene
Q504744.lead: Hellanicus (or Hellanikos) of Lesbos, also called Hellanicus of Mytilene (Greek: Ἑλλάνικος ὁ Μυτιληναῖος, Hellánikos ho Mutilēnaîos; c. 490 – c.

Q504986.label: Demosthenes
Q504986.lead: Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, was an Athenian general during the Peloponnesian War.

Q505640.label: Alcamenes
Q505640.lead: Alcamenes was an ancient Greek sculptor of Lemnos and Athens, who flourished in the 2nd half of the 5th century BC. He was a younger contemporary of Phidias and noted for the delicacy and finish of his works, among which a Hephaestus and an Aphrodite of the Gardens were conspicuous. Pausanias says that he was the author of one of the pediments of the temple of Zeus at Olympia, but this seems a chronological and stylistic impossibility.

Q5064218.label: Cerethrius
Q5064218.lead: Cerethrius was a Gallic king in Thrace. He was defeated in 277 BC, by Antigonus II Gonatas at the Battle of Lysimachia.

Q506550.label: Eteocles
Q506550.lead: In Greek mythology, Eteocles was a king of Thebes, the son of Oedipus and either Jocasta or Euryganeia. Oedipus killed his father Laius and married his mother without knowing his relationship to either.

Q506781.label: Memnon
Q506781.description: mythical Ethiopian king, son of Tithonus and Eos
Q506781.lead: In Greek mythology, Memnon was a king of Aethiopia and son of Tithonus and Eos. During the Trojan War, he brought an army to Troy's defense and killed Antilochus, Nestor's son, during a fierce battle.

Q508188.label: Antalcidas
Q508188.description: Spartan general and statesman (died c. 367 BC)
Q508188.lead: Antalcidas, son of Leon, was an ancient Greek soldier, politician, and diplomat from Sparta.

Q5086536.label: Charmus
Q5086536.lead: Charmus of Kolyttus (fl. mid-6th century BCE) was an Athenian polemarch (557/6) during the Pisistratid dynasty, and also eromenos of Pisistratus.

Q509010.label: Eurycrates
Q509010.lead: was the 11th Agiad dynasty king of the Greek city-state of Sparta, who was preceded by his father Polydorus followed by his son Anaxander. He ruled from 665 to 640 BC.He married to an athenian woman Hesperis of Athens after battle of hysia.

Q5092559.label: Chersias
Q5092559.lead: Chersias of Orchomenus (fl. late 7th century BCE) was an archaic Greek epic poet whose work is all but lost today.

Q5114615.label: Chrysis
Q5114615.lead: Chrysis was the priestess of Hera at the ancient Greek sanctuary of Hera at Argos at the time of the Peloponesian War. She is known for having inadvertently caused a fire that led to the destruction of the temple.

Q5131665.label: Cleolaus
Q5131665.lead: Cleolaus was a name attributed to two men in Greek mythology. Cleolaus, the Thespian son of Heracles and Argele, daughter of King Thespius of Thespiae.

Q5131686.label: Cleon of Sicyon
Q5131686.description: ancient Greek sculptor, fl. c. 380 BCE
Q5131686.lead: Cleon was an Ancient Greek sculptor of Sicyon.

Q514746.label: Xuthus
Q514746.lead: In Greek mythology, Xuthus was a Phthian prince who later became a king of Peloponnesus. He was the founder (through his sons) of the Achaean and Ionian nations.

Q515531.label: Tantalus
Q515531.description: mythological Greek character, son of Thyestes
Q515531.lead: In Greek mythology, Tantalus was a prince of the south of Argolis as son of King Thyestes. He was the brother of Pleisthenes, Pelopia and Aegisthus, and - according to Hyginus - also of Menelaus and Agamemnon.

Q51583754.label: Pelagon
Q51583754.description: Phocian of Greek mythology, with cows

Q51673.label: Mark Antony
Q51673.description: Roman politician and general (83 BC – 30 BC)
Q51673.lead: Marcus Antonius, commonly known in English as Mark Antony, was a Roman politician and general who played a critical role in the transformation of the Roman Republic from a constitutional republic into the autocratic Roman Empire. Antony was a relative and supporter of Julius Caesar, and he served as one of his generals during the conquest of Gaul and Caesar's civil war.

Q518265.label: Aglaurus
Q518265.lead: Aglaurus or Agraulus (Ἄγραυλος, lit. 'living in the fields' or the 'rustic one') is a name attributed to three figures in Greek mythology. Aglaurus, the daughter of Actaeus, the first king of Attica.

Q5200183.label: Cynurus
Q5200183.lead: Cynurus was the son of the Greek hero Perseus. According to the tradition he led colonists from Argos into Cynuria.

Q520551.label: Corycia
Q520551.lead: In Greek mythology, Corycia or Corycis (Kōrukis), was a naiad who lived on Mount Parnassus in Phocis.

Q5211993.label: Damarchus
Q5211993.lead: Damarchus or Demaenetus was a victorious Olympic boxer from Parrhasia (Arcadia) who is said to have changed his shape into that of a wolf at the festival of Lycaea, only to become a man again after ten years. Pausanias investigated the story for his famous work Description of Greece and, while he seems to believe that Damarchus the boxer did indeed exist, he notes that Damarchus' inscription at Olympia mentions nothing about his supposed metamorphosis to a wolf.

Q521203.label: Duris of Samos
Q521203.description: 4th-century BC Greek historian and tyrant of Samos
Q521203.lead: Duris of Samos (or Douris) was a Greek historian and was at some period tyrant of Samos. Duris was the author of a narrative history of events in Greece and especially Macedonia from 371 BC to 281 BC, which has been lost.

Q529472.label: Isagoras
Q529472.description: Late 6th century BC Athenian aristocrat and opponent of Cleisthenes
Q529472.lead: Isagoras, son of Tisander, was an Athenian aristocrat in the late 6th century BC. He had remained in Athens during the tyranny of Hippias, but after Hippias was overthrown, he became involved in a struggle for power with Cleisthenes, a fellow aristocrat. In 508 BC he was elected archon eponymous, but Cleisthenes opposed him, with support from the majority of the population.

Q5308451.label: Dropion
Q5308451.lead: Dropion was the last known Paeonian king.

Q5332383.label: Echetlus
Q5332383.description: ancient Greek mythical hero of the battle of Marathon
Q5332383.lead: Echetlaeus or Echetlus (Ἔχετλος) was an ancient Athenian mythical hero of the Battle of Marathon with the Persians of the Achaemenid Empire. The latter name was also the name of a hero of ancient Thebes.

Q53606.label: Philammon
Q53606.description: musician son of Apollo in Greek mythology
Q53606.lead: In Greek mythology, Philammon was an excellent musician, a talent he received from his father, Apollo.

Q5382860.label: Epidotes
Q5382860.description: divinity worshipped at Lacedaemon and divine epithet
Q5382860.lead: In Greek mythology, Epidotes was a divinity who was worshipped at Lacedaemon, and averted the anger of Zeus Hicesius (Greek: Ζευς Ικέσιος) for a crime committed by the Spartan general Pausanias. Epidotes, meaning the "liberal giver" or "bountiful", occurs also as an epithet of other divinities, such as Zeus at Mantineia and Sparta, and of Hypnos and Oneiros at Sicyon, who had a statue in the temple of Asclepius there, which represented them in the act of sending a lion to sleep, and lastly of the beneficent gods, to whom a second-century senator, Antoninus, built a sanctuary at Epidaurus.

Q540804.label: Glaucus of Chios
Q540804.lead: Glaucus of Chios was a Greek metal sculptor from the island of Chios, who is often distinguished as the inventor of the art of soldering metals (Greek: σιδήρου κόλλησις, lit. "gluing together of iron").

Q5414525.label: Euthydemus
Q5414525.lead: Euthydemus was a tyrant of the ancient Greek city-state of Sicyon in the 3rd century BC. He ruled jointly with Timocleidas, but the two were deposed by the citizens of Sicyon. They replaced Euthydemus and Timocleidas with Cleinias, although the historian Plutarch believed that Timocleidas ruled jointly with Cleinias.

Q54230.label: Nereids
Q54230.description: sea nymphs in Greek mythology, daughters of Nereus
Q54230.lead: In Greek mythology, the Nereids or Nereides are sea nymphs (female spirits of sea waters), the 50 daughters of the 'Old Man of the Sea' Nereus and the Oceanid Doris, sisters to their brother Nerites.

Q542758.label: Styx
Q542758.description: Greek divinity of the river Styx
Q542758.lead: In Greek mythology, Styx, also called the River Styx, is a goddess and one of the rivers of the Greek Underworld.

Q543525.label: Chabrias
Q543525.lead: Chabrias was an Athenian general active in the first half of the 4th century BC. During his career he was involved in several battles, both on land and sea.

Q544528.label: Leaena
Q544528.lead: Leaena is a pseudo-historical figure, described by later tradition as a hetaera and the mistress of Aristogeiton the Tyrannicide. Original versions of the story of Aristogeiton portray him, on the contrary, as the lover of Harmodius, for whom he decided to overthrow the tyrant Hipparchus.

Q548099.label: Eurynome
Q548099.lead: In Greek mythology Eurynome was an Oceanid and the mother of the Charites by Zeus.

Q551847.label: Oxyartes
Q551847.lead: Oxyartes was a Sogdian or Bactrian nobleman and local ruler of Bactria. His daughter, Roxana, was taken as a wife by Alexander the Great.

Q552396.label: Tithraustes
Q552396.description: Early 4th century BC Persian satrap of Sardis
Q552396.lead: Tithraustes was the Persian satrap of Sardis for several years in the early 4th century BC. Due to scanty historical records, little is known of the man or his activities. He was sent out from Susa to replace Tissaphernes in 395 BC, and, after arresting his predecessor, executed him.

Q552420.label: Caranus
Q552420.lead: Caranus, a Macedonian member of the elite cavalry body known as the hetairoi (Greek:ἑταῖροι) , was one of the generals sent by Alexander the Great against Satibarzanes when, for a second time, he had encouraged Aria to revolt. Caranus and his colleagues were successful in achieving their objective by defeating and slaying Satibarzanes in the winter of 330 BC. In 329 BC, Caranus was appointed, together with Andromachus and Menedemus, under the command of the Lycian Pharnuches, to act against Spitamenes, the revolted satrap of Sogdiana.

Q552759.label: Parrhasius
Q552759.lead: Parrhasius of Ephesus was a famed painter of Ancient Greece who lived in the decades around 400 BC. Active during an era when other painters were starting to depict realistic scenes with shading, Parrhasius stood out by sticking to the older technique of line-drawing, and innovated new ways to portray volume using this method. He created new iconographies that future painters would reproduce for centuries.

Q56257517.label: Androgeos
Q56257517.lead: Androgeos or Androgeus was the name of two individuals in Classical mythology. Androgeus, son of Minos and Pasiphaë.

Q5676461.label: Amphimachus
Q5676461.description: Greek mythical character, son of Cteatus, suitor of Helen
Q5676461.lead: In Greek mythology, Amphimachus was one of the leaders of the Elean contingent at the Trojan War.

Q56823038.label: Calliteles
Q56823038.description: ancient Aeginetan sculptor working with Onatas

Q570434.label: Idomeneus
Q570434.description: Greek mythical character, King of Crete
Q570434.lead: In Greek mythology, Idomeneus was a Cretan king and commander who led the Cretan armies to the Trojan War, in eighty black ships. He was also one of the suitors of Helen, as well as a comrade of the Telamonian Ajax.

Q57157139.label: Celusa
Q57157139.lead: In Greek mythology, Celusa or Kelousa personified Mount Celusa or Celossa in Phliasia. She born the river-god Asopus to Poseidon.

Q571969.label: Antenor
Q571969.lead: In Greek mythology, Antenor was a counselor to King Priam of Troy during the events of the Trojan War.

Q572133.label: Anteros
Q572133.description: The God of Selfless Love in Greek mythology
Q572133.lead: In Greek mythology, Anteros is the god of requited love (literally "love returned" or "counter-love") and also the punisher of those who scorn love and the advances of others, or the avenger of unrequited love.

Q5733718.label: Briacas
Q5733718.description: mythical son of Aeginetes the Arcadian

Q57438557.label: Chrysorthe
Q57438557.lead: In Greek mythology, Chrysorthe was a Sicyonian princess as the daughter of King Orthopolis, descendant of the city's founder Apis. By Apollo, she became the mother of Coronus who succeeded her father in the throne of Sicyon.

Q575252.label: Oxylus
Q575252.description: son of Haemon, mythical king of Elis
Q575252.lead: Oxylus, was a mythical king of Elis, who came from Aetolia and was son of Haemon (himself son of Thoas) or of Andraemon.

Q576170.label: Anticlea
Q576170.lead: In Greek mythology, Anticlea or Anticlia was a queen of Ithaca as the wife of King Laërtes.

Q577245.label: Cycnus
Q577245.description: character in Greek mythology, son of Ares, killed by Heracles
Q577245.lead: In Greek mythology, Cycnus or Cygnus was a bloodthirsty and cruel man who dwelt either in Pagasae, Thessaly or by the river Echedorus in Macedonia.

Q577552.label: Antilochus
Q577552.lead: In Greek mythology, Antilochus was a prince of Pylos and one of the Achaeans in the Trojan War. He was the youngest prince to command troops.

Q577769.label: Antimachus
Q577769.lead: Antimachus of Colophon, or of Claros, was a Greek poet and grammarian, who flourished about 400 BC.

Q578378.label: Aphareus
Q578378.description: Greek mythological character, son of Perieres
Q578378.lead: In Greek mythology, Aphareus was a Messenian king.

Q580661.label: Antiochus of Syracuse
Q580661.lead: Antiochus of Syracuse was a Greek historian of Magna Graecia, who flourished around 420 BC. Little is known of Antiochus' life, but his works, of which only fragments remain, enjoyed a high reputation because of their accuracy. He wrote a History of Sicily from the earliest times to 424 BC, which was used by Thucydides, and the Colonizing of Italy, frequently referred to by Strabo and Dionysius of Halicarnassus.

Q5837114.label: Oeroe
Q5837114.description: river goddess of Boeotia, daughter of Asopos

Q58373.label: Amun
Q58373.lead: Amun was a major ancient Egyptian deity who appears as a member of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad. Amun was attested from the Old Kingdom together with his wife Amunet.

Q58461838.label: Comaetho
Q58461838.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and folklore, Comaetho is a legendary heroine who served Artemis Triclaria in Patrae as virgin priestess. Comaetho fell in love with Melanippus, and unable to marry him, she consorted with him in secret inside the temple, earning the goddess' wrath.

Q5862013.label: Philonome
Q5862013.description: daughter of Tragasus in Greek mythology
Q5862013.lead: In Greek mythology, Philonome or Phylonome is the daughter of Tragasus and second wife of king Cycnus, thus stepmother to his children Tenes and Hemithea. She features in a short myth where she falsely accuses her stepson of rape to his father after failing to seduce him herself.

Q59180.label: Diogenes of Sinope
Q59180.lead: Diogenes the Cynic, also known as Diogenes of Sinope, was an ancient Greek philosopher during the period of Classical Greece, and one of the founders of Cynicism. Renowned for his ascetic lifestyle and radical critiques of social conventions, he became a legendary figure whose life and teachings have been recounted, often through anecdote, in both antiquity and modernity.

Q592348.label: Halirrhothius
Q592348.description: son of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q592348.lead: Halirrhothius was the Athenian son of Poseidon and Euryte or Bathycleia in Greek mythology. He was also called the son of Perieres and husband of Alcyone who bore him two sons, Serus and Alazygus.

Q594770.label: Naukydes of Argos
Q594770.lead: Naukydes of Argos (4th century BCE) was a Greek sculptor from Argos. Taught under Polykleitos, he created a statue of gold and ivory of Hebe for the temple of Hera in Argos; also, statues of Hecate, Hermes, of the poet Erinna, and Phrixus.

Q5962287.label: Hysmon
Q5962287.lead: Hysmon was an Ancient Greek pentathlete from Elis. As a boy, he began to practise the pentathlon as a cure for rheumatism.

Q599482.label: Tros
Q599482.description: ruler of Troy in Greek mythology
Q599482.lead: In Greek mythology, Tros was the founder of the kingdom of Troy, of which the city of Ilios, founded by his son Ilus took the same name, and the son of Erichthonius by Astyoche (daughter of the river god Simoeis) or of Ilus I, from whom he inherited the throne. Tros was the father of three sons: Ilus, Assaracus and Ganymede and two daughters, Cleopatra and Cleomestra.

Q599489.label: Euphorbus
Q599489.lead: In Greek mythology, Euphorbus was a Trojan hero during the Trojan War.

Q599737.label: Marsyas
Q599737.lead: In Greek mythology, the satyr Marsyas is a central figure in two stories involving music: in one, he picked up the double oboe (aulos) that had been abandoned by Athena and played it; in the other, he challenged Apollo to a contest of music and lost his hide and life. Literary sources from antiquity often emphasize the hubris of Marsyas and the justice of his punishment.

Q60219568.label: Dysponteus
Q60219568.description: Greek mythical character, son of Oenomaus or Pelops

Q602258.label: Melampus
Q602258.lead: In Greek mythology, Melampus was a legendary soothsayer and healer, originally of Pylos, who ruled at Argos. Melampus was the introducer of the worship of Dionysus, according to Herodotus, who asserted that his powers as a seer were derived from the Egyptians and that he could understand the language of animals.

Q603759.label: Theras
Q603759.lead: Theras was a regent of Sparta, a son of Autesion and the brother of Aristodemos' wife Argeia, a Cadmid of Theban descent. He served as regent for his nephews Eurysthenes and Procles.

Q603937.label: Aletes
Q603937.lead: Aletes was a son of Hippotes, of Dorian ancestry, and a fifth-generation descendant of Heracles. He is said to have defeated in battle the Corinthians, taken possession of Corinth, and to have expelled the Sisyphids thirty years after the first invasion of the Peloponnesus by the Heraclids.

Q606422.label: Arcas
Q606422.description: son of Callisto in Greek mythology
Q606422.lead: In Greek mythology, Arcas was a hunter who became king of Arcadia. He was remembered for having taught people the arts of weaving and baking bread and for spreading agriculture to Arcadia.

Q6070954.label: Pellen
Q6070954.lead: In Greek mythology, Pellen or Pelles was the founder of Pellene in Achaea. He was the son of Phorbas, son of Triopas of Thessaly, and the father of Hyperasius, father of the Argonauts, Amphion and Asterius.

Q60774.label: Medon
Q60774.description: mythical king of Argos, son of Cisus

Q61060088.label: Hyperion
Q61060088.description: King of Megara, son of Agamemnon

Q611171.label: Peitho
Q611171.description: personification of Persuasion or winning eloquence in Greek mythology
Q611171.lead: In Greek mythology, Peitho is the personification of persuasion. She is a goddess of charming speech.

Q6143496.label: Thespia
Q6143496.description: daughter of Asopus in Greek mythology
Q6143496.lead: In Greek mythology, Thespia or Thespeia was the daughter of the river god Asopus and Metope, daughter of Ladon, himself a river god. She was abducted to Thespiae (the city west of Thebes) by Apollo, and the city might have been named after her.

Q615912.label: Myrtilus
Q615912.description: son of Hermes in Greek mythology
Q615912.lead: In Greek mythology, Myrtilus or Myrtilos was a divine hero and son of Hermes. His mother is said variously to be the Amazon Myrto; Phaethusa, daughter of Danaus; or a nymph or mortal woman named Clytie, Clymene or Cleobule (Theobule).

Q622504.label: Thyestes
Q622504.description: King of Mycenae and brother of Atreus in Greek mythologie
Q622504.lead: In Greek mythology, Thyestes was a king of Olympia. Thyestes and his brother, Atreus, were exiled by their father for having murdered their half-brother, Chrysippus, in their desire for the throne of Olympia.

Q622781.label: Asopus
Q622781.lead: Asopus or Asopos is the name of four different rivers in Greece and one in Turkey. In Greek mythology, it was also the name of the gods of those rivers.

Q632592.label: Archelaus of Sparta
Q632592.description: king of Sparta, son of Agesilaus I
Q632592.lead: Archelaus (Ancient Greek: Ἀρχέλαος, Ἀrkhélaos; reigned from c. 790 to c.

Q633120.label: Pandrosus
Q633120.description: daughter of Cecrops I in Greek mythology
Q633120.lead: Pandrosos or Pandrosus was known in Greek myth as one of the three daughters of Cecrops I, the first king of Athens, and Aglaurus, daughter of King Actaeus.

Q634361.label: Damasichthon
Q634361.lead: In Greek mythology, Damasichthon was a king of Thebes and the son of Opheltes, purported to be son to Peneleos (regent of Thebes).

Q635170.label: Onatas
Q635170.lead: Onatas was an ancient Greek sculptor of the time of the Persian Wars and an exponent of the flourishing school of Aegina. Many of his works are mentioned by Pausanias; they included a Hermes carrying the ram, and a strange image of the Black Demeter made for the people of Phigalia; also some elaborate groups in bronze set up at Olympia and Delphi.

Q636796.label: Temenus
Q636796.description: son of Aristomachus, in Greek mythology
Q636796.lead: In Greek mythology, Temenus was a son of Aristomachus and brother of Cresphontes and Aristodemus. Temenus was a great-great-grandson of Heracles and helped lead the fifth and final attack on Mycenae in the Peloponnese.

Q637955.label: Neleus
Q637955.description: mythical son of Poseidon or Cretheus and father of Nestor
Q637955.lead: Neleus was a mythological king of Pylos. In some accounts, he was also counted as an Argonaut instead of his son, Nestor.

Q638008.label: Phalerus
Q638008.description: Athenian mythological character, son of Alcon and grandson of Erechtheus king of Athens
Q638008.lead: In Greek mythology, Phalerus was the son of Alcon from Athens. He is counted among the Argonauts.

Q638578.label: Helle
Q638578.lead: Helle, sometimes also called Athamantis (Ancient Greek: Ἀθαμαντίς, "daughter of Athamas"), was a character in Greek mythology who figured prominently in the story of Jason and the Argonauts. Helle is known for giving her name to the strait of Hellespont ("sea of Helle"), into which she fell while crossing it on the back of a flying golden ram with her brother Phrixus—the same flying ram from which the Golden Fleece derived.

Q64073707.label: Pyrrha
Q64073707.description: daughter of Creon in Greek mythology

Q641993.label: Arene
Q641993.description: wife of Aphareus in Greek mythology

Q643456.label: Arethusa
Q643456.description: nymph in Greek mythology who fled from the river god Alpheus
Q643456.lead: In Greek mythology, Arethusa was a nymph who fled from her home in Arcadia beneath the sea and came up as a fresh water fountain on the island of Ortygia in Syracuse, Sicily.

Q643504.label: Cephalus
Q643504.description: son of Deioneus and beloved of Eos in Greek mythology
Q643504.lead: In Greek mythology, Cephalus or Kephalos was the son of Deion, the ruler of Phocis, and Diomede.

Q644030.label: Argalus
Q644030.lead: In Greek mythology, King Argalus was a leader of the Lacedaemonid Greeks from the age of legend, now treated as being the Bronze Age in Greece.

Q644692.label: Corcyra
Q644692.description: daughter of the Asopos river and the nymph Metope
Q644692.lead: In Greek mythology and religion, Corcyra or Korkyra is the naiad daughter of the river-god Asopos and the nymph Metope, herself the daughter of the river-god Ladon. She is the personification and tutelary goddess of the ancient Greek city and island of Korkyra, now better known as Corfu.

Q644921.label: Erichthonius
Q644921.lead: In Greek mythology, King Erichthonius was a legendary early ruler of ancient Athens. According to some myths, he was autochthonous (born of the soil, or Earth) and adopted or raised by the goddess Athena.

Q649476.label: Argus
Q649476.description: mythological Greek character, king and eponym of Argos
Q649476.lead: In Greek mythology, Argus was the king and eponym of Argos.

Q649624.label: Phoroneus
Q649624.description: son of Inachus in Greek mythology
Q649624.lead: In Greek mythology, Phoroneus was a culture-hero of the Argolid, fire-bringer, law giver, and primordial king of Argos.

Q65087714.label: Lyrcus
Q65087714.lead: In Greek mythology, Lyrcus was the illegitimate son of Abas, king of Argos.

Q652819.label: Moerocles
Q652819.lead: Moerocles was an Athenian orator, native of Salamis. He was a contemporary of Demosthenes, and like him an opponent of the kings Philip and Alexander, and was one of the anti-Macedonian orators whom Alexander demanded to have given up to him after the destruction of Thebes, though he subsequently withdrew his demand on the mediation of Demades (335 BC).

Q654037.label: Europs
Q654037.description: son of Aegialeus, mythical king of Sicyon

Q654257.label: Tiphys
Q654257.lead: In Greek mythology, Tiphys was the helmsman of the Argonauts.

Q6543182.label: Lichas
Q6543182.description: 6th c. Spartan, discover of bones of Orestes
Q6543182.lead: Ancient Spartans with the name Lichas may refer to: Lichas or Liches (Ancient Greek: Λίχης) was a Spartan Agathoergi who played a key role in fulfilling an oracle that required the Spartans to obtain the bones of Orestes in order to conquer Tegea. Lichas discovered a giant coffin under a blacksmith's shop in Tegea, which matched the oracle’s description.

Q656881.label: Tiresias
Q656881.lead: In Greek mythology, Tiresias was a blind prophet of Apollo in Thebes, famous for clairvoyance and for being transformed into a woman for seven years. He was the son of the shepherd Everes and the nymph Chariclo.

Q656887.label: Tityos
Q656887.lead: Tityos or Tityus is a giant from Greek mythology. The son of Zeus and the mortal Elara, Tityos tried to rape the goddess Leto, a former lover of Zeus and the mother of the twin gods Artemis and Apollo.

Q657562.label: Alope
Q657562.lead: Alope was in Greek mythology a mortal woman, the daughter of Cercyon, known for her great beauty.

Q658523.label: Hermione
Q658523.description: daughter of Menelaus and Helen of Troy
Q658523.lead: In Greek mythology, Hermione was the daughter of Menelaus, king of Sparta, and his wife, Helen of Troy. Prior to the Trojan War, Hermione had been betrothed by Tyndareus, her grandfather, to her cousin Orestes, son of her uncle, Agamemnon.

Q66016.label: Muse
Q66016.description: goddess of the inspiration of literature, science and the arts
Q66016.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, the Muses were the inspirational goddesses of literature, science, and the arts. They were considered the source of the knowledge embodied in the poetry, lyric songs, and myths that were related orally for centuries in ancient Greek culture.

Q660196.label: Ascalaphus
Q660196.description: son of Ares in Greek mythology
Q660196.lead: In Greek mythology, Ascalaphus or Askalaphus, was son of Ares and the Minyan princess Astyoche, daughter of King Actor of Orchomenus. Ascalaphus was also a king of the Minyans, and twin brother of Ialmenos.

Q6612.label: Charon
Q6612.description: ferryman of Hades in Greek-Roman mythology
Q6612.lead: In Greek mythology, Charon or Kharon is the ferryman of the Greek underworld. He transports the souls of those who have been given funeral rites across the river (often called Acheron or Styx) that borders the underworld.

Q666525.label: Aristodemus
Q666525.description: one of the Heracleidae in Greek mythology
Q666525.lead: In Greek mythology, Aristodemus was one of the Heracleidae, son of Aristomachus and brother of Cresphontes and Temenus. He was a great-great-grandson of Heracles and helped lead the fifth and final attack on Mycenae in the Peloponnese.

Q666603.label: Aristocles
Q666603.description: Greek sculptor, 5th century BC, son of Cleoetas

Q666652.label: Aristokrates
Q666652.lead: Aristocrates was a name belonging to two ancient Greek rulers in Orchomenus in Arcadia. The elder Aristocrates of Orchomenus was the son of Aechmis.

Q6676329.label: Lophis
Q6676329.description: mythical prince of Haliartus killed by his father because of an oracle
Q6676329.lead: In Greek mythology, Lophis was the young son of a ruler of Haliartus, Boeotia.

Q668054.label: Talaus
Q668054.description: son of Bias in Greek mythology
Q668054.lead: In Greek mythology, Talaus was the king of Argos and one of the Argonauts. He was the son of Bias (or Perialces) and Pero, and brother of Arëius and Leodocus.

Q6691.label: Homer
Q6691.description: reputed author of the Iliad and the Odyssey
Q6691.lead: Homer was an ancient Greek poet who is traditionally credited as the author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, two epic poems that are foundational works of ancient Greek literature. Homer was highly revered in ancient Greek society and is considered one of the most influential authors in history.

Q6707302.label: Lycius
Q6707302.lead: Lycius was an ancient Greek sculptor active in the middle decades of the 5th century BCE. Ancient sources identify him as son of Myron of Eleutherae. He sculpted bronze horses and humans for a cavalry monument dedicated on the Acropolis of Athens.

Q674319.label: Machaon
Q674319.description: character of Greek mythology: son of Asclepius and Coronis, lover of Anticlea; healing hero of the Trojan War; killed by Eurypylus
Q674319.lead: In Greek mythology, Machaon was a son of Asclepius; and the older brother of Podalirius. He and his brother led an army from Tricca in the Trojan War on the side of the Greeks.

Q675699.label: Epaphus
Q675699.description: mythical character, son of Zeus and Io
Q675699.lead: In Greek mythology, Epaphus, also called Apis or Munantius was a son of Zeus and king of Egypt.

Q6783302.label: Masistius
Q6783302.lead: Masistius was a Persian cavalry commander best known for his role in the second Persian invasion of Greece.

Q679716.label: Cychreus
Q679716.description: son of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q679716.lead: In Greek mythology, Cychreus was a legendary king of Salamis Island. He was the son of the god Poseidon and the nymph Salamis.

Q689422.label: Euphrosyne
Q689422.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Euphrosyne is a goddess, one of the three Charites. She was sometimes named Euthymia (Ancient Greek: Εὐθυμία, lit. 'good mood') or Eutychia (Ancient Greek: Εὐτυχία, lit. 'good luck').

Q6896910.label: Molurus
Q6896910.lead: In Greek mythology, Molurus was the son of Arisbas. In a surviving fragment of the poem Megalai Ehoiai, Molurus was killed by Hyettus of Argos when Hyettus caught him with his wife.

Q690603.label: Iacchus
Q690603.description: minor deity in connection with the Eleusinian mysteries
Q690603.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Iacchus (also Iacchos, Iakchos) was a minor deity, of some cultic importance, particularly at Athens and Eleusis in connection with the Eleusinian Mysteries, but without any significant mythology. He perhaps originated as the personification of the ritual exclamation Iacche!

Q690613.label: Tlepolemus
Q690613.lead: In Greek mythology, Tlepolemus was the leader of the Rhodian forces in the Trojan War.

Q6948683.label: Mysius
Q6948683.description: mythical Greek who gave hospitality to Demeter
Q6948683.lead: In Greek mythology, Mysius was a figure meant to provide an etiology for Mysia as a surname of Demeter. He was said to have received Demeter hospitably in his home in Argos as she was searching for Persephone, and to have founded a sanctuary of Demeter Mysia, known as "Mysaeum", located at the distance of about sixty stadia from Pellene; another temple of Demeter Mysia was reportedly situated on the road from Mycenae to Argos.

Q699635.label: Arrhichion
Q699635.lead: Arrhichion (also spelled Arrhachion, Arrichion or Arrachion) of Phigalia (died 564 BC) was a champion pankratiast in the ancient Olympic Games. He died while successfully defending his championship in the pankration at the 54th Olympiad (564 BC).

Q7124090.label: Paeon
Q7124090.description: son of Endymion in Greek mythology
Q7124090.lead: Paeon or Paion, in Greek mythology, was an Elean prince as son of King Endymion, and brother of Epeius, Aetolus, Eurycyda and possibly Naxos.
