From him, the ancient region of Paeonia—on the Axius river, in the northern parts of the modern region of Macedonia—and the tribe of the Paeonians, were believed to have derived their name.

Q712572.label: Philistus
Q712572.lead: Philistus, son of Archomenidas, was a Greek historian from Sicily.

Q713679.label: Timotheus
Q713679.lead: Timotheus was a Greek statesman and general who sought to revive Athenian imperial ambitions by making Athens dominant in a Second Athenian League. He was the son of the Athenian general, Conon.

Q718102.label: Cleombrotus
Q718102.description: Regent of Sparta between 480 and 479 BC
Q718102.lead: Cleombrotus, regent of Sparta between 480 and 479 BC. He was a member of the Agiad dynasty, the son of Anaxandridas II and the brother of Cleomenes I, Dorieus and of Leonidas I. When the latter died, he became the tutor of his nephew Pleistarchus, son of Leonidas, and leader of the Greek infantry at the beginning of the second phase of the Greco-Persian Wars. Cleombrotus was in command of the Spartan and Peloponnesian troops who built the wall across the Isthmus of Corinth that was intended to keep the Persian army out of the Peloponnese.

Q718154.label: Lagus
Q718154.lead: Lagus of Eordaia was a Macedonian courtier and the father of Ptolemy, the founder of the Ptolemaic dynasty. He married Arsinoe of the Argead dynasty and a concubine of Philip II, king of Macedon, who was said to have been pregnant at the time of their marriage, forming the basis of Ptolemy as the son of Philip; but it is possible that this is a later myth fabricated to glorify the Ptolemaic dynasty.

Q7181590.label: Phialo
Q7181590.description: Greek mythical character, lover of Hercules
Q7181590.lead: Phialo or Phillo was one of the lovers of the Greek mythological demigod Heracles. She was the daughter of the Arcadian hero Alcimedon and the mother, by Heracles, of Aechmagoras.

Q7226232.label: Polycles
Q7226232.lead: Polycles, mentioned in Pliny's Natural History (XXXV.8.19), was an ancient Greek sculptor who flourished during the 102nd Olympiad (370 BCE). He was a contemporary of Cephisodotus the Elder and Leochares.

Q7235.label: Sophocles
Q7235.lead: Sophocles was an ancient Greek tragedian, one of three from whom at least two plays have survived in full.

Q7249671.label: Promachus of Pellene
Q7249671.lead: Promachus was a pankration athlete of the Ancient Olympic Games in Olympia, Greece. Son of Dryon, he was from Pellene in Achaea.

Q725286.label: Coronis
Q725286.description: goddess from Greek mythology: princess, daughter of Phlegyas, lover of Ischys and Apollo, mother of Asclepius; killed by Apollon and Artemis
Q725286.lead: In Greek mythology, Coronis is a Thessalian princess and a lover of the god Apollo. She was the daughter of Cleophema and Phlegyas, king of the Lapiths.

Q725527.label: Calchas
Q725527.lead: Calchas is an Argive mantis, or seer, in Greek mythology. Calchas appears in the opening scenes of the Iliad and also has a long literary history after Homer.

Q7257118.label: Ptous
Q7257118.lead: In Greek mythology, Ptous may refer to the following: Ptous, eponym of Mount Ptous in Boeotia on which the town Acraephnium was situated. He was believed to have been a son of either Athamas and Themisto, or of Acraepheus and Euxippe, or of Apollo and Zeuxippe, a daughter of Athamas.

Q727279.label: Cephisodotus
Q727279.lead: Cephisodotus was an Athenian general and orator, who was sent with Callias, Autocles, and others in 371 BC to negotiate peace with Sparta. Again, in 369 BC, when the Spartan ambassadors had come to Athens to settle the terms of the desired alliance between the states, and the Athenian council had proposed that the land-forces of the confederacy should be under the command of Sparta, and the navy under that of Athens, Cephisodotus persuaded the assembly to reject the proposal, on the ground that, while Athenian citizens would have to serve under Spartan generals, few but helots (who principally manned the ships) would be subject to Athenian control.

Q729332.label: Helenus
Q729332.lead: In Greek mythology, Helenus was a gentle and clever seer. He was also a Trojan prince as the son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba of Troy, and the twin brother of the prophetess Cassandra.

Q730625.label: Asius of Samos
Q730625.description: ancient Greek poet, son of Amphiptolemus
Q730625.lead: Asius of Samos was an ancient Greek poet whose work survives in the form of fragments quoted by other ancient authors. All that is known about the man is that he was from Samos and that his father's name was Amphiptolemus.

Q732066.label: Creon
Q732066.description: king of Thebes in Greek mythology
Q732066.lead: Kreon, also spelled Creon is a figure in Greek mythology best known as the ruler of Thebes in the legend of Oedipus.

Q735623.label: Inachus
Q735623.description: river deity and king of the Argolid
Q735623.lead: In Greek mythology, Inachus or Inachos was the first king of Argos. He was one of the three thousand sons of Oceanus and Tethys.

Q736813.label: Deiphobus
Q736813.description: mythical character, son of Priam of Troy
Q736813.lead: In Greek mythology, Deiphobus was a son of Priam and Hecuba. He was a prince of Troy, and the greatest of Priam's sons after Hector.

Q7382381.label: Chione
Q7382381.description: mythological Greek character, daughter of Boreas
Q7382381.lead: In Greek mythology, Chione is a mortal woman, the daughter of Boreas, the god of the north wind, and the princess Orithyia, a daughter of Erechtheus, the king of Athens. In the only myth concerning her, Chione sleeps with the sea-god Poseidon and bears him a son, Eumolpus, but in fear of her father's wrath she casts the infant into the sea.

Q738862.label: Iphicles
Q738862.description: son of Amphitryon in Greek mythology
Q738862.lead: In Greek mythology, Iphicles, also called Iphiclus, was the maternal half-twin brother of Heracles and one of the Calydonian boar hunters.

Q740645.label: Docimus
Q740645.description: Macedonian general of Alexander and Antigonus
Q740645.lead: Antigonos Dokimos, commonly shortened and Latinized as Docimus, was one of the officers in the Macedonian army. After the death of Alexander the Great (323 BC) he supported the party of Perdiccas.

Q741155.label: Nycteus
Q741155.lead: In Greek mythology, Nycteus was a king of Thebes. His rule began after the death of Polydorus, and ended when he was succeeded by his brother Lycus.

Q741632.label: Agasicles
Q741632.lead: Agasicles, alternatively spelled Agesicles or Hegesicles, was a king of Sparta, the 13th of the line of Procles. Son of Archidamus I, he was contemporary with the Agiad Leon, and succeeded his father, probably about 590 BC or 600.

Q7420860.label: Saon
Q7420860.lead: In Greek mythology, the name Saon may refer to: Saon of Samothrace, also called Samon (Σάμων) or Saos (Σάος), son of either Zeus and an unnamed nymph (Nymphe) or of Hermes and Rhene. He was believed to have unified all the inhabitants of the island, who had previously lived in scattered settlements, into one people, which he further subdivided into five tribes named after his sons.

Q743482.label: Phrixus
Q743482.description: son of Athamas in Greek mythology
Q743482.lead: In Greek mythology Phrixus was the son of Athamas, king of Boeotia, and Nephele (a goddess of clouds). He was the older brother of Helle and the father of Argus, Phrontis, Melas and Cytisorus by Chalciope (Iophassa), daughter of Aeetes, king of Colchis.

Q747657.label: Enyo
Q747657.description: Greek goddess of war and destruction
Q747657.lead: In Greek mythology, Enyo is a war-goddess, frequently associated with the war-god Ares. The Romans identified her with Bellona.

Q748963.label: Sterope
Q748963.description: one of the Pleiades in Greek mythology
Q748963.lead: In Greek mythology, Sterope, also called Asterope (Ἀστερόπη), was one of the seven Pleiades.

Q749123.label: Euphemus
Q749123.description: son of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q749123.lead: In Greek mythology, Euphemus was counted among the Calydonian hunters and the Argonauts, and was connected with the legend of the foundation of Cyrene.

Q750236.label: Polyxena
Q750236.lead: In Greek mythology, Polyxena was the youngest daughter of King Priam of Troy and his queen, Hecuba. She does not appear in Homer, but in several other classical authors, though the details of her story vary considerably.

Q750580.label: Pittheus
Q750580.description: son of Pelops in Greek mythology
Q750580.lead: In Greek mythology, Pittheus was the king of Troezen, city in Argolis, which he had named after his brother Troezen.

Q754835.label: Catreus
Q754835.description: king of Crete and a son of Minos and Pasiphaë
Q754835.lead: In Greek mythology, Catreus, also spelled Katreus, was the eldest son of Minos and Pasiphaë, and Minos's successor as king of Crete. Catreus had one son, Althaemenes, and three daughters, Apemosyne, Aerope and Clymene.

Q7563929.label: Sostratus of Dyme
Q7563929.lead: Sostratus is a lover of the hero Heracles mentioned in Pausanias' Description of Greece. According to Pausanias in his description of Dyme, he was from that ancient Achaean city and held in reverence by its inhabitants.

Q760213.label: Auge
Q760213.description: daughter of Aleus in Greek mythology
Q760213.lead: In Greek mythology, Auge, was the daughter of Aleus the king of Tegea in Arcadia, and the virgin priestess of Athena Alea. She was also the mother of the hero Telephus by Heracles.

Q76247521.label: Lysimache
Q76247521.lead: Lysimache I (453 BC - 365 BC), was an Ancient Greek Athenian Priestess. She served as the High Priestess of Athena Polias in the Parthenon Temple of the Acropolis of Athens between 430 BC and 365 BC. Lysimache was the daughter of Drakontides of Bate.

Q762982.label: Patroclus
Q762982.lead: Patroclus, also spelled Patroklos, was a leading official and admiral of the Ptolemaic Kingdom. He is best known for his activity during the Chremonidean War (267–261 BC), when he commanded the navy sent to Greece by Ptolemy II. His early career is obscure, but it must have been distinguished enough for him to rise to the chief priesthood of Alexander and the Theoi Adelphoi in 271/270 BC. After the outbreak of the Chremonidean War, he led a diplomatic and military expedition to the Aegean Sea that expanded Ptolemaic control by establishing bases at Crete, Ceos, Thera, Attica and the Argolid.

Q763268.label: Alcyone
Q763268.description: Greek mythological figure; one of the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas
Q763268.lead: Alcyone, in Greek mythology, was the name of one of the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas and Pleione or, more rarely, Aethra. She attracted the attention of the god Poseidon and bore him several children, variously named in the sources: Hyrieus, Hyperenor, and Aethusa; Hyperes and Anthas; and Epopeus.

Q765456.label: Laodamas
Q765456.description: son of Eteocles in Greek mythology

Q768822.label: Thestius
Q768822.description: son of Agenor in Greek mythology
Q768822.lead: In Greek mythology, Thestius was a king of Pleuronians in Aetolia. He is not to be confused with Thespius, who was sometimes referred to as "Thestius".

Q7696793.label: Telesarchus
Q7696793.lead: Telesarchus was a Syro-Macedonian military commander from the region along the Orontes river. In 279 BC, Antiochus I sent him with a force of 500 men against invading Gauls led by Brennus.

Q770627.label: Taraxippus
Q770627.lead: In Greek mythology, the Taraxippos was a presence, variously identified as a ghost or dangerous site, blamed for frightening horses at hippodromes throughout Greece. Some taraxippoi were associated with the Greek hero cults or with Poseidon in his aspect as a god of horses (Ancient Greek: Ποσειδῶν ἵππειοs) who brought about the death of Hippolytus.

Q771241.label: Polydectes
Q771241.lead: In Greek mythology, King Polydectes is a king of the island of Seriphos in the Cyclades. Polydectes was the ruler of the island when the Argive princess Danaë and her infant son Perseus washed ashore, having been cast away into the sea by Danaë's father Acrisius, who was afraid that his daughter's son would kill him.

Q774101.label: Aura
Q774101.description: divine personification of the breeze in Greek and Roman mythology
Q774101.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Aura is a minor wind goddess, whose name means "breeze". The plural form, Aurae (Ancient Greek: Αὔραι) is sometimes found to describe a group of breeze nymphs associated with Boreas, the god of the north wind.

Q776139.label: Semele
Q776139.description: mother of Dionysus in Greek mythology
Q776139.lead: In Greek mythology, Semele, or Thyone (Ancient Greek: Θυώνη, romanized: Thyṓnē), was the youngest daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, and the mother of Dionysus by Zeus (her own great-grandfather). Certain elements of the cult of Dionysus and Semele came from the Phrygians.

Q7800294.label: Tiasa
Q7800294.description: personification of Tiasa river in Laconia
Q7800294.lead: In Greek mythology, Tiasa was a nymph of a river near Amyclae, Sparta. She was a Laconian princess as the daughter of King Eurotas and Cleta, and thus sister of Sparta.

Q781867.label: Menestheus
Q781867.lead: In Greek mythology, Menestheus was a legendary king of Athens during the Trojan War. He was set up as king by the twins Castor and Pollux when Theseus travelled to the Underworld after abducting their sister, Helen, and exiled Theseus from the city after his return.

Q782764.label: Erato
Q782764.description: Greek mythological figure, wife of Arcas
Q782764.lead: In Greek mythology, Erato was a dryad. She was the priestess and prophetess of the god Pan, verses were attributed to her at an ancient oracle of the god, located at Megalopolis near Acacesium.

Q7832603.label: Tragasus
Q7832603.lead: In Greek mythology, Tragasus or Cragasus (Κράγασος) was the father of Philonome, the deceitful wife of Cycnus.

Q7844848.label: Trochilus
Q7844848.description: Greek mythological figure and the son of Callithyia
Q7844848.lead: In Greek mythology, Trochilus was a member of the Argive royal house as the son of Princess Callithyia (equated with Io "Callithyessa" in her role of the priestess of the Argive Hera).

Q784528.label: Autesion
Q784528.lead: In Greek mythology, Autesion, was a king of Thebes. He was the son of Tisamenus, the grandson of Thersander and Demonassa and the great-grandson of Polynices and Argea.

Q785598.label: Melia
Q785598.description: Greek mythologial figure, daughter of the Titan Oceanus and consort of Apollo
Q785598.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Melia, a daughter of the Titan Oceanus, was the consort of Apollo, and the mother, by Apollo, of the Theban hero and prophet Tenerus. She was also the mother (or sister) of Ismenus, god of the Theban river of the same name.

Q787120.label: Automate
Q787120.description: daughter of Danaus in Greek mythology
Q787120.lead: Automate was one of the Danaids in Greek mythology. According to Apollodorus and others, she killed the (mythical) Egyptian king Busiris, who was betrothed to her.

Q7877819.label: Lynceus
Q7877819.description: son of Aegyptus in Greek mythology
Q7877819.lead: In Greek mythology, Lynceus was a prince of Egypt and king of Argos, succeeding Danaus on the throne. Through his marriage to the Danaid Hypermnestra, he began the Danaid Dynasty that led to Perseus, hero and legendary founder of Mycenae.

Q789715.label: Auxo
Q789715.description: one of the Graces, worshipped in Athens; and/or one of the Horae

Q791446.label: Battus
Q791446.lead: Battus was a figure in Greek mythology who witnessed Hermes stealing Apollo's cattle in Maenalus in Arcadia. Hermes gave him a heifer on condition Battus kept the theft secret.

Q793560.label: Azan
Q793560.lead: In Greek mythology, Azan may refer to the following personages: Azan, king of Azania in Arcadia and the son of King Arcas and the Dryad Erato or Leanira, brother of Apheidas, Elatus and Hyperippe. Azan was the father of Cleitor and Coronis, mother of Asclepius by Apollo.

Q796763.label: Orsippus
Q796763.description: ancient olympics stadion victor in 8th century BC
Q796763.lead: Orsippus was a Greek runner from Megara who was famed as the first to run the footrace naked at the Olympic Games and "first of all Greeks to be crowned victor naked." Others argue that it was Acanthus instead who first introduced Greek athletic nudity. Orsippus won the stadion of the 15th Olympic Games in 720 BC. Later, as a general, Orsippus conquered a neighboring territory for Megara, which had recently become independent from Corinth.

Q79876.label: Isis
Q79876.lead: Isis was a major goddess in ancient Egyptian religion whose worship spread throughout the Greco-Roman world. Isis was first mentioned in the Old Kingdom as one of the main characters of the Osiris myth, in which she resurrects her slain brother and husband, the divine king Osiris, and produces and protects his heir, Horus.

Q79999.label: Uranus
Q79999.description: primordial Greek deity, god of the Sky; one of the Greek primordial deities
Q79999.lead: In Greek mythology, Uranus, sometimes written Ouranos (Ancient Greek: Οὐρανός, lit. 'sky', [uːranós]), is the personification of the sky and one of the Greek primordial deities. According to Hesiod, Uranus was the son and husband of Gaia (Earth), with whom he fathered the first generation of Titans.

Q80398.label: Pericles
Q80398.description: Athenian statesman, orator and general (c. 495 – 429 BC)
Q80398.lead: Pericles was a Greek statesman and general during the Golden Age of Athens. He was prominent and influential in Ancient Athenian politics, particularly between the Greco-Persian Wars and the Peloponnesian War, and was acclaimed by Thucydides, a contemporary historian, as "the first citizen of Athens".

Q804277.label: Bacchiadae
Q804277.lead: The Bacchiadae, a tightly knit Doric clan, were the ruling family of ancient Corinth in the eighth and seventh centuries BCE, a period of Corinthian cultural power.

Q8043551.label: Xenoclea
Q8043551.lead: Xenoclea, who appears as a character in the legend of Hercules, was the Pythia, or priestess and oracle, of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.

Q8249134.label: Boges
Q8249134.description: 5th-century BC Persian official and military commander
Q8249134.lead: Boges was a Persian official and military commander, who functioned as governor (hyparchos) of Eion in Thrace (Achaemenid satrapy of Skudra) under the King of Kings Xerxes I. According to Herodotus, following the Persian defeats at Plataea and Mycale, Boges refused to abandon Eion when it was besieged by the Athenians and Cimon (son of Miltiades) in 476/5.

Q827221.label: Chthonophyle
Q827221.description: daughter of Sicyon in Greek mythology
Q827221.lead: In Greek mythology, Chthonophyle was the daughter of King Sicyon (whose name was given to the city of Sicyon) and Zeuxippe. She and Hermes are the parents of Polybus, another king of Sicyon.

Q82732.label: Aeneas
Q82732.description: Trojan hero, son of Anchises and Aphrodite
Q82732.lead: Aeneas was a Trojan hero in Greco-Roman mythology, the son of the Trojan prince Anchises and the Greek goddess Aphrodite (equivalent to the Roman Venus). His father was a first cousin of King Priam of Troy (both being great-grandsons of Tros, founder of Troy), making Aeneas a second cousin to Priam's children (such as Hector and Paris).

Q830706.label: Hyrnetho
Q830706.description: daughter of Temenus in Greek mythology
Q830706.lead: In Greek mythology, Hyrnetho was a daughter of Temenus, and the wife of Deiphontes, by whom she became mother of Antimenes, Xanthippus, Argeius, and Orsobia. Temenus favored his daughter Hyrnetho and her husband Deiphontes more than his sons, Hyrnetho's brothers, and planned on making Deiphontes his heir.

Q831577.label: Britomartis
Q831577.description: Minoan goddess of mountains and hunting
Q831577.lead: Britomartis was a Greek goddess of mountains, nets, and hunting who was primarily worshipped on the island of Crete. She was sometimes described as a nymph, but she was more commonly conflated or syncretized with the goddesses Artemis, Athena, and Aphaea.

Q831583.label: Phlegyas
Q831583.description: king of the Lapiths in Greek mythology
Q831583.lead: In Greek mythology, Phlegyas was a king of the Lapiths (or the Phlegyans).

Q83160.label: Prometheus
Q83160.description: Titan, culture hero, and trickster figure in Greek mythology who defied the gods; son of Iapetus
Q83160.lead: In Greek mythology, Prometheus is a Titan who is responsible for creating and aiding humanity in its earliest days. He defied the Olympian gods by stealing fire from them and giving it to humanity.

Q83223.label: Asclepius
Q83223.lead: Asclepius is a hero and god of medicine in ancient Greek religion and mythology. He is the son of Apollo and Coronis, or Arsinoe, or of Apollo alone.

Q833806.label: Capaneus
Q833806.description: son of Hipponous in Greek mythology
Q833806.lead: In Greek mythology, Capaneus was a son of Hipponous and either Astynome (daughter of Talaus) or Laodice (daughter of Iphis), and husband of Evadne, with whom he fathered Sthenelus. Some call his wife Ianeira.

Q833826.label: Nauplius
Q833826.description: king of Nauplia, son of Poseidon in Greek mythology

Q83496.label: Cerberus
Q83496.description: three-headed dog that guards the underworld in Greek mythology
Q83496.lead: In Greek mythology, Cerberus, often referred to as the hound of Hades, is a multi-headed dog that guards the gates of the underworld to prevent the dead from leaving. He was the offspring of the monsters Echidna and Typhon, and was usually described as having three heads, a serpent for a tail, and snakes protruding from his body.

Q836311.label: Phocus
Q836311.lead: In Greek mythology, Phocus, was a prince of Aegina and son of Aeacus and Psamathe.

Q837699.label: Evander of Pallene
Q837699.description: mythical character of Greek and Roman mythology, king of Pallantium
Q837699.lead: In Roman mythology, Evander was a culture hero from Arcadia, Greece, who was said to have brought the pantheon, laws, and alphabet of Greece to ancient Italy, where he founded the city of Pallantium on the future site of Palatine Hill, Rome, sixty years before the Trojan War. He instituted the festival of the Lupercalia.

Q8409.label: Alexander the Great
Q8409.description: king of Macedonia and conqueror of Achaemenid Persia (356–323 BC)
Q8409.lead: Alexander III of Macedon, most commonly known as Alexander the Great, was king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon from 336 BC until his death. He was the son of Philip II, born to him by his fourth wife, Olympias, and ascended to the throne at the age of 20 after Philip was assassinated.

Q842435.label: Arion
Q842435.lead: In Greek mythology, Arion or Areion, is a divinely-bred, fabulously fast, black-maned horse. He saved the life of Adrastus, king of Argos, during the war of the Seven against Thebes.

Q843335.label: Sinis
Q843335.lead: In Greek mythology, Sinis was a bandit killed by Theseus on his way to Athens.

Q845112.label: Enceladus
Q845112.lead: In Greek mythology, Enceladus was one of the Giants, the offspring of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky). Enceladus was the traditional opponent of Athena during the Gigantomachy, the war between the Giants and the gods, and was said to be buried under Mount Etna in Sicily.

Q847005.label: Labdacus
Q847005.lead: In Greek mythology, Labdacus was the only son of Polydorus and a king of Thebes. Labdacus was a grandson of Thebes's founder, Cadmus.

Q847268.label: Hyllus
Q847268.description: son of Heracles and Deianira in Greek mythology
Q847268.lead: In Greek mythology, Hyllus or Hyllas (Ὕλλᾱς, Hyllas) was a son of Heracles and Deianira and the husband of Iole.

Q849322.label: Brennus
Q849322.description: Gallic leader who invaded Greece (died 279 BC)
Q849322.lead: Brennus (or Brennos) (died 279 BC at Delphi, Ancient Greece) was one of the Gaulish leaders of the army of the Gallic invasion of the Balkans. While invading the Greek mainland he managed to momentarily reach as far south as Delphi in an attempt to loot the rich treasury of the sanctuary of Apollo.

Q849647.label: Briareus
Q849647.lead: In Greek mythology, the Hecatoncheires, also called Hundred-Handers or Centimanes (Latin: Centimani), were three monstrous giants, of enormous size and strength, each with fifty heads and one hundred arms. They were individually named Cottus (the furious), Briareus (or Aegaeon, the sea goat) and Gyges (or Gyes, the long-limbed).

Q850078.label: Broteas
Q850078.description: son of Tantalus in Greek mythology
Q850078.lead: In Greek mythology, Broteas, a hunter, was the son of Tantalus (by Dione, Euryanassa or Eurythemista), whose other offspring were Niobe and Pelops. Broteas was also one of the Lapiths, killed at the battle of the Lapiths and the centaurs.

Q850192.label: Dirce
Q850192.description: daughter of Ismenus in Greek mythology
Q850192.lead: Dirce was a queen of Thebes as the wife of Lycus in Greek mythology.

Q852011.label: Bupalus
Q852011.description: ancient Greek sculptor and temple architect
Q852011.lead: Bupalus and Athenis (Greek: Ἄθηνις), were sons of Archermus, and members of the celebrated school of sculpture in marble which flourished in Chios in the 6th century BC. They were contemporaries of the poet Hipponax, whom they were said to have caricatured. Their works consisted almost entirely of draped female figures, Artemis, Fortune, The Graces, when the Chian school has been well called a school of Madonnas.

Q853014.label: Thamyris
Q853014.lead: In Greek mythology, Thamyris was a Thracian singer. He is notable in Greek mythology for reportedly having been in love with Hyacinth before the latter's relationship with Apollo and having been the first mortal male to have loved another male.

Q855509.label: Bias
Q855509.lead: In Greek mythology, Bias, was one of the three kings of Argos when the kingdom was divided into three domains. The other kings were his brother Melampus and Anaxagoras.

Q859.label: Plato
Q859.lead: Plato was an ancient Greek philosopher of Classical Athens who is most commonly considered the foundational thinker of the Western philosophical tradition. An innovator of the literary dialogue and dialectic forms, Plato influenced all the major areas of theoretical philosophy and practical philosophy, and was the founder of the Academy, a philosophical school in Athens where Plato taught the collection of philosophical theories that would later become known as Platonism.

Q868.label: Aristotle
Q868.lead: Aristotle was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath. His writings span the natural sciences, philosophy, linguistics, economics, politics, psychology, and the arts.

Q86805.label: Geryon
Q86805.description: mythical king of far western Mediterranean
Q86805.lead: In Greek mythology, Geryon was a fearsome giant who dwelt on the island Erytheia of the mythic Hesperides in the far west of the Mediterranean. A more literal-minded later generation of Greeks associated the region with Tartessos in southern Iberia.

Q869665.label: Cretheus
Q869665.description: in Greek mythology, king and founder of Iolcus

Q871361.label: Protesilaus
Q871361.lead: In Greek mythology, Protesilaus was a hero in the Iliad who was venerated at cult sites in Thessaly and Thrace. Protesilaus was the son of Iphiclus, a "lord of many sheep"; as grandson of the eponymous Phylacos, he was the leader of the Phylaceans.

Q878184.label: Teucer
Q878184.lead: In Greek mythology, Teucer, was the son of King Telamon of Salamis Island and his second wife Hesione, daughter of King Laomedon of Troy. He fought alongside his half-brother, Ajax, in the Trojan War and is the legendary founder of the city of Salamis on Cyprus.

Q8846610.label: Euthymus
Q8846610.description: Olympic boxer and hero from ancient Locris,
Q8846610.lead: Euthymus or Euthymos of Locri appears in ancient tradition as both a celebrated Olympic boxer and a figure who blends into myth. Ancient sources present him not only as an Olympic champion but also as a man who confronted a spirit in Temesa.

Q901224.label: Daedalion
Q901224.description: son of Phosphorus in Greek mythology
Q901224.lead: In Greek mythology, Daedalion or Daidalion was a son of Hesperos, the god of the Evening Star or Phosphorus, god of the Morning Star and the brother of Ceyx. Ceyx describes his brother Daedalion as a great warrior, full of courage and vigour but acknowledged that he could also be harsh, relishing the cruelty of war.

Q905409.label: Dictys
Q905409.description: mythic character, fisherman and brother of King Polydectes
Q905409.lead: Dictys was a name attributed to four men in Greek mythology. Dictys, a fisherman and brother of King Polydectes of Seriphos, both being the sons of Magnes and a Naiad, or of Peristhenes and Androthoe, or else of Poseidon and Cerebia.

Q911084.label: Alpheus
Q911084.description: river and river god in Greek mythology
Q911084.lead: In Greek mythology, Alpheus or Alpheios was the river god who embodied the river of the same name.

Q91111186.label: Phaennis
Q91111186.description: seer born ca. 300 BCE, prophesied invasion of Gauls

Q91121085.label: Critolaus
Q91121085.description: son of Hicetaon, husband of Andromache
Q91121085.lead: In Greek mythology, Critolaus was a member of the Trojan royal family as the son of the Trojan elder Hicetaon, son of King Laomedon of Troy. He was the brother of Melanippus, Thymoetes, and possibly, Antenor.

Q91121089.label: Admetus
Q91121089.description: son of Augeias, represented in Iliupersis painting at Delphi
Q91121089.lead: In Greek mythology, Admetus was a Trojan warrior and son of Augeas. On the night of the fall of Troy, he wounded the Greek hero Meges in the arm, but was later killed by Philoctetes.

Q912772.label: Deiphontes
Q912772.description: son of Antimachus in Greek mythology
Q912772.lead: Deiphontes was king of Argos. He was a son of Antimachus, and husband of Hyrnetho, the daughter of Temenus the Heracleide, by whom he became the father of Antimenes, Xanthippus, Argeius, and Orsobia.

Q9160370.label: Arsinoe
Q9160370.description: daughter of Leucippus, mother of Asclepius

Q916442.label: Telephus
Q916442.lead: In Greek mythology, Telephus was the son of Heracles and Auge, who was the daughter of king Aleus of Tegea. He was adopted by Teuthras, the king of Mysia, in Asia Minor, whom he succeeded as king.

Q917719.label: Sarpedon
Q917719.description: Greek mythology character, son of Zeus and Europa

Q918382.label: Calamis
Q918382.lead: Calamis was a sculptor of ancient Greece.

Q9250158.label: Echephron
Q9250158.description: mythical son of Heracles and Psophis

Q928411.label: Cranaus
Q928411.lead: In Greek mythology, Cranaus or Kranaos was the second King of Athens, succeeding Cecrops I.

Q929768.label: Megara
Q929768.description: mythical wife of Heracles and daughter of Creon
Q929768.lead: In Greek mythology, Megara was a Theban princess and the first wife of the hero Heracles.

Q930518.label: Cleonymus
Q930518.description: Pretender to the Spartan throne, son of Cleomenes II
Q930518.lead: Cleonymus was a member of the Spartan royal family of the Agiad dynasty.

Q930914.label: Protogenes
Q930914.lead: Protogenes was an ancient Greek painter, a contemporary rival of Apelles.

Q931271.label: Tisias
Q931271.lead: Corax was one of the founders (along with Tisias) of ancient Greek rhetoric.

Q93172.label: Gaia
Q93172.description: Greek primordial deity, the personification of the Earth
Q93172.lead: In Greek mythology, Gaia, also spelled Gaea, is the personification of Earth. She is the mother of Uranus (Sky), with whom she conceived the Titans (themselves parents of many of the Olympian gods), the Cyclopes, and the Giants, as well as of Pontus (Sea), from whose union she bore the primordial sea gods.

Q932325.label: Marpessa
Q932325.lead: In Greek mythology, Marpessa was an Aetolian princess and a granddaughter of Ares.

Q932708.label: Glaucus of Carystus
Q932708.lead: Glaucus of Carystus, the son of Demylos, was a boxer and one of the most celebrated Ancient Greek athletes. He was a περιοδονίκης (winner at all most important games of Ancient Greece), having gained one Olympic, two Pythian, eight Nemean, and eight Isthmian victories in boxing.

Q935433.label: Elpenor
Q935433.lead: Elpenor was the youngest comrade of Odysseus in Greek mythology. While on the island of Circe, he became drunk and decided to spend the night on the roof.

Q939149.label: Eurytus
Q939149.lead: Eurytus of Oechalia (Οἰχαλίᾱ, Oikhalíā), Thessaly, was a skillful archer of Greek mythology who was even said to have instructed Heracles in the art of using the bow.

Q940138.label: Cabeiri
Q940138.lead: In Greek mythology, the Cabeiri or Cabiri, also transliterated Kabeiri or Kabiri, were a group of enigmatic chthonic deities. They were worshipped in a mystery cult closely associated with that of Hephaestus, centered in the north Aegean Islands of Lemnos and possibly Samothrace—at the Samothrace temple complex—and at Thebes.

Q94066.label: Eileithyia
Q94066.description: Greek goddess of childbirth and midwifery
Q94066.lead: Eileithyia or Ilithyia was the Greek goddess of childbirth and midwifery, and the daughter of Zeus and Hera. In the cave of Amnisos (Crete) she was related with the annual birth of the divine child, and her cult is connected with Enesidaon (the earth shaker), who was the chthonic aspect of the god Poseidon.

Q94072.label: Autonoë
Q94072.lead: In Greek mythology, Autonoë was a Theban princess as the eldest daughter of Cadmus, founder of Thebes in Boeotia, and the goddess Harmonia. She was the wife of Aristaeus and mother of Actaeon and possibly Macris.

Q947753.label: Acacallis
Q947753.description: daughter of Minos in Greek mythology
Q947753.lead: Acacallis in Greek mythology, was princess of Crete. The Bibliotheca calls her Acalle (Ἀκάλλη).

Q949770.label: Euphranor
Q949770.lead: Euphranor of Corinth (middle of the 4th century BC) was a Greek artist. Pliny the Elder provides a list of his works including a cavalry battle, the Twelve Gods, a painting of the feigned madness of Odysseus, and a Theseus, Euphranor said regarding his statue of Theseus, that Parrhasius's Theseus had lived on a diet of roses, whereas his own was a beef-eater.

Q950523.label: Gorgophone
Q950523.description: daughter of Perseus and Andromeda in Greek mythology
Q950523.lead: In Greek mythology, Gorgophone was queen of both Messenia and Sparta and one of the Perseids, as a daughter of Perseus and Andromeda. Her name means "Gorgon Slayer", a tribute to her father Perseus who killed Medusa, the mortal Gorgon.

Q952188.label: Thespius
Q952188.description: legendary founder and king of Thespiae, Boeotia
Q952188.lead: In Greek mythology, Thespius or Thestius (Ancient Greek: Θέστιος, romanized: Théstios) was a legendary founder and king of Thespiae, Boeotia. His life account is considered part of Greek mythology.

Q956906.label: Thrasymedes
Q956906.lead: In Greek mythology, Thrasymedes was a prince of Pylos and a participant in the Trojan War.

Q960237.label: Eurysthenes
Q960237.lead: Eurysthenes was king of Sparta and one of the Heracleidae in Greek mythology. He was a son of Aristodemus and Argia, daughter of Autesion.

Q962546.label: Lacestades
Q962546.description: son of Hippolytus in Greek mythology

Q976463.label: Hippomedon
Q976463.description: son of Talaus and one of Seven Against Thebes in Greek mythology
Q976463.lead: In Greek mythology, Hippomedon was one of the Seven against Thebes. He lived near the lake Lerna in Peloponessus; the foundations of his house on Mount Pontinus at Lerna were shown in Pausanias' times.

Q977434.label: Ceryx
Q977434.description: son of Eumolpus in Greek mythology
Q977434.lead: In Greek mythology, Ceryx was a member of the Athenian royal family as the son of Hermes by either of the princesses Pandrosus or Agraulus.

Q978079.label: Harmonia
Q978079.description: ancient Greek goddess of harmony and concord, spouse of Cadmus; her opposite is Eris
Q978079.lead: In Greek mythology, Harmonia is the goddess of harmony and concord. She is traditionally the daughter of Aphrodite, the goddess of love, and Ares, the god of war.

Q978308.label: Olen
Q978308.lead: Olen was a legendary early poet from Lycia who went to Delos, where his hymns celebrating the first handmaidens of Apollo in the island of the god's birth and other "ancient hymns" were still part of the cult at Delos in the time of Herodotus: Arge and Opis came at the same time as the gods of Delos and are honoured by the Delians in a different way. For the Delian women make collections in these maidens' names, and invoke them in the hymn which Olen, a Lycian, composed for them; and the rest of the islanders, and even the Ionians, have been taught by the Delians to do the like.

Q981302.label: Amphoterus
Q981302.description: son of Alcmaeon in Greek mythology
Q981302.lead: In Greek mythology, Amphoterus was the son of Alcmaeon by Callirrhoe (daughter of the river god Achelous), and brother of Acarnan.

Q993387.label: Eurylochus
Q993387.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurylochus appears in Homer's Odyssey as second-in-command of Odysseus' ship during the return to Ithaca after the Trojan War. He is portrayed as an unpleasant, cowardly individual who undermines Odysseus and stirs up trouble.
